MOTIONS
Congratulatory Message—Birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of
Cambridge

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I seek leave to move a motion without
notice on the birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of Cambridge.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There
is not.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I move, That the House put on record its congratulations to
Prince William, the Duke of Cambridge, and Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, on the
birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of Cambridge.  The birth of a second
child is an exciting time for a family. It is a time of great joy and immense celebration,
and part of th at joy is observing the reaction of the older brother or sister as they meet
the new little member of the family. I am sure that the duke and duchess are cherishing
this special time with both Prince George and their new daughter.
The birth of Prince George was one of the most eagerly anticipated in recent history.
It is moving to see that the public is just as excited at the birth of the princess. I am sure
she will bring the same delight as we watch her grow. It is a pleasure to observe the
strong family unit bonded by love and mutual support that the duke and duchess are
creating with their children. I have joined with other leaders across the Commonwealth
and the world in congratulating Prince William and the duchess on the arrival of their
daughter, and I am sure that the other members of this House and the public of New
Zealand support the good wishes expressed to them.
I would also like to note that in a few days’ time New Zealand will be welcoming
His Royal Highness Prince Harry, who will be visiting our country for the first time. It
will be an opportunity for New Zealanders to pass on personally their best wishes to the
royal family on the birth of Princess Charlotte. New Zealand’s official gift to the royal
couple is a handcrafted teddy bear and a box set of woollen baby items made from wool
of unique Stansborough sheep bred in the Wairarapa. The teddy will be specially made
by Cheryl Eldridge of Stansborough and will have the special touches to make it unique
for the princess. I might add that it is in the colour of dusky pink.
On behalf of the people of New Zealand, I am pleased to be able to put on the record
of this House our congratulations to the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge and to Prince
George, and to welcome the newest member of the royal family into the world.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: Speaking as the Leader of Her
Majesty’s loyal Opposition, can I also join the Prime Minister and the many New
Zealanders congratulating the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge on the birth of their
second child, Princess Charlotte Elizabeth Diana. Welcoming a child into the world is a
very happy occasion for any family. Princess Charlotte, of course, arrived under the
3130 Motions 5 May 2015
scrutiny of hundreds of media and millions more waiting in anticipation, including, of
course, the street vendors keen to get their supplies of ceramic mugs and tea towels on
to the streets’ shelves.
As many in this House will know, I was actually in England for the  days leading up
to the royal birth . Despite the fact that I am a committed republican, it did not stop my
wife Leigh from insisting that I bring back a ceramic mug or tea towel, or several of
them, but, sadly, that did not happen on this occasion.
In spite of my personal views, I know that the Queen and her family are held in high
regard by many New Zealanders. I acknowledge the important role different generations
of the family are making today around the Commonwealth as standard -bearers for
comity and community. For example, I note that Princess Charlotte’s grandfather Prince
Charles, after whom I understand Princess Charlotte has been named, gave the most
eloquent and touching addresses at the Gallipoli commemorations over Anzac weekend.
I see that the new princess carries the name “Diana”. That will be greeted warmly by the
millions who continue to hold her grandmother in high esteem for her charity work
around the world.
On behalf of the Labour Party I once again respectfully congratulate the Duke and
Duchess on the birth of their daughter, Princess Charlotte, and look forward to meeting
her uncle Prince Harry when he arrives this weekend.

items.speaker: Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM
items.text: The Green Party congratulates Prince William
and the Duchess of Cambridge on the birth of their second child, Charlotte Elizabeth
Diana, Princess of Cambridge. The birth of a happy and healthy baby girl is always a
cause for joy, and the name “Charlotte” has, apparently, ranked first in recent years by
way of choice for a girl’s name in New Zealand. But this royal baby is special for a
particular reason. Charlotte will be the first female heir to the  British throne to have her
place in the line of succession guaranteed over younger male siblings and other male
heirs. Blissfully unaware she may be, but as she beams out on the world she personifies
constitutional progress for the Realm of New Zealand.
As we debate this motion today the New Zealand Flag Consideration Panel is starting
its work. Whether changing the flag is necessary or not is a different issue, but that does
show that New Zealanders are interested in discussing the issues that symbolise us as a
nation and tell the story of who we are. The Green Party welcomes that debate. We
should not take for granted that our symbols of nationhood today will be relevant
tomorrow. We take this opportunity to wish the British royal family in London well.

items.speaker: TRACEY MARTIN
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. New
Zealand First joins with the rest of the House in extending our congratulations to the
Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. W e welcome Charlotte Elizabeth Diana and we wish
both her and her family, her older brother, and extended family a safe and happy life.
Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr
Speaker. Kia ora tātou. Ko tāku he whaiwhai haere i ngā mihi a te Pirimia ki te uri o
Irihāpeti, kua puta mai ki te whaiao, ki Te Ao Mārama.
[Thank you , Mr Speaker . Salutations to us . I am merely following up the Prime
Minister’s sentiments to the descendant of Queen Elizabeth who has emerged into the
world of light and understanding.]
As a representative of some of Her Majesty’s Treaty partners, I stand to follow on
from the Prime Minister’s statement and acknowledge the bir th of e kī ana te kōrero he
taonga ki te ao [as it has been stated, a worldly treasure].
I acknowledge the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, but I probably want to pay more
tribute to the grandparents, being a grandfather myself on the birth of my mokopuna. I n
our household our mokopuna is the princess —in fact, she is probably the queen, to be
5 May 2015 Motions 3131
truthful, in everything that she does, from the time she wakes up until the time she goes
to bed. So in our household she is the queen, not just the princess. I wish the m all the
very best in the years ahead. In particular, I hope that the House thinks very much of the
grandparents today, as we consider this very important last couple of days for the birth
of a taonga ki te ao, arā noa atu ngā taonga o te ao [ a worldly tr easure, and there are
many other treasures of the world]. Tēnā tātou katoa.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: On behalf of the ACT Party, I would like to
offer our warmest congratulations to Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge on
the birth of Princess Catherine—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Charlotte.

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: —sorry, Charlotte —a healthy,  strapping 8 pound, 3 ounce
baby. Thank you.
Motion agreed to.
SPEAKER’S RULINGS
Tabling of Documents—Procedure

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Last Thursday Metiria Turei raised a point of order seeking my
advice on the procedure for seeking leave to table a document. To assist members, I
have given this further consideration and I have also examined the rulings of previous
Speakers. What I will require of members when seeking leave to table a document are
three things, and that the members identify these three things in this order: the source of
the document, when it was published or produced, and to very succinctly inform the
House of its nature. This way an informed decision can be made by members as to
whether the document should in fact be tabled.
Seeking leave to table a document is not an opportunity to make a political statement
that a member wishes to be heard. It is intended for placing before the House material
that informs members of matters that are not otherwise readily available to them. Briefly
describing for the House the nature of the document is not an opportunity to quote
passages from it. If members persist in doing so, the leave will not be put to the House.

items.speaker: CHRIS HIPKINS
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.
That is a considered ruling and I understand the point you are raising. The only
challenge for members in descri bing the document is that I think there must be some
necessity to explain the relevance for tabling a document at that point. Otherwise, we
can get into a situation where members can be seeking to table all sorts of things, and
part of the narrowing -down o f the rules around tabling is to prevent that from
happening. So although the description does need to be succinct, it also needs to relate
the nature of the document to the question or the speech in question, otherwise it is
simply a pointless exercise.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think my ruling is very clear. There is an opportunity to succinctly
describe the nature of the document, and on various occasions that will require more
depth than on other occasions. But I repeat the point that it is not the opportunity for
members to make a political statement, which I see it being used for on many occasions.
If I sense that that is the purpose of the member who is seeking to table the document, it
is likely that the leave will not be put in the first place.
Overseas Investment—Agriculture and Housing
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does
he stand by all his statements; if so, why?
3132 Oral Questions 5 May 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because I believe them to be correct at
the time they were made.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that he would “hate to see
New Zealanders as tenants i n their own country”; if so, why did his Government so
avidly support Shanghai Pengxin Group’s purchase of farms in the central North Island
and now 10 dairy farms south of Kaikohe in Northland?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: In answer to the first part of the question, yes.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Supplementary question, the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Opposing investment in Northland again.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Oh, here is “Big Ears” again. He l ost in Northland pretty
badly.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I am going to invite the member to
stand and ask the supplementary question.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Why has his Government encouraged China to contro l so
much of New Zealand’s dairy infant formula, from production testing through to
marketing and sale of New Zealand’s premium agricultural product?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The position of the Government is not necessarily to
encourage investment from anywhere but to allow a framework whereby if people want
to invest they are free to do so, but they have to meet the conditions set out in the
Overseas Investment Act. They have to be approved by the Overseas Investment Office.
Actually, the Govern ment thinks investments by  Inner Mongolia Yili  Industrial Group
Co. Ltd, Yashili New Zealand Dairy , and Bright and others have actually been sensible
investments in the same way that we think Fonterra’s investment in Beingmate was also
a sensible investment.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: When will the National Government understand the law of
supply and demand, which sees Auckland housing demand massively inflated by record
levels of immigration into Auckland and record levels of buying Auck land homes by
offshore interests, and do what the Australian Federal Government has done?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: As I understand it, in Australia what they have done is they
have stopped, in theory, non -residents from buying existing properties, but in fact the
actions of the Australian Government over the weekend essentially are saying that those
measures were not working and required greater enforceability —a testimony to why
those things are very difficult to enforce. The second thin g is that despite the steps the
Australian Government has taken, I am pretty sure I am right in saying that Sydney
house prices have risen at the same rate as Auckland’s, but I actually think they have
risen at a faster rate.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Do not all those answers add up to the fact that this
Government, whilst making dog whistles about foreign ownership before the general
election, has done absolutely nothing to stop it since?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: There is fore ign investment. If one looks at a table —and,
funnily enough, I looked at one this morning —the bulk of that foreign investment
actually comes from Australia. China, if the member is being specific about China, is
quite a small investor in New Zealand. But, interestingly enough, what I think is really
important is that anybody who comes to New Zealand from overseas to invest follows
the Overseas Investment Act. I am interested to note, of course, that the author of that
Act was the Rt Hon Winston Peters.

items.speaker: Rt H on Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Answers to
parliamentary questions are meant to be terse and to the point. That last statement was a
demonstrable lie.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I would also be grateful i f the member could , equally, ask
short and terse supplementary questions.
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3133
Inflation—Crown Revenue
2. TIM MACINDOE (National —Hamilton West)  to the Minister of Finance :
What reports has he received on low inflation in New Zealand, and how does that
benefit households and businesses?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As the published figures have shown,
New Zealan d is experiencing very low inflation —or, more accurately, in the last 6
months actually we have had deflation. Usually in an economy growing at 3 percent,
inflation is rising, not falling. However, it is good news for New Zealand households
and businesses, which can expect to see interest rates and inflation stay lower for longer
than they expected, and this is likely to help to reduce unemployment and sustain real
wage growth.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What impact does lower than expected inflation have  on
Government revenue?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Very low inflation and lower interest rates and lower
commodity prices mean that growth in the dollar value of what New Zealand produces
each year is a bit lower than expected. Treasury now expects that the dollar value of
what we produce each year over the next 4 years will be around $15 billion less than
forecast in Budget 2014, even though the economy will actually grow slightly faster
than we expected in Budget 2014. This poses some real challenges for Government
revenue, because it means less PAYE, less company tax, and less GST. In total,
Treasury expects the Government will collect $4.5 billion less tax revenue over the next
4 years than it expected at the last Budget.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that question and answer, is it in fact correct that
“lower than expected inflation” actually means lower Government expenditure as well?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: As it turns out, the inflation impact on Government
expenditure is considerably less than the impact on spending and the impact on tax
revenue. That member had better figure it out, because his other members are always
advocating more spending when he is advocating bigger surpluses.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: How is lower revenue having an impact on the Government’s ability
to return the books to surplus in 2014-15?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Back in December Treasury forecast that the deficit for the
2014-15 year would be around $570 million, whi ch is just 0.2 percent of GDP. It is fair
to say that the forecast for the 2014 -15 year has deteriorated a little since December, so
we expect the Budget to forecast a slightly bigger deficit for 2014 -15, and a slightly
smaller surplus for 2015 -16. So, whi le progress is slower than expected, we remain on
track to achieve surpluses and to start repaying debt.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: What steps has the Government taken to get on top of spending and
return the books to balance?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Government has been very thoughtful about its new
spending, and very thoughtful about what drives existing spending. If you want a
measure of that, in the last six Budgets, the total annual cost of new initiatives has been
just under $3 billio n. By comparison, the last six Budgets of the previous Government
totalled $20 billion of extra costs —$20 billion as opposed to $3 billion. But despite the
fact that we have had very constrained spending, we have been delivering better public
services with better results for New Zealanders.
Ministers—Conduct
3. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
enforce high standards of conduct on all his Ministers, including himself?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes. However, in respect of my actions at a
Parnell cafe, my conduct clearly upset the staff member in question. I sincerely
3134 Oral Questions 5 May 2015
apologised to her at the time that I became aware of that, and I have continued to do so
publicly.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he accept that repeatedly pulling a woman’s hair who was just
trying to do her job, despite her indicating to him to stop, was unworthy of any grown
man, let alone the Prime Minister?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I accept I misread the situ ation. I have apologised for
that.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he accept that through his embarrassing and weird behaviour
he has now made the office of the Prime Minister of New Zealand an international
laughing stock?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOH N KEY
items.text: No, but I do accept I have to take responsibility for my own
actions.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Has he read the section of the Cabinet Manual  that states:
“incumbent Ministers should ensure that any requests they make for advice or
information from their officials is for the purposes of their portfolio responsibilities and
not for party political purposes.”; if so, was the advice and information Simon Bridges
sought from the New Zealand Transport Agency used in National’s Northland bridges
policy?

items.speaker: Hon Simon Bridges
items.text: Information.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: My understanding is that information was asked for —I might
need to check that—and that is appropriate.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why is he allowing a Minister wh ose portfolio conflicts with the
alleged actions of his own brother to remain as Minister, and why does he not follow the
high standard I set in temporarily standing down Carmel Sepuloni in similar
circumstances?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! It is a very  marginal call. I am going to allow the Prime
Minister to deal with it.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Firstly, because I took advice on the day that I became aware
of it. The advice was very clear that there had been no conflict up to that point and a ny
potential conflict could be managed. I think all members of this House appreciate that
there are potential conflicts, as an electorate MP right through to a Cabinet Minister,
and they need to be managed. In relation to the actions that he took with Carm el
Sepuloni, I personally think he made the wrong call.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he stand by his statement made after Mike Sabin resigned that
Mr Sabin could have been a Minister, and what does that say about the standards he sets
for ministerial office?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, I do stand by that statement. In the time that Mike Sabin
was part of our caucus I actually found him to be a very thoughtful, hard -working
member of Parliament. He had good policy ideas and I think he could have made a very,
very good Minister.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Is it not true that he is allowing Ministers off the hook because he
has lost his moral authority and that is why Judith Collins is sharpening her knives?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Supplementary question. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Just before I call the member, I am waiting for a bit of
assistance from my left.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Does this mean that his subterranean standards are so low
that Judith Collins, despite the appalling Oravida scandal and numerous gaffes, is soon
to be welcomed back into Cabinet?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: The great news on this side of the House is that we have a
caucus full of talent and opportunity. Judith happens to be one of its members. There are
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3135
many others, and if one day an opportunity opens itself, I am sure that Judith, along
with many others, will be wanting to put her hand up. It is ni ce to have some fantastic
people to choose from.
New Zealand International Convention Centre Act 2013 Repeal Bill—Fiscal
Impact

items.speaker: DAVID SEYMOUR
items.text: My question is to the Minister for Ec onomic
Development and reads as follows—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! There is just too much noise from my left -hand side. I will
ask the member to start his question again.
4. DAVID SEYMOUR (Leader —ACT) to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: What are the fiscal risks to the Crown from Tracey Martin’s New
Zealand International Convention Centre Act 2013 Repeal Bill, if any?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If the bill was to
pass—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I am about to lose my patience with
one member in particular. There has just been perpetual interjection from one member,
particularly, in a very loud voice. If it happens again I will be asking that member to
leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: If the bill was to pass and the New Zeal and International
Convention Centre Act repealed, the risks would be high. In terms of direct Crown
liability, to begin with, the Government would be liable for half of the design costs up
to a maximum of $10 million. But following the signing of a buildin g works contract
that liability would rise potentially to the value of the concessions, which would be in
excess of $400 million, as set out in clause 22 of the agreement. Also important is the
reputational risk. If a Government is to be able to contract, other parties to that contract
need to be able to trust that the Government will follow through. Subsequent
cancellation of a contract of this magnitude would mean that other parties would be less
likely to contract with the Government in the future, or pr ice in that risk. I am pleased,
therefore, that that member and others on this side of the House will not be supporting
the repeal bill.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that Mr Seymour was in support of my
bill until, one, he saw the polling in Northland, and, two, he received a phone call—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! No, there is no ministerial responsibility for the bill in that
question. If the member wishes to ask a question that relates to the ministerial
responsibility I will accept it. The way it is phrased at the moment it will be ruled out of
order.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. Can I rephrase the question to
meet the—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have given the opportunity for the member to rephrase it.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Thank you very much. Can the Minister confirm that Mr Seymour
was in support of my bill until he received a phone call from the Minister himself?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question is not in order.

items.speaker: Dr Russel Norman
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. In the Minister’s answer he
introduced the bill and said that the ACT Party member was sup porting it. It is perfectly
reasonable for a follow -up supplementary question to address the answer that the
Minister gave.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will listen again to the question. The way it was phrased, in my
mind, I have made absolutely the correct decision. There must be a ministerial
responsibility. If the member can relate it to the ministerial responsibility, then I will
accept the question. I am trying to assist the member.
3136 Oral Questions 5 May 2015

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can the Minister confirm—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Start again.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can the Minister confirm whether he has seen any reports indicating
Mr Seymour’s support of the bill until he received a call from the Minister himself,
pressuring him to change his position?

items.speaker: Hon Gerry Brownlee
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. There is absolutely no
ministerial responsibility—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I listened to the question. It is a very easy question for the
Minister to address. The Minister was asked whether he had seen any reports.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Yes, I have seen reports. I am not sure that I could verify
those reports, exactly; they were from a media outlet. But I have seen the reports.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can the Minister explain why he and the questioner, David
Seymour, are now asserting the sanctity of contract law around my bill, in light of the
fact that Skycity has already indicated that it is in breach of a core platform of this
particular contract? [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the Minister did not hear the question I can get it repeated.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not sure that that member is correct. What I can tell
her, though, in relation to her bill, is that she does say at the outset of her bill, I
understand through the press release, that she is very keen to minimise costs to
taxpayers. I agree with her that that  is important, but the simple reality is that the bill
that she is proposing would actually dramatically increase costs to taxpayers.

items.speaker: Tracey Martin
items.text: Can the Minister confirm that it was he who negotiated this
contract, which included clause  22, and whether it will cost the New Zealand taxpayer
more or less than they have paid for the Novopay contract debacle he was supposed to
be fixing?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No, I did not personally negotiate the contract with Skycity.
I did sign the contract on behalf of the Government, and I can confirm that the Skycity
contract as constructed says quite clearly that the concessions are in response to the
construction of the New Zealand International Convention Centre, and as such it would
be considerably cheaper than the Novopay contract signed by the previous Labour
Government.

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: What can we learn about the role of Governments in commercial
enterprises, and has the Minister seen any reports of other parties prop osing such
enterprises in their manifestos recently?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I think the —[Interruption] Order! The first part of the question can
be answered.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I think Governments should always be careful in their
involvement with commercial enterprises and be seeking to transfer the risk to, for
example, the private sector, as has been done, for example, in the ultra -fast broadband
contract that is being supported by this Government. That has transferred the risk to the
private sector and resulted in a very competitive development of ultra -fast broadband in
this country, as compared with, for example, Australia, where the taxpayer took on the
commercial risk and it has cost masses and masses of billions of dollars.
Business Research and Development—Funding
5. PAUL FOSTER-BELL (National) to the Minister of Science and Innovation :
What is the Government doing to grow business-led research and development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Recently the Prime
Minister and I announced that, as part of Budget 2015, the Government will inve st an
additional $80 million in research and development growth grants over 4 years, to
encourage more private sector research and development and grow New Zealand’s
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3137
research and development ecosystem. Research and development growth grants are
non-discretionary and meet 20 percent of the cost of an eligible firm’s research and
development programme. To qualify, they must commit to spending at least $300,000
and at least 1.5 percent of revenue a year on research and development, conducted in
New Zealand. Th e new funding is equivalent to a 14 percent increase in Callaghan
Innovation’s total research and development grants budget, and contributes to the
almost $1.5 billion the Government will be spending and investing in science and
innovation in the coming financial year.

items.speaker: Paul Foster -Bell
items.text: How does investing more in business -led research and
development further diversify the New Zealand economy?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Research and development growth grants are a crucial part
of our efforts to boost levels of private sector research and development in New Zealand
and lift innovation. A strong emphasis on research and development helps to diversify
and strengthen the New Zealand economy and ensure our companies maintain
competitiveness internationally. This is borne out by the range of industries investing
more in research and development in New Zealand these days. The top two industries,
by value, in 2013 -14 were manufacturing with 54 percent, and information and
communications technology with 23 percent, of the research and development growth
grants funding. This compares favourably with countries where research and
development tax credits are in place and where the research and development tends to
simply match the profile of exi sting industries —for example, in Australia, where
mining and financial services are apparently the most innovative industries.

items.speaker: Paul Foster-Bell
items.text: What examples has he recently seen of New Zealand companies
growing internationally through their investment in research and development?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Hundreds of New Zealand companies are now succeeding
on the world stage through their research and development, in many cases supported by
Callaghan Innovation. For example,  just last week I was privileged to be in Latin
America and officially open the new Sao Paulo offices for growth grant recipient Tait
Communications, which is succeeding very well in Latin America. [ Interruption] I also
visited research and development pro ject grant recipient ADInstruments from Dunedin,
which is doing a great job producing data acquisition and analysis systems for the life
sciences industry, and is expanding its presence in South America. The success of these
and other innovative Kiwi compa nies around the world is lifting New Zealand’s export
revenue and growing jobs and incomes for Kiwis, including for people from Dunedin,
Mr Clark.
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
6. ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) to the Prime Minister: Does he
stand by his statement in relation to achieving a surplus that it is like “landing a 747 on
a pinhead”?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: Yes, because history shows that fiscal
forecasts and out -turn move around quite substantial ly. For example, in Budget 2008
the then Minister of Finance was forecasting a $1.3 billion operating balance before
gains and losses surplus in 2008 -09. As it turned out, he left the Government books in
deficit by $3.9 billion that year, and Treasury told us that we faced never-ending deficits
under the previous Government’s policies. So, yes, forecasts can move around a lot,  but
this Government is making good progress on fixing up the hash of it that Labour made.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why is he trying to minimise the importance of achieving a surplus
this year, when he has made it a core part of his Government’s cred ibility for the past 4
years; why can he not just admit he has failed?
3138 Oral Questions 5 May 2015

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: We are not trying to minimise it. We are pointing out that
there are a number of factors that make it a little bit trickier —and that is, for instance,
that inflation is so much lower, which is great for consumers, and that there are a
number of areas where there has been a re -evaluation by Treasury. But if we just take a
step back for a moment and say that in 2011 what the deficit was, the answer was $1 8.4
billion. The Half Year Economic and Fiscal Update forecast for this year’s deficit is
$585 million. I will point out that every single attempt to either raise revenue or cut
expenditure by this Government has been opposed by the Labour Opposition.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Does he accept that he would now likely be on track to surplus if his
Government had not spent $36,000 on sending Ministers to Northland, had not wasted
tens of millions of dollars on Novopay, had not lost hundreds of millions of  dollars in
dividends due to the asset sales, and was not blowing the Budget on everything from
charter schools to Inland Revenue Department computers?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: No. I will point out that Novopay was something that came
along under  the previous Labour Government. When it comes to the hundreds of
millions of—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I cannot hear the answer with that sort of noise.

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: When it comes to the hundreds of millions of dollars more that
we might have got under the mixed -ownership model, that was money that was literally
blown by the reckless policies of Labour, so firmly rejected by the New Zealand public.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Why does he say that low inflation  is to blame for his failure to
reach surplus, when low inflation saves the Government money just as it saves the
taxpayers from paying more tax; why does he always greet failure with excuses rather
than fronting up?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I am hugely fearful that the Leader of the Opposition is getting
his economic advice from Grant Robertson. He needs to go and read a decent speech on
economics, and he would see one from the Minister of Finance where he quite
accurately pointed out that becaus e of lower inflation over the next 4 years, the
Government’s revenue will be $15 billion less and the tax revenue the Crown receives
will be $4.5 billion less. Low inflation is great for consumers, great for business; it just
ain’t great for Government revenue.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: When will he admit that his Government acting as a bystander at the
dairy auctions rather than building a more diverse economy is the real reason his
economic promises are falling away as fast as the milk price?

items.speaker: Rt Hon JOHN KEY
items.text: I do not know whether I misinterpreted the question from the
Leader of the Opposition, but he seems to be saying that the Government should be in
there buying milk powder in the auction. If he is, that is an interesting use of
Government resources.
Budget 2015—Employment Standards
7. SARAH DOWIE (National —Invercargill) to the Minister for Workplace

items.speaker: Relations and Safety
items.text: How will Budget 2015 help strengthen compliance with
minimum employment standards?
Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE (Minister for Workplace Relations and
Safety): Today I announced that Budget 2015 will invest $32 million more over 4 years
to support employment relations services to help strengthen compliance with minimum
standards. It will boost the labour inspectorate, strengthen education and information
services, and address breaches of employment law. The funding will se e six new labour
inspectors for  Auckland, building on last year’s Budget, which funded six more in
Christchurch. The latest boost shows that the labour inspectorate staff numbers
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3139
comprise a 57 percent increase on the size of the 2008 inspectorate that this Government
inherited.

items.speaker: Sarah Dowie
items.text: How does this announcement build on other work the Government is
doing in this area?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: This funding will support the recently announced
package of measures to strengthen the enforcement of minimum employment standards,
including tougher sanctions. A bill to put these measures in place is expected to be
introduced mid -year. It also follows the passing last week of the Immigration
Amendment Bill (No 2) , which imposes heavy penalties on employers exploiting
migrant workers including 7 years’ imprisonment and a $100,000 fine, or deportation.
This Government is committed to protecting the integrity of the labour market and
ensuring fair and productive workplaces. Budget 2015 will provide an excellent
example yet again of that commitment.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: How will the fact that he has allowed migrant workers to work
in New Zealand for 6 months without the pro tection of New Zealand employment law,
and supports labour inspectors being told to “butt out” when they try to enforce the
Minimum Wage Act, impact the ability of the six extra labour inspectors to strengthen
minimum employment standards?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: As the member knows, it is the Minister of
Immigration who has allowed those workers to come in under special purposes, but I
stand by the labour inspectorate’s investigation into the welfare of those workers. Their
welfare has been well supported, and I accept that.
Housing Market—Auckland
8. KEVIN HAGUE (Green)  to the Minister of Finance : Does he stand by all his
statements?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes, in the context in which they
were made.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: As the Minister is happy to have the problems of success, as he told
the The Nation television programme on the weekend, could he tell the House whether
it is a mark of this Government’s success that the homeownership rate is at its lowest
since 1951, and whether he is happy about that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I know the Greens do not like any kind of economic success;
they regard it as an attack on the environment. But we think that on balance it benefits
most people, so, yes, in answer to your first question, we are happy to have the
problems of success . Secondly, with regard  to homeownership rates, the member may
not be aware of the HomeStart programme, launched on 1 April —I hope he is advising
his constituents about it —which will assist particularly young New Zealanders into
homeownership. The steady decline in homeownership since the late 1950s tells us, I
think, a bit more about demographic change —the change in the nature of households
and so on; particularly, say, for instance, in the fast growth in the sole -parent
household—and is probably a stronger explanation than some others that the member
has in mind.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Is it another mark of this Government’s success that the median house
price in Auckland has now reached $753,500, with an average sale of more than
$800,000, and is he happy about that?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I am not happy about it, and I am particularly unhappy
with the kind of planning approach that the Greens advocate, which is part of the cause
of the rapid escalation in house prices. The Greens have advocated anti-growth and anti-
densification policies for years. They have been far too influential, and that is cutting
low and middle income Aucklanders out of the possibility of decent housing or of
3140 Oral Questions 5 May 2015
owning their own house. I hope that the Greens will change their views and help us to
change the Auckland Council’s vie ws so that we can allow Auckland City to grow and
to have affordable housing.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Is it a problem of this Government’s success that its housing accord
partner, the Auckland Council, has put the building of 2,000 to 3,000 supposedly fast-
tracked homes on hold around Huapai because the Government refuses to properly fund
much-needed transport links to this area?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am sure that there will be ongoing discussion with the
Auckland Council, but my underst anding is that, quite independent of the Government,
it appears at least to have reduced its own infrastructure budget at a time when the city
is under pressure to grow. That is a wee bit hard to understand, and I am sure we can
have further productive dis cussions with the city, but it should be clear —as the Greens
should be clear —that the long -term answer to affordable housing in Auckland is more
houses on the ground, faster, and the Government will relentlessly focus on that
objective.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Is it a problem of success for this Government that the Auckland
Council is actually caught between a rock and a hard place when it comes to housing,
with Auckland ratepayers being the rock, and working with this Government being the
extremely hard place?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The Auckland Council would not have to work with the
Government if it built enough houses fast enough for the people who want to go to
Auckland and pay rates. But it is also caught with dealing with community gro ups
fostered and encouraged by the Greens to oppose new building of houses in Auckland
communities when we need them.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Does it make the Minister happy that he and his Government wilfully
ignore the advice of organisations such as the OECD and the Reserve Bank and rule out
introducing a capital gains tax to curb property speculation, which is driving up house
prices in Auckland?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member may be aware that New Zealand already has
tax law that tax es gains from speculation, as if it is income, at the marginal income tax
rate. So, no, I am not unhappy to be considering OECD or Reserve Bank advice and not
necessarily taking it, because what we have discovered in this whole process is that
planning law—such as that advocated by the Greens —that tries to restrict the growth of
Auckland creates inequality for low and middle income households that cannot afford
housing, and it creates very high and volatile house prices. We will continue to work
hard to und o the damage of the previous 20 years, when that philosophy was put in
place. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption] I am just waiting for Mr Twyford.

items.speaker: Kevin Hague
items.text: Is it not insulting to tell young Aucklanders who are desperately
trying to buy a house and are being outbid at auctions week after week by property
speculators that this Government’s policies, which do absolutely nothing to address the
demand side of the housing market, are a success?

items.speaker: Hon B ILL ENGLISH
items.text: What would be insulting to tell young Aucklanders is the
Greens saying to them that they should have cheap houses but the Greens are opposed
to roads, to cars, to digging up the ground, to creating subdivisions, and to building
houses. That is  what is insulting to young Aucklanders. It is Labour and the Greens
saying: “You should have cheap houses but you’re not allowed to do any of the things
that ensure that more houses get built faster.”

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. My point of order is
that that answer does not fulfil the requirements of the Standing Orders where
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3141
ministerial answers are concerned. It was all about some other party’s so -called
stance—totally irrelevant to the question being asked.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: On this occasion, when I consider the start of the question, “Isn’t it
insulting”, the Minister, I think, has addressed the question. It would have been helpful
if he had not used it as an opportunity to attack the Green P arty to the extent he did. I
accept that point.
Surgery, Elective—Waiting Lists for Orthopaedic Services
9. Hon ANNETTE KING (Deputy Leader —Labour) to the Minister of Health :
Are New Zealanders who require elective surgery receiving it in a timely manner?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Yes, the number of
elective surgeries has increased by 44,000 a year in the last 6 years under this
Government—a remarkable turn -round, given that elective surgeries fell by 2,000
between the years of 2000 and 2006. By doing more and more operations, the number
of New Zealanders waiting over 6 months has reduced from nearly 7,000 New
Zealanders in 2006 to a handful today.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: In light of that answer, why did Dr John Cullen, a highly
respected clinical leader at Waitematā District Health Board , tell the chief executive
officer less than 1 month ago that in addition to raising the threshold at which people
can get an operation that leads to clinical risk, “The situation is controlled by the use of
a suspended list.”?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: If any member reads that article in the New
Zealand Herald on Saturday morning, they will know that Mr Cullen then retracted his
statement. Over the last 6 years at Waitematā District Health Board, elective surgery has
increased by 51 percent. That is a total of 6,500 more operations every year, 21,000
extra operations for people in that district health board area in total, and we have
delivered more than 13,000 more first appointments there. The answer to increased
demand is to do more operations, and nationally we have done 44,000 more operations
and delivered 50,000 more first specialist appointments —a lot better than that person’s
record when she—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table a letter from Dr John Cullen, clinical leader,
Waitematā District Health Board , dated 10 April 2015, entitled “An impossible
situation”, setting out why the management of both elective and acute surgery is
increasingly difficult.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The document has been described. It is a letter by Dr John
Cullen. Is there any objection to that document being tabled? There is not. It can be
tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Why did Dr John Cullen send an email to the chief executive
officer of Waitematā District Health Board on 10 April 2015 saying that the operations
manager of orthopaedic surgery is concerned at the potential adverse publi city
following the return of patients to their general practitioner even after they were given
certainty for surgery?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: The member would have to ask Mr Cullen that,
but he has actually since retracted his st atement. What we do know is that those people
who were sent back to their general practitioner went back because there was
incomplete information in the referral, because more testing was needed, and also, very
importantly, because surgery was not appropri ate. This member is trying to make
something out of nothing, but what remains is that we are doing more surgery at
3142 Oral Questions 5 May 2015
Waitematā District Health Board  and providing more appointments, whereas that
member actually provided fewer.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table the email from Dr John Cullen dated 10
April 2015 raising concerns about sending patients back to their general practitioner
after being given certainty—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Leave is sought to table that particular email. Is there any
objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is he aware that district health boards are either raising the
threshold at which patients can get surgery or introducing measures such as suspended
lists and patient pathways in an effort to meet the Government’s targets, which are
virtually impossible to meet with the financial resources they have?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JON ATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Look, that is completely incorrect. The
information I have is that there are no hidden lists. What I can tell you is that people go
back to their general practitioner because surgery is not appropriate, because the referral
is incomplete, or  because they need more testing. But we are doing 44,000 more
operations and 50,000 more appointments, so more surgery, more appointments —a lot
better than that member’s record.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Is another way to manage the waiting list s to refer patients back
to their general practitioner, like the Taranaki District Health Board, which has
increased the number of people refused an orthopaedic first specialist assessment by 142
percent under the last 3 years of this Government?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: What I do know is that that data is very
incomplete. But what is a fact is that there have been 1,216 more electives performed in
Taranaki under this Government and there has been a 5,000 cumulative increase in fir st
specialist appointments, unlike when Annette King was Minister, when—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has completed his answer as far as I am
concerned.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: I seek leave to table an Official Information Act rel ease from
the Taranaki District Health Board dated 19 March 2015 showing a 142 percent
increase over the last 3 years of letters refusing first specialist appointments for people
wanting orthopaedic surgery.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Leave is sought to table that particular Official Information Act
release. Is there any objection? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: I seek leave to table a document showing that
we are doing 1,216 more electives a year in Taranaki and delivered—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I need the source of the document and the date.

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: This is current information compiled by health
officials. You will not find it anywhere else, so I suggest—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Is it very recent information?

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: Very recent.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will put the leave.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: What’s the date?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It is very recent. That will do on this occasion. [Interruption] Order!
The members themselves can decide. I will put the leave. Leave is sought to table this—
[Interruption] Order! Leave is sought to table this particular information from the
Ministry of Health of a recent date. Is there any objection?
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3143

items.speaker: Hon Dr JONATHAN COLEMAN
items.text: It is compiled by health officials, including
advisers, and the date is today.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: That is of assistance. We have now dated it to be today. Is there any
objection to it being tabled? There is none. It can be tabled.
Document, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [Interruption]

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: You show yours and I’ll show mine.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have no intention, I can assure you.
Sign Language Fund—Sign Language Week
10. STUART SMITH (National—Kaikōura) to the Minister for Disability Issues:
How is the Government’s investment in the New Zealand Sign Language Fund helping
sign language users to promote and maintain the language during Sign Language Week?

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Sign Language Week is
a chance to celebrate one of New Zealand’s official languages. It is a language th at is
spoken by over 20,000 Kiwis every day. The Government has invested $350,000 to
raise awareness about this unique language during Sign Language Week 2015 and
provide all New Zealanders with an opportunity to get involved and connect with the
Deaf community. This is in addition to the $11 million the Government has invested
over 4 years to support deaf children and their families by helping school -aged and
preschool children learn sign language and provide more sign language support and
tutors in schools.

items.speaker: Stuart Smith
items.text: How can New Zealanders take part in New Zealand Sign Language
Week?

items.speaker: Hon NICKY WAGNER
items.text: Hundreds of events are taking place across New Zealand
this week. There are tours of galleries and museums with sign l anguage interpreters,
comedy shows, pop-up sign language cafes, and over 745 New Zealand Sign Language
taster classes being available. Raising awareness of sign language helps the Deaf
community and other users of the language to connect with all New Zeala nders. I
encourage us Kiwis to get out and give it a go. Happy Sign Language Week.
Climate Change—Native Species
11. EUGENIE SAGE (Green)  to the Minister of Conservation : Does she agree
with Professor Mark Urban that New Zealand’s indigenous species are at greater risk of
extinction from climate change than species in many other parts of the world; and if not,
why not?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Has she ever tried to convince her Cabinet colleagues to protect our
native species at risk of extinction from climate change by adopting policies that reduce
New Zealand’s emissions; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I have spoken to my Cabinet colleagues and caucus and
this House on many occasions about the need to preserve and protect more of our
endangered species. In terms of the climate change part of your ques tion, that is best
directed to the Minister for Climate Change Issues.

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Does the Minister accept that if New Zealand contributes to a more
than 2-degree warming of the planet by our emissions increasing by 50 percent over the
next 10 years, as the Ministry for the Environment predicts, this will increase the
extinction risk for our indigenous species?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: I refute the so -called facts in that member’s question and
disagree with them.
3144 Oral Questions 5 May 2015

items.speaker: Eugenie Sage
items.text: Well, how can the Minister, as the Minister of Conservation, stand by
while climate change increases the extinction risk for our threatened species to 14
percent, as Mark Urban predicts?

items.speaker: Hon MAGGIE BARRY
items.text: This Government  and I as the Minister of Conservation
are certainly not standing by. An example I would draw the member’s attention to is the
Battle for our Birds, which was a direct response to what happened with a masting —
that is, a very extensive seeding of the beech trees. Many people understand that the
reason that triggers the mast of a beech forest is to do with temperatures. Warmer
temperatures mean higher seeding, which means plague proportions of rats—25 million.
We planned for that, we analysed it, and we unrol led a strategy called Battle for our
Birds, which resulted in the successful turn -round of the decline of at least 12 of our
native species. It was a highly successful campaign.
Government Financial Position—Return to Surplus
12. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour —Wellington Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: Does he stand by his statement that “returning to surplus and repaying debt
are among the most important things the Government can do to e nsure New Zealand
can withstand future shocks and build a more competitive economy based on exports
and new jobs”; if so, will there be a surplus for the 2014/15 year?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLI SH
items.text: In answer to his questions, yes, I do
stand by my statement and, no, there will not be a surplus for that year. But I want to
thank our public servants for their role in the very substantial progress the Government
has made on get ting back to surplus. They have worked hard to provide more for less,
and despite the fact that for many public services there has been no new money, public
trust in public services is higher than it has ever been —certainly, it is higher than the
period when the previous Labour Government was pouring cash into every service.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, why did he make the promise to New
Zealanders in September last year that No. 1 of his five fiscal priorities for the next 3
years was “Return to surplus this year and maintain surpluses over the next 3 years”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Because it still is our very high priority to get back to
surplus. The analogy I used the other day was if you set out to lose 10 kilo s and you
lose 9.9 kilos, you are almost there, and we are almost there with the surplus.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer from the Minister, if he was trying to lose
10 kilos to fit into a suit for his brother’s wedding and he lo st only 9.8 kilos, he still
does not fit into the suit, and is that not a failure?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: He can just borrow one of yours.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Yes. It was my niece’s wedding an d the suit was a bit tight,
but I wish I had borrowed the member’s.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: In light of that answer, and as someone with some knowledge of
weight loss in recent times, can the Minister finally admit that he has failed to meet the
promise he made to New Zealanders at the last election to get into surplus this year, and
will he finally ditch the excuses and front up?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: There are no excuses. I mean, before Christmas the
Government published the updated forecast, which showed a deficit. The member might
have only just figured that out, but that was actually 6 months ago. So in 2014 -15 we
will not quite get to surplus. In 2015 -16 and the following years, the member will just
have to wait for the Budget.  But we are on track. Actually, I have a much easier life
than that member, who gets up in the House every day saying the surplus should be
bigger, when all his caucus are saying that we should spend more money.
5 May 2015 Oral Questions 3145

items.speaker: David Seymour
items.text: Can the Minis ter confirm Treasury reports that this Government
will be in surplus every year from the mid -2020s for decades, and is that a greater
priority than making surplus this year; if so, what is the Government doing about it?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The Hon Bill  English—any one of those three supplementary
questions.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I admire the way the member makes us all look very “short
termist” here. We are focusing on a surplus now, but the member is quite correct to have
understood that the Government is making decisions, particularly around the way it is
approaching long-term welfare dependency, that will be having an impact on surpluses
in the 2020s. For instance, the number of sole parents under 20 has dropped by 40
percent in 3 years. New Zealand will be making savings because of that intervention for
the next 20 or 30 years.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: It is a privilege and an honour to take the final call
in the second reading of the Human Rights Amendment Bill before the House. This bill
obviously amends the Human Right s Act 1993. It has two particular areas of purpose.
The first is to enable the establishment of a full -time commissioner with responsibility
for leadership in disability rights within the Human Rights Commission and the second
is to make changes to the rol e and the structure of the commission to strengthen its
performance.
People may not know that, actually, this was initiated on 20 October 2010. The
Minister at that time was the Hon Tariana Turia. As the Minister for Disability Issues
she announced the es tablishment of a full -time Disability Rights Commissioner within
the commission, but to formally establish this role would indeed need an amendment to
the Act. This provided an opportunity to review the structure of the Human Rights
Commission and to explo re options for change in three key areas: firstly, in the
composition of the commissioners who were there in place in its status quo; secondly,
the governance arrangements; and, thirdly, the functions and powers of the commission
itself.
5 May 2015 Human Rights Amendment Bill 3147
There were 42 sub missions that were made to the Justice and Electoral Comm ittee
and 19 oral submissions that were submitted. I would just like to take us through some
of those submissions that I think are important and that also give weight to the
recommendations that have  been made by the Justice and Electoral Committee in
particular. One of the areas was just in regard to one of the challenges of the
improvements. In consultation with the commission and other Government agencies,
the Ministry of Justice has identified som e improvements that could be made to the
composition. These were in regard to improving efficiency, the lack of effectiveness of
the current composition of part -time commissioners, the inflexibility resulting from the
way that specialised commissioners rol es are provided for under the Act, and then,
lastly, there sometimes being an unclear and incomplete description of the functions of
the commissioners in the Act as it currently stands.
There are a number of things that I think are quite important in this  legislation,
especially for the disability community in particular. We know that New Zealand
ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on 25
September 2008. Article 33 of the convention requires States to “maintain,  strengthen,
designate or establish within the State Party, a framework including one or more
independent mechanisms, as appropriate, to promote, protect and monitor
implementation of the present Convention.” We believe that the review and these
amendments will definitely go a way to approving that.
A full-time commissioner position with responsibility for leadership and disciplinary
rights will be created within the commission, and we think this is quite critical. The
creation of these roles requires an a mendment to the Act, as it currently enables
commissioners formalised leadership roles in only two areas: race relations and equal
employment opportunities. The changes to these roles, we think, are going to be quite
significant. The Act currently provides  for full-time and part-time commissioners. This
will be changed to permit a composition of three full -time commissioners, and then also
up to five part -time commissioners who will be part of that composition as well.
Although we are removing the statutory  roles of the Race Relations Commissioner and
the Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner, we are requiring commissioners to
be appointed to lead the work in these areas.
I just want to quote from the departmental report from which we heard submission s,
and, again, from the Chief Human Rights Commissioner himself. In 22 of those
submissions they were in support, indeed, of having the establishment of a disabilities
commissioner in particular. The Chief Human Rights Commissioner submitted that it is
quite critically important to be addressing these issues for the disability community as
well.
Consultation with the Minister of Justice was also challenged. There was an issue in
which we felt it would breach the Paris principles of independence of the Huma n Rights
Commission. This was an issue of concern. In fact, 13 submitters opposed any reference
to consultation with the Minister being included in this bill. Again, the Human Rights
Commission actually submitted that this consultation with the Minister cu rrently occurs
at present, so, in effect, it was not seen that there was a breach, in fact, in regard to the
Paris principles of independence for the human rights commissioners.
This bill will enable the chief commissioner to formally designate commission ers.
We think this area here will then allow them to establish areas of importance that may
be relevant in that current context in time for our communities. In some of the 42
submissions that were made there were references to, for instance, areas of the r ights of
women, and that potentially the Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner role
could include looking at the rights and responsibilities for women under that as well.
There was also another submission that talked about issues around the fairness in the
3148 Human Rights Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
Act around Treaty of Waitangi claims. That was another submission that was made. We
feel that the amended changes will allow for the commissioner to be able —with
consultation on the strategic direction of the commission —to potentially appoint part -
time commissioners to this role as well.
There was some concern that was expressed around the rebranding and existence of
the specialised commissioners by removing the titles of the Race Relations
Commissioner and the Equal Employment Opportunities Commiss ioner, which may be
perceived as lowering the profile of these particular areas of focus. We do not believe
that the proposed changes will negatively impact on the commissioners’ leadership role
of protecting and promoting these particular areas of importa nce as well. There will be
identified commissioners leading the work in each area, and the commissioner will be
the face and the contact point in being able to negotiate these areas of importance as
well.
We feel the recommendations that have been made ade quately address the issues of
the review plus the concerns. We feel, as a select committee, that our recommendations,
approved by the Minister, are appropriate but also give both the flexibility and the
clarity for the commissioner to conduct his roles and  responsibilities. On behalf of the
Government, I also do commend this bill to the House in its second reading.
The question was put that the amendments recommended by the Justice and Electoral
Committee by majority be agreed to.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be agreed to.
Ayes 73
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand First 12; ACT New Zealand 1; United
Future 1.
Noes 48
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; Māori Party 2.
Question agreed to.
A party vote was called for on  the question, That the Human Rights Amendment Bill
be now read a second time.
Ayes 73
New Zealand National 59; New Zealand First 12; ACT New Zealand 1; United
Future 1.
Noes 48
New Zealand Labour 32; Green Party 14; Māori Party 2.
Bill read a second time.
Third Reading
Debate resumed from 30 April.

items.speaker: Hon TREVOR MALLARD
items.text: When I was sort of rudely
interrupted by the clock at 6 o’clock last Thursday, I was indicating to the House that I
thought that although Nathan Guy is a nice chap, he has been pretty ineffectual in this
area. He has been very ineffectual in getting the r esources necessary to have a proper
and independent service that focuses on animal welfare particularly in the area of
primary production. I think he relies on the Royal New Zealand Society for the
Prevention of Cruelty to Animals pretty heavily within dom estic arrangements but what
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3149
he does not have is a good force out on farms ensuring that the small minority of
farmers who treat animals badly are dealt with properly.
I also indicated that the Government’s approach to allow cruelty to animals to
continue for another 15 years—so practices that this Minister accepts are cruel and must
go do not have to go for another 15 years —in my opinion is just not good enough. As
well as being cruel and wrong —cruel and wrong —those practices are not in New
Zealand’s economic interests. It is in the interests of our farmers for New Zealand to
have a reputation of being world leading in farming production practices. Generally,
most of our farmers are, but there are some whose practices are awful. They are
generally—but not o nly—centred in the pork and the poultry industries. That is where
the biggest problems come from. The most obvious problems come from there but we
also have some very poor examples of farmers in some other areas as well.
If we want to grab hold of the opp ortunities, especially in Europe but actually in a
number of other countries as well —increasingly in the United States and even in parts
of the middle class in Asia —we need to be aware that there is more and more focus on
the way we treat our animals in a way that is similar to the way that we treat our
environment. If we are not seen to be world leading in this area, over a period of time
we will go backwards. Unfortunately, it is often the fact that we mistreat our pigs that
will end up being a problem fo r our sheep. The fact that we mistreat our poultry will
end up being a problem for our beef offshore, because it is a country’s reputation across
all of the cruelty practices that is, in my opinion, very important. I am holding up now a
sheet of paper that is the area that will be the area available to chooks, including size 18
and size 20 chooks, under National’s new advanced 2022 rules. Under the rules that will
come into effect then, a chook will have 750 square centimetres —a tiny area. A decent
chook will have trouble turning round. It might be a wee bit of progress, but, frankly, it
is not good enough.
In conclusion, I want to thank again Mojo Mathers for the work that she did. I thank
the Government for running out of other business so it could get on with getting this bill
through. I say that eventually we are going to have to look at the real question and that
is to allow all farmed animals the right to go outside. If we do not let all farmed animals
have the right to go outside, we will be regarded as cruel and our exports will suffer.
Thank you.

items.speaker: IAN McKELVIE
items.text: It gives me no great pleasure to follow
the expert on animals from Hutt South, Trevor Mallard. He clearl y is an expert on the
life and times of the moa but knows very little about farm animals, in my view. I want
to make just a couple of comments on the comments he just made, because I think it is
grossly unfair to include all farmers in the general statemen ts that he just made. What I
do want to make the point about is that the Ministry for Primary Industries has a very
strong team out in the provinces. It has a great understanding of farmers and farmers’
ability to handle livestock, and I am quite sure the ministry is well aware of where the
challenges are for the farmers. I certainly admit that there are farmers who are not
perfect but I also want to make the point that I think they do a pretty good job on the
whole, and we certainly do our best to work within the rules.
Now I want to get back to the topic of the day, the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill.
This bill is critical to New Zealand’s future. I do agree with the previous speaker on that
point. It is probably one of the most important bills that will co me through this House,
along with, perhaps, the biosecurity bill and one or two other bills, interestingly, that
affect the primary production sector, because that is a sector that keeps this country
going. They have a very strong underlying influence, I g uess, on how New Zealand’s
economy works and how the primary production sector works. The economy is driven
by agriculture, and it in turn is driven by these hugely important bills or Acts of
3150 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
Parliament that impact on a food industry that is worth some $40  billion to New
Zealand, and a livestock industry that contributes a large bit of that $40 billion to the
food industry.
We have amongst the best animal welfare codes in the world. We are very good
practitioners in this field. I will talk a little bit mor e about the codes of animal welfare a
little later, but first I want to get on to a number of other issues that, I guess, have
challenged the Primary Production Committee during the course of this bill, which was
in the select committee for quite some time.
We dealt with household pets, for example —and 70 percent of all households in
New Zealand have pets. Gareth Morgan has picked on one very topical one: the cat.
Most of our wild cats in New Zealand started off as household pets, perhaps even in
Hutt South. They have been dumped in our rural parts of New Zealand, and,
consequently, that is a large piece of what causes the major cat problem that Gareth
Morgan frequently refers to. There are also, obviously, a large number of dogs as pets in
New Zealand, and many other animals. I am not saying for a minute that households do
not look after their pets pretty well —I think that on the whole they do —but they
certainly come under pressure. The other challenge we have with those household pets
is the large, large number of unregistered dogs—dogs that cause all sorts of problems in
New Zealand’s communities. In fact, we see some quite horrific injuries caused by
those dogs when they attack children, or even adults. Those are pets that have clearly
not been maintained as they should be. They are also pets that come under the control of
this very piece of legislation that we are talking about.
I want to briefly mention the greyhound industry. The greyhound industry came in
for a lot of focus in the course of discussion on  this bill. Greyhound racing is, I guess, a
sport. It also contributes to the New Zealand economy. It is challenged by the fact that
when you breed an animal for performance, you do not always get the performance you
anticipate. We have to find other ways of dealing with those. Greyhounds are clearly
dealt with under the Animal Welfare (Dogs)  Code of Welfare . So the issues that were
raised by people with relationships to the greyhound racing industry are, in my view,
satisfactorily dealt with in the Animal Welfare (Dogs) Code of Welfare.
The other issue that is very topical is one of pests, and I guess you could put that in
the same category as hunting. Pests —all introduced, of course —are possums, cats,
stoats, rats, etc. Mice are also a significant pest. W e spend an awful lot of time keeping
them out of our food chain, keeping them out of places that we need to keep secure. We
also have a great deal of problems with possums, particularly in our native bush and
forest. Cats, stoats, and rats likewise cause g rievous damage to our native birds. There
was some quite significant discussion on those topics during the course of the
consideration of this bill in the select committee, and I think, again, they are well dealt
with under the relevant codes that apply to those issues.
In New Zealand we farm some 45 million animals —probably a lot more, in fact, but
we have an official count of 45 million - odd. We dealt with numerous issues in respect
of them, including —and I am not counting birds and things like that, so  I am not
accounting for the poultry industry in that —microchipping, tagging, ear -marking,
horses’ teeth, blacksmiths’ operations, and all sorts of operations that take place on a
daily basis in respect of animals. They were all dealt with in the course of the discussion
on this bill. If I go to some of the things like horses’ teeth —which were, I guess, dealt
with in the discussion around surgical procedures that are undertaken in respect of
animals—for a long time, very good practitioners with no qualifica tions have dealt with
things like horses’ teeth, and a number of other issues. In terms of blacksmithing, in
some parts of the world you have to have a ticket to enable you to shoe a horse under
their welfare codes. In my view, New Zealanders are a much mo re adaptable people. I
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3151
think there are a large number of those procedures that can be undertaken extremely
safely by people who have a great understanding of animals. So that came in for a lot of
discussion in the course of this bill as well. I think we satisfactorily resolved that.
I want to talk, briefly, about the live export of animals. Clearly, we have an
understanding that there will be no live shipments for slaughter in New Zealand. We do,
of course, sell a large number of horses overseas both for s port—racing—and for other
uses. We sell a large number of breeding animals—sheep, dairy cattle—overseas for the
same reason. I guess that if you look at the food trends of the world, it is quite
conceivable that sometime in the future there will be an oppo rtunity to export very
small numbers of very high -priced animals for slaughter —well, I would not call it
slaughter; I guess there will be a more practical term they will use for it. By the time
they get to that point, there will be a more practical term. A nd we did not, during the
course of this consideration, outlaw the potential for live export of animals; it is just that
we have an understanding in this country that we will not do it, and I think wisely so.
But there may well come a time in the future wh en we can in fact export for human
consumption again, in a smaller and, I guess, much more enlightened way.
I want to talk about codes of welfare for a moment. I have here the Dairy Cattle Code
of Welfare. Anyone who was concerned about the activities of “NAWAC”, the National
Animal Welfare Advisory Council, which produced the codes of welfare for the
Minister for Primary Industries, will realise that these things are hugely comprehensive,
in my view. I think this is a very good document. I would have cons idered, I suppose,
