that as a farmer I do not need this kind of stuff, but I think, unfortunately, we do need to
set a standard. These codes of welfare set a very clear standard, and I think they do a
great job. There was some significant discussion around the make-up of the National
Animal Welfare Advisory Council. The Minister has the ability to appoint those
members, and I think not only are they a very broad cross -section of the New Zealand
animal-industry experts but also there are some independents on the council who are
very competent people. I think it is more than adequate.
I just want to talk very briefly about the Minister and the select committee.
Obviously, as I have said, this bill is a very important part of what we do. It has been
around for a while. In fact, four of the select committee members who dealt with this
bill have left this House: Shane Ardern, Eric Roy, Colin King, and Shane Jones. They
added a whole lot of value to this bill in the course of it. And, of course, the current
committee, of which most are in this House right now, were also on that committee last
year, with the exception of a couple of new members on our side of the House, and the
man sitting in the Speaker’s Chair himself, Deputy Speaker Chester Borrows. We have
considered 1,721 submissions in the course of this bill, including 12 industry groups, 20
advocacy groups, and eight professional bodies. It was a pretty big job. I think  that on
the whole the committee did an outstanding job with this bill, and I am very please d to
see it coming through. I congratulate the Minister on getting what will be one of New
Zealand’s key pieces of legislation through the House. Thank you.
Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast - Tasman): I must say that,
despite being a longstanding member of the Primary Production Committee —of which
the previous speaker, Ian McKelvie, is, of course, the chair —I did actually stand aside
for the Hon Trevor Mallard, who takes the role of animal welfare within our caucus. So
I was not there for a number of the hearings, but I have followed this very closely,
because, as has previously been said by speakers, this does go to the heart of New
Zealand’s production systems. As a passionate advocate for primary industries, I know
the things that we need to protect, starting, of course, with biosecurity and food safety.
Animal welfare probably comes third in terms of the hierarchy of the things that we
need to uphold, both in a re ality sense and in a reputational sense, because if New
3152 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
Zealand is to continue to export food, then the people who have to pay —or should
pay—a little bit more for quality food want to know that it has been grown and
produced ethically. Indeed, this piece o f legislation moves us forward some way in that
area. So Labour will be supporting it.
It is an interesting time because we have a society that is becoming further
disconnected from the realities of production. They want meat but they do not want
slaughter, and this bill is one more realistic step to address the issues, to minimise any
potential harm to animals, but to still leave in place the reality that animals are grown
and produced for slaughter. There will be some who are vegan and who do not want to
eat that. That is true and that is their right. The vast majority of people in the world need
protein, and we produce it. We produce it in a very sound and ethical way, in a safe
way, and in a way that does minimum harm to the animals in the system for th e most
part. We want to continue with that.
We are making technical changes with the bill. We are addressing some tricky issues
like the use of animals in the area of experimentation, and I will say a little bit more
about that later. Not only is there a dilemma across society around wanting meat but not
wanting it to come from a slaughter process; they also want cheap meat and cheap
food—but, of course, they do not necessarily want to deal with the reality that we have
to have commercial systems of produc tion that some say are factory. By international
standards, most of New Zealand’s systems are pretty much organic. Indeed, if you look
at the sheep grazing out in the Mackenzie Country, you would see that they are as close
to the basic first step in the ev olutionary process as you could imagine —freedom to
roam and handled probably two or three times a year. New Zealand is blessed with
systems that are as close to ideal as you can get, but there are, in some areas, systems —
particularly in the area of egg pro duction, poultry production, pork and, increasingly, in
the area of dairying —that are getting to the point of intensity, where the public are
asking whether there is a better way than the ways that have been conducted over recent
years.
The National Anima l Welfare Advisory Committee, the organisation referred to by
the previous speaker, Ian McKelvie, is an independent organisation set up to address
these quite challenging ethical areas in an appropriate and independent way. I think it
does a very, very goo d job. We have got the issues of colonies and cages for poultry,
what size they should be, and what the normal range of behaviours for those chickens is.
What has happened over recent years is we have moved —as a country and through
legislation—to expand the areas in which chooks live to give them more movement and
to give them more freedom. My colleague the Hon Trevor Mallard says that just about
all those animals should have the right to go outside. We have some systems like that in
the country but not all of them. If we were to move to those systems within a set period
of 2, 3, 4, or 5 years, then there would be a cost to the consumer and the producer, and
some might say that that is a perfectly reasonable cost. There is a reality, of course, in a
low-paid economy, particularly under a National Government that seems to like zero -
hour contracts, that people cannot afford to pay for that food.
There are transitional provisions here, and the exceptions and the extensions to what
are deemed not ideal condition s are necessary to allow that transition to occur in a
commercially realistic way. I think we have to accept that —well, some of us or perhaps
my colleague is more reluctant to. Some of us see that as a normal and sensible
transition. But the reality for Ne w Zealand, as the producer of fine -quality food, is that
we will have to move in that direction —that is, with eggs, poultry, and pork. I think
those industries have accepted that.
The difficult issue of dairying is one that is yet to be resolved because o f some
Europeans, I have to say, in reality, who have come into this country and think they
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3153
know how to show us how to milk cows. They want to put all the cows inside in an
intensive, housed farming system. I would suggest that they are not making money th is
year at the payout from Fonterra, so it might clip their wings and their enthusiasm. That
intensive system, despite having some advantages over effluent management, does
move a long way from the pastoral system that we have known —and if not perfected,
certainly developed well —and that has been the hallmark, I guess, of our production
systems. So dairying is heading in the other direction at a time when other sectors are
moving to a less intensified system that provides the animals with a bit more scope, a bit
more freedom, and, I guess, the range of natural movement, as deemed. I think we have
to warn the dairying industry here that when moving down that path, it has to be very
cautious about what that might mean to New Zealand’s brand reputation. It is n ot
something I think we should encourage. The costs of production simply climb to the
point where we are at risk of years of low payout, where those farmers —and more if
they get encouraged into those systems—will go broke.
I come back to the legislation. It does include some good objectives. One in
particular that I quite like is that there will be encouragement for the labelling of animal
products that creates a commercial incentive for improved animal welfare standards.
That is a value proposition for those people who are moving their production systems to
a better one for animal welfare, and it should be labelled, it should be identified, and the
consumers should know, if they are going to pay a bit more for the food, why they are
doing so. Why, then, do es the National Government not endorse country -of-origin
labelling for other foods? Why will it not buy into that? I suggest it is because the
supermarkets, its mates, will simply bully it into avoiding that. The fact is that we have
trans-Tasman standards . Australia buys into country -of-origin labelling and New
Zealand does not. So although this legislation encourages labelling for better animal
welfare standards, which I think is a good thing, there is nothing from the Government
to say that they should i dentify where the food was produced in the first place. So it is
quite a bizarre contradiction in the legislation that once this is passed, we will be
encouraging labelling on the one hand and, in fact, avoiding it on the other hand.
As I said, the extens ion that was proposed under the legislation will now be closed
down. In transitioning from the current standards to better standards of animal welfare
and production systems, the reality is that we must allow that transition to occur. If they
were chopped off, that would be unrealistic, uneconomic, and, indeed, undesirable for
many of the consumers across the country.
All in all, I think this is a good piece of legislation. The question I would like to ask
at the end of this is around John Key calling in t o Saudi Arabia and, we are told, having
discussions about the renewal of the live export trade to that country. I have not heard
too many people asking for that or thinking that it is a good thing, other than the Prime
Minister perhaps promising his Saudi counterpart that we will get this under way. So I
think it is incumbent upon the Government and the Prime Minister to answer the
question: are we going to resume live exports for slaughter or not? Although there was a
hint from the previous speaker—

items.speaker: Hon Nathan Guy
items.text: No.
Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR: No. Well, as the Minister for Primary Industries has
said no, that is good. It is good to hear that, because I do not think there is any benefit,
and I am pleased to hear him say that . So I hope he tells the Prime Minister, his boss,
that it is no good kidding the Saudi Arabians that we might get a renewal of that trade.
The last thing I would say is that we do not agree with animal testing for cosmetics.
Indeed, it is pleasing to see , as the father of five daughters, that cosmetics and make -up
are kind of on the way out. I think that is great. It will save me a fortune. Out of all the
women around here, I do not see one who needs those cosmetics, and, indeed, we do not
3154 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
need the animal testing to try to improve them. This is a wise piece of legislation but the
Government has got to follow through on what it says it is doing here.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: It is a p leasure to speak on the Animal
Welfare Amendment Bill. I was one of the new members to the Primary Production
Committee and unfortunately did not go through any of the process with this bill, so I
commend the members of the select committee for the fine jo b that they have done.
Agriculture underpins our economy —in fact, it pays for our way of life. We would not
enjoy the same standard of living that we enjoy now if it were not for cows and sheep,
in particular. So I think to a large extent we ride on their backs in terms of our economic
well-being. Agriculture earns $25 billion from livestock and it contributes to our
economy. So it is absolutely huge in terms of New Zealand’s gross national product. I
use the term gross national product deliberately. Too of ten we focus on GDP. Actually,
“GNP” is how we pay our way in the world —and that term means “gross national
product”, for anyone who is not familiar with that term. I think that I would like to see a
lot more focus on that term.
Animal welfare is absolute ly vital, but I think that People for the Ethical Treatment
of Animals are currently running a campaign in Australia that does their cause no good.
In their latest campaign they claim that 25 percent of the world’s wool is grown in
Australia and that it is  made from 100 percent cruelty. That is just a ridiculous
statement. I agree wholeheartedly with the Victorian Farmers Federation, which said
that the campaign denigrates, offends, belittles, and insults every Australian’s
intelligence. I think that although we care very deeply about animal welfare, to take it to
that level in a campaign really just runs the risk of putting everyone offside from that
organisation’s particular argument. If you keep running into a crowded theatre calling
“Fire!”, people will not listen to you for very long after that. So I think that they are not
doing themselves any good.
New Zealand is, in fact, ranked first equal in the world for animal welfare, and that is
fantastic. It is great, but that does not mean that we should rest on our laurels; we should
always attempt to improve. I think that trade is so vital. The previous speaker, Damien
O’Connor, mentioned that we are a trading nation, we are a niche producer, we sell into
niche markets, and we actually command a premium for our products. The fact that
people who buy our products are paying a little more than they pay for those they buy
from others is based around things like our animal welfare. They do care about that. It is
not something that they necessarily do a lot of res earch on, but if it comes up, they
certainly do care about it. Although animal welfare has not been a big issue in Asia —
and the Asian market is becoming an increasingly important market for lots of our
goods—over time we have seen a distinct change in valu es around the environment in
Asia, and I believe we will see the same thing with  animal welfare. So it is incumbent
upon us to have really good rules around that, and this bill really does go a long way
towards that.
Sixty-eight percent of New Zealand households own a pet. Although most of our talk
and focus has been on farm animals, by numbers of population most people’s contact
with animals is with the family pet, and we should not forget that in this discussion. As
my colleague said earlier, dogs not on ly damage humans, which we often see when
there is a dog attack, but they also attack other dogs quite often, and are often trained to
be vicious.
This bill deals with a lot of those issues and I commend the Primary Production
Committee and the Minister f or Primary Industries for dealing with it in that way. This
bill seeks to amend the Animal Welfare Act 1999. It brings a higher degree of
transparency to the Act, and I think that is much needed. It has a much greater
enforceability, it increases the range of enforcement tools, and, in fact, it brings in more
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3155
appropriate penalties. I think that is really important because we too often see well -
meaning Acts of Parliament with little enforceability or inappropriate penalties. If
people do offend, then they de serve to feel the full weight of the law, and we need to
make sure that it really is a deterrent.
The bill provides a framework for suitable regulations, and the Minister, at their
discretion, is able to bring in regulations as things change. Over time, attitudes to animal
welfare change considerably. We have just gone through the Anzac Day celebrations.
One hundred years ago 10,000 horses went off to the First World War. I can guarantee
to you that the attitude to animal welfare 100 years ago was consider ably different from
what it is today. Not many of those horses came back and the way in which they were
disposed of is perhaps best not focused on too much these days. Those things would not
happen in the New Zealand of today under the current rules, and t he rules are tightened
further still under the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill.
The issues that this bill tackles are complex, and I commend the select committee for
the work it did on this. It is not easy to deal with these complex issues, but we are not
elected to do the easy things; we are elected to make good law and do things that are
sometimes a bit tough. I actually commend both the Minister, in particular, and also the
select committee for tackling these things head -on and dealing with them in the wa y
that they did.
I think it is worth noting that not all New Zealanders —in fact, very few New
Zealanders—actually deal with farm animals or have any link with farms. Going back
only a few generations, most New Zealanders had a direct link to a farm throug h their
family or good friends. Nowadays most people probably do not have any interaction
with farms at all. Farmers deal with animals every day, and the reality of dealing with
animals every day is quite different from the interaction that people have wit h a pet.
Often, seeing what goes on in a farm can be upsetting for some people. A sheep being
shorn, for example —although the sheep does not actually relish the process, it really
enjoys getting the wool off its back when it gets outside.
Surgical and painful procedures were covered, and these were alluded to earlier in
the process. I have had some feedback from veterinary surgeons in my electorate who
were concerned about the docking of tails on dogs. In particular, those surgeons did not
want to see the law changed because they felt that some dog owners would take that
procedure on themselves rather than doing it through a veterinary surgeon with adequate
anaesthesia and sterile conditions. Although I have some sympathy with their position ,
the reality is that we do not like that sort of procedure in New Zealand and it has really
got to end. We do have to draw a line in the sand somewhere, and I am pleased to see
that that line has been drawn.
There are 16 codes of animal welfare issued un der the Animal Welfare Act and
developed by the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee. Those codes are being
strengthened by new regulations, which I alluded to earlier. I think it is really important
that the regulations will have some teeth rather t han just being codes. I think that that is
a fantastic innovation.
There has been some talk about factory farming, and I really just want to mention a
little bit about that. If we do rush into banning so-called factory farming in terms of how
we treat hens and farrowing crates, etc., there will be a cost. The cost will be borne by
the consumer, and all we will likely see is consumers switching to cheaper products that
have come in from offshore, and you are simply shifting the animal welfare  issue out of
this country and into another country. In terms of the animals you are not really making
any difference whatsoever. You may be salving your conscience but you are not helping
animal welfare. I think it is sensible to have a good lead -in time. Patoa Farms , which is
New Zealand’s biggest pork producer, processes 2,000 pigs a week, so it is a significant
3156 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
producer. It does not in fact use farrowing crates, but it has taken some time for it to
develop that process, and it will take the rest of the industry som e time to catch up with
those practices. I think it is quite right and proper that we give them some time to do
that.
Wild animals, pest management, and hunting have been touched on by others, but I
want to speak just a little bit about those issues. As a hunter myself I know that it is easy
to be a little flippant about these things. Ultimately, the aim is to actually kill an animal,
but we should be doing it in a way that is humane. I think it behoves us as human beings
at the top of the animal pyramid to treat those animals right and properly. It is with great
pleasure that I commend the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill to the House. Thank you.

items.speaker: MOJO MATHERS
items.text: I would like to start by thanking previ ous speakers,
particularly Trevor Mallard and the Minister Nathan Guy, for their generous affirmation
of my work on this bill. At the second reading, I spoke of our hope that the Government
would still be prepared to support a ban on animal testing of cosm etics despite having
rejected it during the Committee of the whole House stage. I am thrilled that my work
has been justified. I applaud the Government for finally agreeing to a ban on these cruel
tests, and I thank all parties in the House for supporting this amendment.
We can be proud of the fact that New Zealand is now the first country in Australasia
to ban cosmetic animal testing , showing leadership on an important animal welfare
issue of our time. The announcement of a ban on cosmetic animal testing h as met with
worldwide acclaim and affirmation, and has spurred renewed efforts to get these cruel
tests banned in other countries. Doing our part to support a global ban on cosmetic
animal testing was a major motivation for getting this change incorporated  into the bill,
and I look forward to the day when no animal, anywhere in the world, is subject, in
these cruel tests, to chemicals being dripped into their eyes or rubbed into their raw
skin.
I also welcome a small but important change in the bill that will require animal ethics
committees to consider alternatives to animal testing when considering applications to
test on animals. Alternatives to animal testing is an area that is making rapid progress at
the moment, but, sadly, it is one that New Zealand i s lagging behind in. Animal testing
often involves extremely high levels of pain and suffering. One of the most traumatic
things that I had to do last year, in the discussions on the Pyschoactive Substances Bill,
was actually to watch a video of what was i nvolved in toxicology testing, and it
absolutely broke my heart. We should be doing everything that we can to reduce the
number of animals suffering in these cruel tests, and we have a moral and ethical
obligation to do so.
If we are to be confident that unnecessary animal tests are not being carried out, it is
essential that animal ethics committees are kept up to date with the latest developments
in non -animal tests. For example, just recently, over in Australia, a major company
decided to use the liver chip model to test the potential cure for hepatitis B instead of
using the much more painful and cruel animal test. I want to encourage the Ministry for
Primary Industries to investigate ways of ensuring that this information about the latest
developments in alternatives to animal testing is shared between the different animal
ethics committees in order to guide their decision making. I have spoken to former and
current members of animal ethics committees, and they have told me that they would
welcome this information because they do not actually have it.
This is particularly important in light of the fact that we know that different animal
ethics committees are making different decisions about controversial tests. At least one
animal ethics committee has ap proved three applications for the controversial and
outdated LD50 test, whereas another says it would never have approved these because
they do not meet the “Three Rs” of animal research. This inconsistency is concerning
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3157
because it undermines the ministry’ s claims that we can trust the decisions of animal
ethics committees. In my view, they have a long way to go yet.
Another welcome change in the bill is the partial removal of the loophole that allows,
for an indefinite period of time, the development of r egulations that breach the purpose
of the Act. This is long overdue. These loopholes are the ones that have previously
allowed cruel factory farming practices such as factory cages and sow crates to remain
legal. I had an amendment that removed that loopho le, and the Primary Production
Committee heard good submissions from the public in support of my amendment. The
Green Party fully agreed with Trevor Mallard that the current transitional provisions in
the bill are too generous and that 7 years is sufficien t time for farmers to make the
change away from cruel practices such as farrowing crates. The fact is that there are
successful pig farmers, such as Havoc farm, that do not rely on farrowing crates, and it
gives lie to the argument that they are needed.
Many people in the House will remember the footage shown on Campbell Live last
year that showed very different conditions on different pig farms. The first programme
focused on exposing the awful conditions on a pig factory farm in the Waikato. That
footage was horrific, showing pigs that were absolutely depressed, cramped in confined
conditions, unable to turn round, and unable to express natural behaviour, and that did
not have anything like a normal existence. Those conditions were typical of many
intensive pig farms and they amounted to legalised animal cruelty. Sadly, this bill will
do little to address these conditions. The second programme showed a completely
different vision for how farming can be done in New Zealand. It showed Havoc farm, a
free-range farm in South Canterbury. It said that the mothers there are able to roam
freely with the piglets and that there is access to warm shelters, litter to snuggle down
in, and an ability to explore and interact. That is the way that farming should be done if
we are going to farm for meat, and these are the only kinds of conditions that the Green
Party considers to be acceptable.
Despite some of the really positive aspects of this bill, it is our overall view that this
bill still represents a missed opportunity  to get it right for the millions of animals
suffering on factory farms. My concern is that this bill will not only continue to sanction
these kinds of cruel conditions of factory farming but that it may entrench them  even
further, and that is because it n ow elevates practicality and economic impact in the bill
as explicit factors that can be considered when developing regulations. There was
already the ability to take these factors into account, and, historically, these factors —
practicality and economic im pact—were precisely the arguments used to justify codes
of welfare that enabled animals to be kept in factory cages and in sow crates that were
in clear breach of the provisions in the Act. In our view, this move sends the wrong
message about which factors  are important in developing codes of welfare in
regulations.
I also want to say that another main area of concern that has just come to light is the
area of live exports. As everybody has mentioned previously, there is an effective
prohibition, via an ord er under the Customs and Excise Act, on live exports for
slaughter, and many submitters wanted an outright ban in this bill. The advice and the
assurance that we had from Ministry for Primary Industries officers was that the
intention is for the current pr ohibition to be maintained via regulation under the Act,
once the bill is passed. I know that many of us have felt very concerned about the recent
comments by the Prime Minister, when he was visiting Saudi Arabia, that this was one
of the areas that was being looked at. It would be absolutely shameful if we allowed our
current policy to be weakened when the regulations are developed, just for the sake of a
trade deal. That would be horrific. Nothing could be more damaging to our international
reputation than if we were to resume live exports of animals for slaughter, because we
3158 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
know that causes significant suffering, and many farmers do not want it and the public
do not want it.
Although we are pleased that some changes will become enforceable, much will
depend on which standards get lifted into the regulations. We also remain concerned
about the resourcing of animal welfare monitoring and enforcement. Currently, less than
1 percent of complaints result in prosecution, and we still want to see significantly
increased funding for monitoring and enforcement, including proactive enforcement.
Thank you.

items.speaker: RICHARD PROSSER
items.text: I am very pleased to rise to take a call in the
third reading of the Ani mal Welfare Amendment Bill on behalf of New Zealand First. I
want to pick up on a couple of points that Mr McKelvie made earlier, and one of them
was actually about pest control. He talked about the pest species of animals that we have
in this country. It is quite interesting that at this time the subject of 1080 is topical,
because 1080 is actually an extremely inhumane form of pest control. It is curious, in
fact, that it was not included in the ambit of this bill, but perhaps that is a question for
another day. It is something we can revisit.
Mr McKelvie also spoke about the export of live animals for slaughter, and Mr
O’Connor touched on that, and the Minister has said a word about it as well. I want to
talk primarily about the export of live animals because it is probably the major lingering
concern that New Zealand First still has with regard to this bill. During the first reading
I expressed some reservations that New Zealand First held regarding the export of live
animals for slaughter. Of course, un der the existing Act, this is prohibited unless it is
specifically authorised by the Director -General of the Ministry for Primary Industries.
We asked at the time whether or not, that being the case, this bill presented an
opportunity to do away with that provision altogether.
New Zealand used to export animals for slaughter on quite a large scale, and the
practice was brought to a halt by Parliament some years ago for what were very sound
reasons at the time. There were, and are, of course, other reasons as well, economic
reasons, but the motivation at the time was primarily centred on the conditions the
animals were subjected to while they were being transported to other places and the
conditions that they were subjected to when they arrived at the other end.
New Zealand First has got no objection to the export of live bloodstock, because we
understand full well just how valuable the thoroughbred industry is to this country. We
know that our bloodstock is highly regarded and highly sought after internatio nally, and
that many thousands of jobs and literally hundreds of millions of dollars are generated
in the economy through the export of live horses. But horses are treated in an entirely
different manner from sheep and cattle intended for slaughter in the way they are
transported and cared for.
Horses are airfreighted to their destinations in pressurised, air -conditioned comfort.
They are housed in safe, secure environments while on the aeroplane and they have
veterinary care. And, of course, on arrival, t heir fate is not to be taken to the nearest
abattoir but rather to a training track or a stud farm. These are valuable animals and they
are cared for accordingly. Breeding heifers are similarly afforded a better lot than the
cattle and sheep that left thes e shores a decade or so ago destined for the
slaughterhouses of distant places. New Zealand First does not believe that we should be
exporting such animals either, but we recognise that while it is legal, there are people
who will see it as good business and who will look to profit from it.
We are opposed because we believe that such practices are short -sighted, and, as I
have said in debates on other legislation, notably the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act ,
we believe that business activity of this type will come back and bite New Zealand. The
reason for that is that one day the dairy bubble is going to burst. We have allowed
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3159
ourselves in this country to come to the belief that because we hold such a major
position in terms of global cross -border trade in  dairy products we are somehow
significant in terms of world milk production, and we are not. New Zealand produces
only around 3 percent of the world’s milk.
Most dairy produce worldwide is consumed domestically in the country of origin,
and international  trade comprises only a very small proportion of the total. At the
moment, there is a shortfall between supply and demand, and it is this that allows New
Zealand to profit from being in a position to supply, from our disproportionately large
dairy producti on relative to our population and domestic demand, to buyers from
overseas. But in helping to grow production overseas through joint ventures, and by
selling heifers to foreign dairy producers, we are only hastening the arrival of the day
when demand for d airy products in the countries that are presently our export markets
will be met from production in those countries. For that reason, we do not believe that it
is sustainable or even a good idea to export live dairy cows, regardless of the conditions
under which they are transported.
Of course, New Zealand does also export other animals for breeding purposes,
including cattle, sheep, goats, deer, and even chickens. Our animals are very much
sought after worldwide because they are known to be, for the most part, from very good
stock lines and are, for the most part, free from any of the nasty diseases that are
endemic in some other parts of the world. Again, animals that are exported for breeding
purposes are treated better and transported in far greater saf ety and comfort than those
that are destined for the pot.
The issue of live exports for slaughter has not gone away. In fact, it raised its head
only last week with the Prime Minister’s efforts towards securing a free -trade deal with
the nations of the Mi ddle East’s Gulf Cooperation Council . This deal has been on hold
since 2009. Coincidentally, one of the sticking points is the fact that New Zealand
halted live sheep exports in 2004. Apparently, an investor from Saudi Arabia lost quite
a bit of money as a result of the cessation of exports,  and we are told that the Saudis are
still a wee bit sore about that. But, that aside, these exports were put on indefinite hold
at that time for very good reason.
As a nation, we have engaged in live export for slaughter for more than 20 years
prior to that, but in 2003 something like 5,000 sheep died on one ship under what can be
described only as quite horrific conditions while being transported from Australia to
Saudi Arabia. They died from heat stress, overcrowding, and a lack of food, water, and
sanitation during a sea voyage that had lasted something like 2 months longer than it
should have. New Zealand First is very much concerned that such exports may be
resumed and that the provision for their resumption still exists under the bill.
We are concerned on a number of fronts, but they all come back to animal welfare in
one way or another. Obviously, we are concerned that if live exports for slaughter were
to be resumed, we would be faced with a return to the very same conditions that led to
their being curtailed in the first place. It is hard to see how that can be avoided, because
these things are driven by money. Sheep are crammed into overcrowded boats because
the cost of transporting them has to be kept down. A live sheep being exported for
slaughter is not worth very much. In fact, it is probably the lowest return for both the
farmer and the nation that can be received for a sheep that has been grown for
consumption.
We do know that things have not improved very much in that regard in the last 10 or
15 years, because live exports from Australia have continued pretty much unabated
since that time, and the standard of transport today is much as it was then. In fact,
collateral losses for sheep exports from Australia to other parts of the world are ru nning
at about 7 or 8 percent —maybe a little bit less than that, but it is still too much, by any
3160 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
measure. It is the minimal value of the animal and the minimal return to the farmer and
to “New Zealand Inc.” that we oppose, and for the same reasons we do n ot wish to see
any part of our primary sector reduced to a simple exporter of bulk commodities.
The second concern that we have is around the conditions that might meet livestock
exported for slaughter when they arrive at the other end of their journey. W e know that
the Director-General can grant an exemption if he or she is satisfied that the abattoir in
the destination country meets the standards that we demand here, but the reality is that
in too many cases live animals are sought in other parts of the world for reasons of ritual
slaughter in accordance with the requirements of various religious and cultural
practices. These practices by their very nature are not able to meet the minimum
standards of animal welfare that we demand of our own meat processe s. Animals are
required to be fully conscious when they are put to death, which is at odds with our own
requirement that they be stunned first. They are frequently transported in the boots of
cars, even in the back seats of cars. They are not properly rest rained. They are subjected
to quite brutal and stressful treatment prior to slaughter.
We have an objection also to the granting of the exemption being placed in the hands
of the Director -General, however professional he or she might be. The practice of
exporting live animals for slaughter was stopped by politicians through the
parliamentary process, and we believe that if it is to be resumed, then that decision must
be made in the same way. We do not believe that it is good enough for a Minister to be
able to hide behind a bureaucrat if and when this decision ever is to be made.
Governments need to take responsibility for changes of this magnitude, and we believe
that if a Minister wishes to restart the export of live animals for slaughter, then he or she
should be required to put their money where their mouth is, stand behind that decision,
and stand up for it if and when necessary. And whether it is necessary is a salient point,
because over the last decade or so we have shown that exports of live sheep f or
slaughter from New Zealand are not necessary.
The New Zealand farming sector has got on quite well without them for the last
decade, and it appears that customers in the Middle East have got on quite well without
those exports, as well. So it is simply  not necessary, and we ask again why it has not
been removed altogether, and why we did not make provision for prohibiting it in total
when the bill went through. But all that said, on balance this is still a very good bill,
which will deliver very much be tter and improved outcomes for animal welfare in New
Zealand, and New Zealand First continues to support it. I commend it to the House.
Thank you.

items.speaker: BARBARA KURIGER
items.text: It is a pleasure to
be speaking this afternoon on the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill. To begin, I will
make just a couple of comments about comments made by the member for Hutt South,
the Hon Trevor Mallard, this afternoon about  the Ministry for Primary Industries and
about it perhaps not being out there doing its job in the field. I have to say that, in my
experience—prior to my becoming a member of Parliament, I did substantial work with
the Ministry for Primary Industries on v arious committees in the area of animal
welfare—a lot of work has been done with industries to help them to improve the
practices in which they partake in order to earn an income.
Although there has been some reference today about this bill having been aro und for
a long time—and as one of the newer members of the Primary Production Committee,  I
will acknowledge those who have gone before me —that does not mean, actually, that
nothing has been happening out there. People who farm animals are really keen to ma ke
a difference. They know what the market perceptions are. They know what people are
saying about their practices. There is a lot of work constantly going on, all the time, to
make sure that they are upholding the best practices that they possibly can.
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3161
We have heard a bit today about the 16 codes of welfare that are covered under the
Act, and, of course, these codes will be strengthened by the new regulations. In recent
weeks I have been lucky enough to see some good presentations from people, in the
likes of the poultry industry, who are actually transitioning to a phase where they are
looking at moving from cages into colonies. So they are looking at actually taking the
animals in that process out of those cages as fast as they economically can. Sometimes
it is economically difficult to do some of those things in a hurry. But I am really
heartened by the attitude of that industry, in terms of being able to effect some change.
There was a reference today about sheep shearing. In Te Kūiti, in the heart of my
electorate of Taranaki - King Country, we have just had the New Zealand shearing
championships. I have seen some of the graphics that have been coming out of Australia
as well. I have to say that I did not see any sheep in distress, and there were hundred s—
probably thousands—of sheep shorn over that weekend. Those people are professionals
who know the technicalities of shearing a sheep. I am sure that if I got hold of a sheep
and tried to shear it, it would probably panic, but when you watch the likes of a
champion like David Fagan shearing a sheep, it is very professionally and very well
done.
We have also heard this afternoon about animals being outside rather than inside. I
think I will be really interested to see what happens there. Some of the latest requests
out there, in terms of getting rid of our pests in New Zealand, have been calls from
some people in society to keep cats inside. So it is going to be really interesting because
we have got people asking to get farm animals outside but then to keep cats inside.
It is surprising to me, in this bill, that it has taken such a long time for us to realise
that animals are sentient beings. Even though we know it, it is going to be nice, actually,
to see it finally written in legislation. I would also like  to commend Mojo Mathers for
her clauses around banning cosmetics testing on animals.
What I would really like to highlight this afternoon is the fact that we are talking
about being productive and competitive —and trade is very important to this country.
Yes, there is a need to have high standards. We are in a transition phase with a lot of
industries. Earlier this year the Government released the New Zealand Animal Welfare
Strategy. This sets a direction. It sets a vision. I think we would be arrogant to think that
we in this House are the only people who are the experts on animal welfare. Industries
have the ability to debate, to construct evolving standards, and to work with the
Ministry for Primary Industries. People who work with animals do care about animals.
The proposals in this legislation have been through rigorous consultation. They are set
to act at a pace that our communities can live with. I think it is really important that this
legislation has made that clearer and more transparent, and that we can navigate our
way through this legislation much more clearly than we could before.
There is also one thing that I would like to point out around trade and biosecurity,
and that is the move to avoid unnecessary delays in urgent national biosecurity
responses. Clause 5 inserts into section 3 of the Act the new subsections (2A), (2B), and
(2C) to provide for exemption from the requirement to seek approval from an ethics
committee before killing an animal in such circumstances. Sometimes we just do not
have time to go through big long rigorous processes that could end up being
substantially more dangerous to society than to the animal, or animals, concerned in
those situations. So I am really, really pleased to see that that is changing in this bill.
This bill also clarifies what constitutes a significant surgical procedure that can be
carried out only by a vet, without defining it so narrowly that farmers cannot do routine
procedures. So that is just another clarification that means people will not be able  to
say: “I did it because I didn’t know.” Things are unclear in the Act and people go ahead
3162 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
and do things, and then find out later. So it is really important that people do know
exactly what is in the legislation and exactly what they are allowed to do.
The other thing is that there will be greater sanctions for those who mistreat animals.
I think that is really important because, at the end of the day, we do have laws to protect
us from those people who perhaps do not see things in the same way as the res t of us.
That is not only farmers; that is pet owners and a whole raft of other people. We have
also included wild animals in this. It is really important that just because they were not
pets or owned by somebody, they we re not protected under our law. I a m pleased to see
that there are greater sanctions for those who do mistreat animals, because, for those
who watch not only the daily 6 o’clock news but also social media, which is a classic
these days, there are people showing pictures of mistreated animal s, so it is certainly
important to get on top of that one.
Under this legislation, the vast majority of New Zealanders who take care of their
animals very well will not see any major changes in terms of the way they are expected
to behave towards their an imals. I think it is going to deal with those people who, as I
said, really do not have the feeling for animals. We need to deal with those people
because one thing is for certain: those people in society who have trouble respecting
animals often have trouble respecting people as well. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The next call is a split call. Steffan
Browning—5 minutes.

items.speaker: STEFFAN BROWNING
items.text: I am pleased to be able to speak to the Animal
Welfare Amendment Bill and congratulate those involved with getting the
improvements into the bill, particularly my colleague Mojo Mathers. What I want to see
when this legislatio n is fully enacted is other elements of animal welfare law that are
already enacted put into practice by this Government. I am thinking particularly, as I
speak tonight, of the hundreds of cows that died from the herbicide -tolerant swede issue
in Southland, the many, many more that were visibly ill, and the many, many more with
subclinical issues. So poor was the condition of some of the surviving cows that there
was a question of their suitability as culled cows for processing.
I have been looking at some  Official Information Act material on this. There is what
they call a natural toxin that seems to be the cause of the distress of these cows. This
was a serious animal welfare issue. Was that product, which clearly is at the base of this
issue, withdrawn? Was it banned? Or was there a cover -up? There was a cover -up. We
still do not have a proper report on what happened last winter, and into early spring, to
those cows in Southland. The only way we can find anything is through Official
Information Act materi al, and in that I find the very valid questions that I put to the
Minister and I see how they were treated as just generalisations. It says that if the group
is asked about this, it should just stick to these messages and not go down the track of
trying to answer any questions.
There is a chemical involved here as well. It is not just the glucosinolates —we call
them GSLs for short, as everybody else does, for good reason. A glucosinolate is natural
toxin. It forms in the leaves of swedes and other brassicas. It can get to quite high
levels, and under certain conditions it can get to a toxic level. But what we find here is
that the herbicide -tolerant swedes have way more than the non - herbicide tolerant
swedes. The glucosinolate levels are 4 to 16 milligrams per kilo in the leaves—the bulbs
are lower, down on the ground, 1 to 4 milligrams per kilo —but non - herbicide tolerant
ones are just 1 milligram. Something is going on in PGG Wrightson’s Cleancrop
system, with swedes at least, and we are not too  sure about the turnips, rape, and other
products under that system. It cheated New Zealanders and it cheated farmers by going
down a system of production of those herbicide -tolerant ones and by dodging the
genetic engineering route that it already had for  that same product through a chemical
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3163
mutagenesis thing—just as much a DNA muck up—so that it did not have to go through
the Environmental Protection Authority and be open to submissions and testing for
safety. PGG Wrightson dodged it and this Government has let it dodge it.
This is an animal welfare issue. It is also an issue for the people who consume the
products from those animals, and for the other animal products in this country from
animals that are fed products containing lots of herbicides, whethe r it be glyphosate or
whether it be chlorothal onil, which is in these herbicide tolerant swedes and is banned
in China. In here, in the Official Information Act stuff, I find that they are saying: “Is
there enough other herbicide if we move away from these  crops?”. They are so locked
into PGG Wrightson’s crop. We have got to change the way we farm. We have to go
down the organic route, and this Government has got to help with regulation for the
organic sector. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Sue Moroney—5 minutes.

items.speaker: SUE MORONEY
items.text: It is a pleasure to rise and support the Animal Welfare
Amendment Bill at its third reading on behalf of the Labour Party. I just want to note
for regular viewers of, and listeners to, parliamentary debates that they will have noticed
something a little different happening in the House this afternoon. It is a Government
day where Government measu res are going through the House, and the Government
members are making very fulsome contributions to this debate. It is good to see that
occur, but, of course, it is a sign that the Government is not that keen to get through all
this legislation very fast because it does not have much legislation on the Order Paper at
the moment. That is because the Government has run out of ideas, so it has finally
found its voice and is wanting to talk rather a lot about its legislation, one piece of
which is the Animal W elfare Amendment Bill, and that is what is consuming our
interest today for the next little while in the House.
Labour is supporting this bill and we are very pleased to do so, although we wish it
went an awful lot further and we wish that the measures ca me in more quickly. Once
Parliament determines, as it has, that certain practices are harmful and are not in the
interests of animal welfare, then our question is: why wait 15 years to bring in those
measures? If we have determined that these practices are harmful, we should act as soon
as we can. I noticed that the last Government member who spoke on this bill used a
phrase where she said that people were doing this “as fast as they economically can”.
That is a phrase that I have not heard used a lot befor e, but I think it is very telling in
terms of where the priority lies in this regard. I would prefer, and the Labour Party
would prefer, that the welfare of the animals was the priority and that people were urged
to treat animals in a more respectful way m uch more quickly than taking 15 years for
those harmful practices to be phased out. So that would be our criticism of this bill.
However, we are pleased that there is some progress being made.
One of the most important reasons that personally I am pleased  to see some progress
made on animal welfare is the very close and now well -documented link between those
who are prepared to abuse animals and be harmful towards animals and those who
therefore turn out also to be abusive towards fellow human beings. Ther e is now
actually a lot of evidence that tells us this. The young men whom I think were
eventually caught undertaking that heinous act of clubbing the seals to death down
south—this happened about 18 months ago, maybe 2 years ago now. Actually, when
people show a lack of empathy towards animals in that way —albeit these animals were
out in the wild, not someone’s pet —they almost certainly have that same lack of
empathy towards others in vulnerable situations, like children, like other fellow human
beings, like women in their lives as well.
So I think it is very important not only for the issues of animal welfare, which in its
own right is very important, and for the issues that many other members have pointed
3164 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
out about how we are placed within the internatio nal market and how animal welfare is
seen in those terms, but it is also important because we know of the impact and the
direct correlation and relationship between people who get a buzz out of hurting animals
and how that probably means that they get the same buzz out of hurting, and have the
same lack of empathy for, their fellow human beings. I am not going to take up too
much more of Parliament’s time. This is an important measure not only for animals but
for people. It is important for our place in the  international market. Labour supports its
passing.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: I just find it absolutely
amazing that when Opposition members speak in support of a Govern ment bill, they
make such good sense. So I just want to commend Sue Moroney’s on some of her
thoughts there, and also—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Oh, be careful—be careful.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Yes, be careful. I have been warned to be careful.  That is
right. You will not get any more credit from me.
The Animal Welfare Amendment Bill is a very important bill, I think, for most New
Zealanders—well, all New Zealanders —and, certainly, for those who have a kind
consideration and thought towards anim als. In fact, about 70 percent of New Zealand
households have a pet, and I was just thinking about the pets that I have had throughout
my life. I started off with tadpoles. I am sure that everybody else here might have had a
tadpole in their room, in a lit tle jar with a bit of oxygen weed. Then I had guinea pigs,
cats, and calves. I had a pet pig once, called Patsy. I had lambs, horses, and dogs, of
course. All of these things, I think—

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Horses in your bedroom?

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: —have made me a very empathetic person. Thank you very
much, Ms Moroney.
I think that there is some validity in the comment that the way we treat our animals is
indicative of the sorts of attitudes we have towards ourselves —human beings—and it is
always good to see animals treated with respect and care. I think that in our country we
are horrified when we see abuse and cruelty to animals. It comes across our TV screens
far too often, and there is an outcry when despicable things are done.  I think it is
indicative of the fact that New Zealand is, by and large, a very decent society. So it is no
wonder that we are bringing through the House this piece of legislation, by and large
with support right across the House, wanting to improve the st ate and the being of
animals. I am sure that there are going to be differences on some finer points —as
different members have spoken about—but, by and large, we are together on this.
One of the things that my colleague Barbara Kuriger said —she understands animals
very well, she being from a dairy background —was that this bill talks about the
sentience of animals: their ability to feel, to perceive, and to experience. I think that the
more science reveals this, the more of an obligation there is upon humanit y to deal with
animals in a very humane way. I think also that the comments made by Damien
O’Connor are pertinent, in that we live in a world that consumes protein. So that is the
other balance of it. There are some people who abhor the thought of a steak or a ham
sandwich or, you know, sausages on a barbecue. But, you would say that—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Oh!

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: It would not be Mr Faafoi, by the look of it. He is a man
who would like a beautiful lamb curry, no doubt, and also a steak on a barbecue, or a
beef sandwich.
But the other side of it is that we understand that animals, whether they produce
dairy products, wool, milk, or meat, have contributed to our way of life and to our
economy here —to the point where each year around 50 percent of export earnings
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3165
comes from animals and animal products. I think that is the reality. For myself,
whenever I go to the supermarket, I always buy eggs that are free range. That is because
I believe in animal welfare, and also because the y seem to be the biggest and the nicest
eggs. I think there is something in that; that we can have not only a reputation around
positive animal welfare but also products that are far superior because of it. I think
people in the industry need to realise that they will not be hurt by the transition, but that,
actually, they will end up with products that are far superior. Having minimum
standards is an important aspect of this.
We pride ourselves on our place in the world with regard to animal welfare. There  is
a global charity, called World Animal Protection, that recently ranked 50 countries
across the world on their animal welfare standards. This index placed New Zealand in
first place, alongside the United Kingdom, Austria, and Switzerland. That is good t o
see, but we cannot afford to be complacent just because we might be top -ranking. We
must always look for improvements. One of the things Mr Mallard said was that this
transition away from caged hens is taking far too long —15 years. Well, in the bill, it is
10 years. Yes, there is an opportunity for a person to apply for a one -off exemption of 5
years, but for the vast majority, the strong expectation is that it should take no longer
than 10 years. I believe also that over that period of time you would have to have a good
reason for why it was going to take that long. There is no reason why people cannot be
proactive in moving ahead.
It is not just legislation that controls this; it is also market appetite. It is what the
market wants. Increasingly, we will  find, not only in New Zealand but also around the
world, that the market is deciding its food products and the products that animals
produce—milk or whatever it may be —based on ethical farming. That is the way the
world is going. People are listening to t hat message. If they are interested in staying in
business, they need to listen.
It has been 14 years since there was a review of the Animal Welfare Act, so this bill
is long overdue. It is a very important piece of legislation. This legislation will updat e
and strengthen animal welfare in New Zealand. This bill is the result of a
comprehensive review of the Animal Welfare Act 1999. It was found that although the
principles of the existing legislation are sound, the time is right to update and improve
how it operates.
In that regard, I want to put a shout out there for my former parliam entary colleague
from Taranaki - King, Country Shane Ardern, who was the chair of the Primary
Production Committee. He did a tremendous amount of work on this bill. We are ver y
pleased now to have Barbara Kuriger, who is the member for Taranaki - King Country.
That electorate starts in Taranaki and ends nearly in South Auckland. I think it is a
nation-size electorate.

items.speaker: Jacqui Dean
items.text: A townie.

items.speaker: JONATHAN YOUNG
items.text: Yes, that is right. And she is a townie in a dozen towns up
and down our country. Barbara has a tremendous knowledge of and experience in
animal welfare, and it is great to have her in our caucus.
Minimum standards are important. Sometimes it is a real shame that you have to
legislate for minimum standards. You would hope that people would always, all the
time, be seeking to be the best and to develop and promote excellence in their industry.
But minimum standards of animal care do change over tim e, as scientific views lift on
what animal management practices are and on what is acceptable. An example of this is,
of course, what has recently captured the attention of New Zealanders, through
campaigns, and that is the use of sow stalls and battery ca ges—both of which are being
phased out. I think that is an important point to make.
3166 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
When transitioning from one type of farming practice to another, we have to
acknowledge that it is an expensive process. We have put into this bill a transitional
period of time. The purists might be upset at that and they might say: “Do it tomorrow.
Do it whatever the expense is. You just have to do it.” Not only do we need to consider
the well-being of our farming and poultry industries but we also need to understand that
the way of life that has been passed on to New Zealanders is something that we need to
protect. These transitional measures are being put in place because we do expect a
transition, but we are not going to do it just tomorrow, although we expect the indus try
to be proactive in this and make every effort to do it in a very timely way. Thank you.

items.speaker: RINO TIRIKATENE
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Speaker. I am
pleased to make the penultimate contribution in the third reading of the Animal Welfare
Amendment Bill. Even though I am not a member of the Primary Production
Committee, I know that this is a very, very important piece of legislation that we are
debating in the House today. It fur ther enhances our reputation as a quality food -
producing nation and exporter to markets around the world. It is a very important piece
of legislation.
We have heard in previous contributions that we as Kiwis feel very deeply about
animal welfare, and that is true. We have heard that two -thirds of households have pets.
We have heard that our export industries are largely underpinned by our food
production and our food product exports. I need not go into the detail of how important
it is in terms of our way of life and our standard of living that we do have strong
primary industries. We are fair -minded as Kiwis. We do like to see our animals treated
well. We are horrified when we see examples of abuse conducted on animals whether it
be on farms or in other si tuations. All of those matters are sought to be addressed
through this bill. We are supporting this bill based on that underlying principle and
policy.
Again we have heard numerous contributions from the Government side of the
House about the importance o f animal welfare in terms of our primary industries, but
again it has failed to even mention the importance of the seafood industry to our
country. I repeat that the seafood industry is very important. It is a $1.5 billion export
industry, and it is very i mportant in terms of the communities that it services. I think of
communities in my own electorate, such as Bluff or Kaikōura, or even over on the
Chatham Islands. It is a very important industry.
Animal welfare, under the application of this bill, is equ ally important to the seafood
industry. The No. 1 export product in the seafood industry now is live lobster. The very
fact that our lobster, which is potted here in the waters of Aotearoa, has to live in a tank
in a restaurant, principally in North Asia, is incentive enough for the industry to ensure
that the animals are absolutely treated with the highest standards of handling and
transportation all the way from —dare I say it —a rock over on the Chatham Islands
through to their handling on the plane to Asia.
The seafood industry has come about only in the last, say, 15 to 20 years. It is an
industry that has flourished, and now the No.1 product in our seafood industry is
lobster, and that is principally based on animal welfare, handling, and the catch methods
that are applied to live lobster. I am very pleased to say that the fishing industry has a
very good relationship with the Ministry for Primary Industries in terms of the
protocols, or codes of practice, that are in place, for example, for live lobster.  I would
imagine that the industry is looking forward to those codes of practice eventually being
put into regulation, again because the value lies in the very fact that the product has to
be live. That is where the value lies, and that is where the premiu m is paid to our
exporters. Ultimately, the returns flow back to our fishing industry, our fishers and their
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3167
families, through the very fact that that lobster is handled and is received live by our
customers.
It does not really stop there because opportun ities abound for further live exports.
We know that there are small bits of trade that are happening around live pāua exports.
We have significant live shellfish exports that take place. All of these are enhancing the
value that we are earning as a seafood  industry, which ultimately benefits our country.
The one area of opportunity that is yet to be developed is in the live fin fish export
trade. If you go into any restaurant in North Asia, in China and southern China
especially, live fish is a very much hi ghly prized dish in the Chinese market. If we are
able to actually export live fish, that can turn a low - value species fish in New Zealand
into a high -value fish, just by ensuring that we look after that fish or that animal, and
making sure that it is delivered in good condition to the customer.
It not only goes to the fact that the fish is alive but it goes further in terms of the
appearance. Our customers in North Asia like colourful fish. They like stripes; they like
distinctive looking and highly pri zed fish that will end up on their plates. Opportunities
abound for our seafood industry and I know that it will be working with the Ministry for
Primary Industries to ensure that there are very appropriate regulations or codes of
practice put in place to ensure that we can unlock the value to generate further foreign
exchange earnings, which will ultimately benefit our nation.
This is a very important piece of legislation. I do, though, want to take issue with the
Minister for Primary Industries, because I do believe he was being slightly disingenuous
in his comments about how the Government is doing so much to support animal welfare
and enforcement. The Minister mentioned that there have been extra front -line animal
protection officers appointed, or put on to the job, to ensure that there would be on -farm
inspections, compliance, and the like. But that is not entirely correct because a fair
portion of the actual animal welfare inspectors that the Ministry for Primary Industries
does engage at the moment, o r employ, are actually fisheries officers. They are those
good men and women whose job is to actually detect and investigate breaches of our
fisheries legislation. Yet those fisheries officers are now being shifted into roles that
require them to be animal  welfare inspectors as well, or biosecurity officers to
investigate incursions that take place. Again, the fact that the Government is, sort of,
fudging the numbers in terms of what is actually going into the front line is slightly
disingenuous.
Finally, can I also say that the Minister has talked about the fact that resources are
going into animal inspections. Can I say that when it comes to fisheries, the fishing
industry pays over $35 million each year in cost -recovery compliance, and $10 million
of those cost-recovery levies that are imposed on, and paid by, the fishing industry is
supposed to go on compliance. Unfortunately, now we are finding that the fisheries
officers are having to be animal welfare inspectors as well. It is easy to take money
from an industry, but the Government needs to make sure that it is actually delivering
services to that industry for those costs. Thank you.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: I am very pleased to stand in the third
reading of the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill. When I was contemplating what I
would say in my contribution to this third reading, I went back, as always, to my
electorate, which is a large southern rural electorate that is a big producer of a number
of commodity products, which are duly exported overseas.
This led me to think about an occasion when I was in Hong Kong. I was taken to a
wet market and then to a dry market and supermarkets to have a look at primary
produce, particularly New Zealand beef and lamb at the time. I was very kindly
chaperoned by a local gentleman who was an importer of New Zealand beef and lamb
products and who was a local representative of Beef and Lamb New Zealand. Many
3168 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015
tourists go to the we t markets because you can see chickens being slaughtered right
there, and there are concrete floors. People go to the market and buy each meal because
of the culture and because they like the freshest of food. We went from the wet markets
on to a supermark et where New Zealand beef and lamb —in this instance, lamb  in
particular—was packaged for Hong Kong consumers, as it is packaged for Singaporean
consumers, European consumers, Chinese consumers, or wherever it is in the world that
New Zealand exports its animal products.
A couple of things struck me, and I reflected on a couple of aspects that I think relate
to this bill. One of them was the context around the meat product —and it was lamb in
this case. It was that the offering on sale was a package maybe twice that size, and there
were little slithers of thinly sliced lamb that were being sold. I was thinking: “Gosh, that
doesn’t look like a leg of lamb.”, which is what I’m used to buying or growing. But it is
the form in which the Hong Kong consumer buys the lamb for the dinner that night, and
it might end up being a hotpot, which, from memory, is one of the dishes that New
Zealand lamb is used in. So I noted the differences in expectations of the different
markets for our product, and I also noticed, when  I was looking at the labelling, that
New Zealand sells itself on having not only a wonderful environment and a clean, green
environment—which, I have to say, this Government—

items.speaker: Stuart Nash
items.text: Has destroyed.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: —is doing a  lot to enhance. You see, there we have the
Opposition, because it is the Opposition and it can only think to oppose, saying
“destroyed”.
Let me say to that member of the Opposition that this Government has done much
more to enhance the quality of our envi ronment—and particularly of water —than any.
In fact, if I recollect, the Labour Government in the previous term had its water plan of
action. Does anybody who has been around here for a while remember Labour’s water
plan of action? Well, it was so bad —so b ad—that officials at the Ministry for the
Environment termed it, in public, the water plan—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. I am relating this  to the bill
because of our international reputation in terms of quality. Although we do have some
parties in the House that would seek to destroy New Zealand’s international reputation,
this Government is working very strongly to enhance our international  reputation, and
this Animal Welfare Amendment Bill certainly adds to our reputation.
I know when speaking to some of our vets, for example, in and around the Waitaki
district that they have long been concerned —particularly those who are involved in the
export markets and who service the farmers, farming operations, and freezing works
that export internationally. They are absolutely aware of and support not only New
Zealand’s efforts to enhance our environmental reputation —because this is “New
Zealand Inc.”, after all —but also the need for us to maintain our reputation for good
animal husbandry standards. And I believe we do.
What I have also seen over the years, particularly around the Waitaki Valley, is the
expansion of dairying as a result of irrigation —another wonderful initiative of this
Government in supporting this development. It is not only supporting it but also
providing incentive funds, and research and development funds for the development of
irrigation, which is increasing productivity and jobs in the regions. Particularly, I want
to zero in on the Waitaki Valley because we now have irrigation from the top of the
valley—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: This is a third reading speech.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker. What that has meant is that we
now have dairy farming expansion along the main road. When you have dairy farming
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3169
expansion along the main road, the travelling public —both visitors and New Zealand
citizens alike—get to see farming operations up close. In fact, people will often stop and
park their cars to take photos of dairy cows and sheep when they can find them —there
are fewer sheep in my area than there used to be. One of the consequences of having
dairy farming on show is that animal husbandry, as of necessity, needs to lift its game,
consequentially—not just because it can be seen from the main road and it is New
Zealand’s reputation at stake but also because farming has lifted its game substantially
over the past few years, and that is just my observation.
I did not sit on the select committee that considered this bill —I know that a number
of members here did—so I have not had the opportunity to scrutinise fully this bill. But
I am pleased that one of the obje ctives of the bill is to provide for clear and enforceable
standards of animal welfare. In that, I do hope that attention was paid to the growth of
smallholdings and hobby farmers in New Zealand. I think that Federated Farmers have
often raised the point t hat small farmers also need to have a high standard of animal
husbandry. It may not be that they are exporting —probably not; the likelihood of small
farms exporting is probably pretty low —but none the less, even if those animals are
being raised for home kill or on-farm killing, or for sending down to the local abattoir to
be killed and then dressed at the butcher and then sent home again, which is what we
used to do when we had a small farm, the level of animal husbandry needs to be
maintained by that sector as well.
I did a visit to Alliance Group’s Pukeuri freezing works some years ago —probably 4
or 5 years ago. This was just as the local MP, because I was interested in the export of
lamb, and they tried to play a trick on me at Pukeuri. We went right to the top of the
chain—and it is quite a long trek from the bottom, where they cut up the cuts with the
saws, all the way up back to the kill. This is a halal plant, and so the sheep were killed
very humanely. In fact, they had no idea what was coming —so it was a very humane
kill—and then they proceeded down the line. I could see the workers looking at me —a
local sheila turning up —and thinking: “Who does she think she is —the local MP? I
know, we’ll get her.”
As the sheep was coming down the line, it came time  to top the sheep’s head off.
What the freezing workers did was pop it on the ground looking at me, with the hope of
my saying: “Oh, isn’t it awful. It’s a sheep’s head.” Well, little did they know that we
had been involved in home killing down on the farm  for 20 years or so by that stage, so
that did not work. But I have to say that I know a lot of the freezing workers out at
Pukeuri, which is probably why they played the trick on me. I have to say that I know
Pukeuri freezing works very well. I also know Silver Fern Farms up at the northern end
of my electorate. I have met with the management. I have met with the freezing
workers. They do uphold the highest standards of animal welfare, because they have to.
They understand that for the animals’ sake it is important and also that in terms of our
international reputation and our export markets it is critical. Thank you.
Bill read a third time.
SOCIAL ASSISTANCE (PORTABILITY TO COOK ISLANDS, NIUE, AND
TOKELAU) BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 29 April.

items.speaker: CARMEL SEPULONI
items.text: Kia orana, fakalofa lahi atu, and
taloha ni. It is a privilege to speak to this bill, the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook
3170 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 5 May 2015
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill, and out of respect for our Pacific brothers and sisters
to whom this bill relates, I greet this House in those three languages.
I want to start by contextualising this bill. Many New Zealanders are, actually,
unaware of the unique relationship that New Zealand has with our Cook Island, Niuean,
and Tokelauan nations. Those three Island nations hav e a constitutional relationship
with New Zealand, which I am sure we are aware of but which many people outside of
this House have no knowledge of. They are technically part of the Realm of New
Zealand. As such, they have free association with New Zealand and are New Zealand
citizens by right. They can move freely between their Island homes and ours. As such,
we have a responsibility as a Parliament to make sure that we exercise the same duty of
care to them as we do to New Zealand - based citizens.
It is appropriate to recognise the service of men and women from those countries to
our country —particularly in light of the recent Anzac Day commemorations. Our
Pacific Realm brothers and sisters fought alongside New Zealanders during World War
I and World War I I—many of them under our flag, the New Zealand flag. The
contributions that they have made to this country, whether to our economy, our sports
fields, our workforce, our academia, our arts, or through fighting for this country, are
unquestionable. The Labo ur Party and, I think, this whole Parliament value the unique
relationship that we have with these countries and will do what is required to honour
that relationship.
In brief, this bill will give effect to the Government policy on portability of New
Zealand superannuation and the veterans pension to the Cook Islands, Niue, and
Tokelau. This is an omnibus bill that seeks to amend the New Zealand Superannuation
and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and the Social
Security Act 1964. The aim of this bill is to allow eligible people who live in the Cook
Islands, Niue, or Tokelau to apply from any of those countries for New Zealand
superannuation or the veterans pension and to be paid those benefits in those countries
or in other specified Pacific countries.
In August 2013 the Hon Murray McCully, Minister of Foreign Affairs, announced
changes to the special portability arrangement that would allow eligible residents to
apply for their pension or veterans pension from the Cook Islands, Niu e, or Tokelau.
Under the current rules, people wishing to retire to the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau
have to be resident and present in New Zealand at the age of 65. Residents of those
countries or that territory would still need to qualify for New Zeala nd superannuation.
They must have been resident and present in New Zealand for more than 10 years since
