The concern about the siloed Government approach that Steven Joyce raised is raised
in the paper by officials —the 38-page list of concerns that they have put in front of the
House—as are the privacy concerns that the bill presents. Identity theft in the US has
been a problem with similar systems, and we see that this is something that concerns
also the officials who are advising on the bill. I have no doubt —no doubt at all in my
mind—that my colleague Clare Curran will have a little more to say about the
Government’s track record on privacy issues and the risks that are presented by identity
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3191
theft. That is her specialist area, and  I am sure she will tell us a little more about that in
her contribution.
The repeated registration processes at the moment in dealing with the Government
cost New Zealand businesses up to $34 million in lost productivity every year, says the
Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment estimate in the papers we have been
supplied with. The ministry’s concern is that this unique identifier will not become a
unique identifier because of the way it is implemented, but that instead it will join the
list of other business numbers produced by the Government that are part of this constant
churn of reregistration, of working out which number to deal with when you are dealing
with the Government, rather than being the simple system that ought to be in place.
Again, it says: “Maintaining core business data with government agencies costs
businesses up to $26 million each year; between 50 and 60 percent of business details
are replicated on over 250 government forms.” These are shocking numbers. This is the
shocking reality of a Government that seems to be out of ideas. It has been very slow to
move on these issues, and here again is moving with a half-baked solution.
I think that perhaps one of the most telling paragraphs in this regulatory impact
statement is paragr aph 16 in here. It states: “The NZBN has already been allocated to
companies in New Zealand. Ministers would like to extend the NZBN to all businesses
to enable a digitally-based economic infrastructure.” That is all well and good, but then
it says: “Our options are therefore constrained to consideration of the best way to extend
the NZBN to all businesses.” Therein lies the rub. The officials have recognised that
despite their 38 pages and further nine pages of concerns, Ministers are determined to
press ahead with this, regardless of the consequences. They want to be seen to be doing
something about making business easier and business compliance easier, but the real
test will be when the rubber hits the road, and I am sure we will hear from businesses
when they present to the select committee on whether this will really work for them.
This is a Government, of course, that came in strong on promises but seems to be
becoming stronger and stronger on excuses. It is a Government that seems to be tired
and out o f ideas. Now we have some half -baked ones being thrown up. We hope they
can be knocked into shape in the select committee so that they really do make a
difference for business in New Zealand because we do need our small business sector to
prosper for the g ood of all New Zealand. We will support this bill to the select
committee, and we will see what comes of it there. Labour will be concerned to see that
it really does make life simpler for those people who risk their shirt every day in order
to better thei r own lot, and to better the lot of the families around them and the people
they care about—the New Zealand business people. Thank you very much.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: It is a great pleasure to rise to speak on this first reading
of the New Zealand Business Number Bill. Before I actually talk a little bit about the
substance of the bill, I would like to commend the member who just sat down, David
Clark. I look forward to working with him and his colleagues opposite in the Commerce
Committee because I think we do actually work quite well together. Having said that, I
commend the member for saying that he does not like an extra layer of bureaucracy. I
think the member came  in in 2011 and does not really remember the times when the
previous Labour Government was in power and there were extreme layers of
bureaucracy that this Government has been spending a lot of time unravelling.
This New Zealand Business Number Bill is par t of the Government’s Better Public
Services agenda. It aims to reduce the cost to businesses of dealing with the
Government by 25 percent by 2017. I know that Dr Clark, just before he sat down, said
that he wants this to benefit the hard -working community—people who work for their
families, and, you know, everyone. That is everyone, not just businesses. He mentioned
the fact that there are already 1.1 million New Zealand Business Numbers extended to
3192 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
companies, and what this bill does is to extend it even f urther, to those that are not
necessarily companies—to those sole traders, partners, and trusts that also need to have
this number in order to operate better and take the benefit from what we are doing.
All key Government agencies that work regularly with  businesses will be required to
recognise and use the New Zealand Business Number by 2017. I actually have to
applaud that. The New Zealand Business Number is a 13 -digit number —a single,
unique identifier in a New Zealand - specific numerical series provid ed by GS1, which
is a global standards organisation. Each number uniquely identifies a business and may
be used in interactions with the Government and also with other businesses. The bill’s
purpose is to enable certain business entities to obtain or be al located with a New
Zealand Business Number. The New Zealand Business Number will make it easier,
quicker, and less complicated for businesses to interact with the Government.
I guess it is sort of like going back to one’s country of birth. My country of b irth
actually has a registration number for all citizens who are born there. We are identified
with a unique number for ourselves, as well as the birth date and the year that we are
born. We are actually identified by a number. I suppose that is how the so cial security
number works in the United States. To make sure that your unique number actually is
specifically for you, Mr Deputy Speaker, you and I would have a different number so
that you and I would not be confused. This is exactly the kind of idea, ef fect, that this
New Zealand Business Number will have on businesses, so that businesses will not be
confused—so that one business will not be confused with another. They will have a
unique number, specific to their business.
This has significance because New Zealand Business Numbers will make it easier for
businesses to work and interact with the Government as well. Businesses will no longer
have to continuously update their data with a myriad of different Government databases,
as businesses currently have  to use multiple numbers issued by different Government
agencies. I think of when I did a company search when I was a journalist. Every time I
logged on to try to find a company, I was given a number. Every time I did it again, I
was given another number, and another number. It was a constant numbers game. If I
had one number identifying myself as a constant user of that website, and I was
identified as a specific person who was allowed to use and connect with the
Government agency, I think it would have made life so much easier.
Also, I think, small businesses operating in New Zealand are often sole traders that
have to do everything. Not only do they have to work the job but also they have to
invoice, do marketing, and drive as well. Often time is of the essence, and time spent
dealing with office work and dealing with administration means time that is not spent
on making the dollars for their families and their businesses. Anything that we can do to
reduce the number that is spent on administration is som ething that is great, I think. As
working mothers, even when we are doing internet banking or mobile banking, when
we have an app that can actually identify our payees immediately so that we do not have
to punch in the numbers all the time or constantly, i t reduces the time that we spend on
the internet doing these things. So for a business that is actually spending a lot of time
on admin, if we can at least do something to reduce the time that it is spending on
admin, I think that is something that is wonderful.
I say that, specifically for the ethnic migrant communities who do business, admin is
an added burden, often, because of the language barriers. This time spent on admin is
extra, on top of the language issues that they already face. So if we can ma ke life easier
for them, I think it is a wonderful thing.
The bill sets up a New Zealand Business Number Register, where business
information will be held, publicly viewable, and searchable. However, it is also
designed to protect the security and confide ntiality of information under this bill, and
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3193
the privacy of individuals in business. I think that is paramount. I agree with the
member Dr David Clark, who actually talked about the security issue. I think we all
worry about the security issue.

items.speaker: Kanwaljit Singh Bakshi
items.text: You should have taken his number.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I look slightly different from him, I think. I think the security issue
is a very important one, and nobody wants a breach and identity theft. We have had
issues, even before this Business Number. We have had in the past instances where
people’s identities had been stolen, and I think that will continue to happen. We try to
put security protection in there to actually prevent people from stealing other people’s
identities, but when somebody purposely goes out to steal somebody else’s identity,
with the pu rpose of committing a crime, I am unsure as to whether anything could
actually prevent them from doing so. So it will be very interesting to hear the public
submissions on this bill. I look forward to the discussions that the select committee will
have on these issues. I look forward to the advice we will get on that particular aspect of
the bill.
In the future, once the regime is fully implemented, businesses will be able to update
their details in one place. That has to be a good thing —to automatically u pdate others
without businesses having to go through a complicated and time -consuming process, as
I had earlier alluded to. This means less time and effort on Government administration
and more time for business owners to focus their efforts on productivit y, growth, and
exporting their goods. Having been to Korea to sign a free -trade agreement deal, I think
anybody who can grow their business, grow New Zealand, is doing a great job, and we
should reduce the workload that they have in admin.
This is a great bill. I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: This is a fascinating bill. I am
actually really looking forward to the discussion in the Commerce Committee on this,
because, as the Minister for Economic Development said in his opening remarks, it is
really about modernising the way that businesses interact with the Government—

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Potentially.

items.speaker: CLARE CURRAN
items.text: —potentially—and tryin g to provide the best possible
framework for that to happen. Labour is supporting this bill to the select committee; you
have already heard that.
I have mixed views on my first reading of the bill, the regulatory impact statement,
and some of the submissi ons that went into the consultation around the development of
this bill. On the one hand, I think the modernising of that relationship is critical; on the
other hand, you have got to have in place the checks and balances to protect the privacy
of businesses and those who sit behind the businesses. And you have got to ensure that
you have got that balance right. On my first reading of the bill and the information
accompanying it I am not sure that that balance is right.
To put that in context with the enthu siasm of the Minister getting up and talking
about how, you know, it is all a great new world and everyone will have a New Zealand
Business Number, and it is all going to make things work a lot more smoothly, etc., I
think you have got to look at the track  record of this Government around its
management of IT across the Government —or its lack of management of IT processes
across the Government —and also its management of privacy and its devaluing of
privacy. I am certainly looking forward to the contribution s that will be made by
submitters on this bill, because this is where the rubber hits the road in terms of the
ability of the Government to act in an efficient and modern way while ensuring that the
entities that it is relating to are protected.
The phras e that came to mind when I was reading this bill was that it has the
potential to be a big data -grab. That is where I would be raising questions and doing a
3194 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
bit of flag -waving. This is the era of big data. This is the era of data analytics, of the
ability of entities to use their ability to get as much data as possible to give them
leverage. The Government is a big entity. How it manages the data that it gets from its
citizens and from businesses is a matter of trust. It is a very important relationship of
trust. My concern is around where the checks and balances lie in this piece of
legislation.
I will use the analogy of security and privacy. In any society it is absolutely critical
that you have got an equal relationship between security and privacy. At t he moment—
and for those who are listening to Parliament by radio, I am holding up my hands in an
equal way—in any society, security and privacy should be equal pillars. In our society,
the security side has gone up in terms of the way that national securit y legislation has
been given more of a priority, and personal privacy has been given a lesser priority.
Well, what we are talking about in this bill is the privacy of companies, of businesses,
and of entities, and my concern is that there could be some com promising of that
privacy under this bill. What we have to ensure is that there is level pegging around
privacy and the ability for the Government to gather data and to use that data, and
around what that data is being used for.
Just to illustrate that, I am going to quote from the Cabinet paper that lies behind this
piece of legislation. This is all about the scope of this piece of legislation. It says: “We
propose: extending the NZBN to all entities trading in the New Zealand economy,
including sole trad ers, non -incorporated partnerships and trading trusts, and to state
sector and not -for-profit entities; businesses not to be charged for allocation of an
NZBN or to remain on the NZBN register; a new legal register, managed by MBIE,”.
The most important pa rt of that proposal is to extend the New Zealand Business
Number to all entities trading in the New Zealand economy, including sole traders, etc.
So what that means is that the scope of this bill includes the individuals who are
operating as companies, and  there are concerns raised within the regulatory impact
statement around that —around what that actually means and what the implications of
that are.
There are concerns raised around whether or not it is compulsory to be on this
register, and there are con cerns raised around what sort of information is being
collected. All of those things are absolutely critical. In this day and age it is time for us
to have this debate. Therefore, my mixed views around this bill are such that I am
concerned about the track record of this Government. But I certainly think that it is time
to have this discussion. As I said, this is the era of big data, and the ability to collect
data is really important, but it should be done in the most ethical manner —the manner
befitting a Government in a democratic society, one that is progressive and one that puts
privacy at the top of its agenda. This Government does not put privacy at the top of its
agenda, and this is going to be the challenge in this debate.
I just want to draw the Hou se’s attention to the regulatory impact statement, where it
says—this is in the table below paragraph 22 of the regulatory impact statement —that
“Overall privacy risks to individuals and cost to society of identity fraud are likely to
outweigh benefits to business and to government”. This is actually being specified in
the regulatory impact statement as being a key risk. The Privacy Commissioner did
provide advice, alongside other entities such as Business New Zealand. It is noted that
the bill takes into account some of that advice, but it certainly does not take into account
all of it. So that is why the submissions from the Privacy Commissioner and anyone
who cares about privacy are going to be very important.
In the regulatory impact statement the Priva cy Commissioner has set out a series of
issues that he thinks are critical, which includes that this bill should include “a clear
statement of purpose for the NZBN and the register that is not overly broad or unclear; a
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3195
specific limitation that restricts t he use of the NZBN to business purposes only and a
prohibition on its use for non -business purposes such as social service purposes; a
definition of the personal information that may be collected; clear maintenance of the
Privacy Act prohibition … against an agency requiring an individual to disclose a
unique identifier for a purpose other than that for which it was issued; [and] an explicit
prohibition against agencies using the NZBN for a purpose other than that set out in
legislation”. I am not sure that  that exists in this legislation. Finally, the Privacy
Commissioner says that “an explicit prohibition to prevent agencies from requiring an
individual to provide a New Zealand Business Number in order to receive”—

items.speaker: Mr DE PUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member, but her time has
expired.

items.speaker: KANWALJIT SINGH BAKSHI
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity to
speak on the first reading of the Ne w Zealand Business Number Bill. First of all, I
would like to congratulate the Minister for Economic Development, the Hon Steven
Joyce, who has initiated the process of best practice in New Zealand. This legislation
allows the allocation of unique identification numbers to businesses such as sole traders,
partnerships, and trustees of trusts. This National -led Government has done a lot of
fantastic work in the past 6 years. This current legislation will further enhance the
capability of providing better pub lic services to all New Zealanders. Providing better
public services, of course, is one of National’s key priorities.
This National -led Government is in no doubt that we need to continually strive to
improve New Zealand’s economic performance if we are to continue to live the
enviable Kiwi lifestyle. In our economic performance as a country, that will determine
whether we have jobs, our incomes are on the rise, our standards of living continue to
improve, and we provide top-notch services that all Kiwis need and are truly entitled to.
By way of this legislation, it is estimated that the Government will reduce the cost of
doing business by 25 percent by the year 2017. This will, in my mind, without doubt
lead to a more competitive and productive economy. That is what is required.
We need to create opportunities for businesses. Small businesses that are engaged in
export have increased from 13 percent in 2007 to 21 percent in 2014. Similarly,
medium-sized businesses that are engaged in export markets increased from 21 percent
in 2007 to over 28 percent in 2014. It shows that businesses are growing and looking
towards export, and that is what we need. We need more jobs, we need more growth,
and we need new markets.
This Government has been focused in the past 7 y ears on opening up doors for
businesses to the international market. The recent signing of the free -trade agreement
with South Korea is an example of where we have created opportunities for other small
and medium sized  businesses. The easier and the simple r we make it for businesses  to
operate, the more time and energy we give to our entrepreneurs towards the expansion
of their businesses, and towards using innovative ideas to create products and services
that put New Zealand on the world map. The chain eff ect of all this, of course, is a no -
brainer. We are creating highly skilled and high -paying jobs for our current and future
generations. These jobs will create products and services that will build our exports,
increase innovation, make our workplaces and lives safer, and build our natural
resources and infrastructure for all of us to make use of.  The effect of our pragmatic
approach towards assisting Kiwi businesses and Kiwis with our economic management
will ensure that the world-leading growth performances that New Zealand has shown in
the past couple of years turns into a long-term, sustainable future for our economy.
This legislation will mean that rather than updating their data on a number of media,
businesses will need to use just a single medium.  The New Zealand Business Number
will lead to smart administration solutions for all stakeholders —businesses, suppliers,
3196 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
and Government. This will save time and effort, allowing all to focus on the real work.
Furthermore, this information will be shared among st Government agencies, so that
each time a business needs to interact with a Government agency, it will need to provide
its New Zealand Business Number. There will no longer be a requirement to fill out
multiple forms and go through bureaucratic rigmarole . We are also working closely
with our Australian counterparts towards developing mutually recognisable Australian
business numbers.
Even in our conservative estimate, New Zealand businesses stand to save $60 million
with this single piece of legislation. It is now up to businesses to take up this
opportunity. The sooner all of them sign up, the sooner benefits will flow to all
businesses. As I said at the start of my speech, this is only one of the several positive
pieces of legislation that this National -led Government has presented in this House and
to New Zealanders. I hope that during the select committee process we will have more
interaction with businesses and see how they can benefit. With these words, I commend
this bill to the House.

items.speaker: JAMES SHAW
items.text: It is a pleasure to stand to speak on the New Zealand
Business Number Bill. The overarching aim of the Green Party’s economic
development policy is to facilitate the transition to a smart, green econom y, and so, to
that end, initiatives to support businesses to reduce their time and administration costs
are to be welcomed. The Green Party will be supporting the New Zealand Business
Number Bill.
Before I get into why we are going to be supporting the bil l, I just want to set a little
bit of context. A number of previous speakers have spoken about the intended benefits,
mostly to do with the efficiency gains that may be available to businesses as a result of
having these unique business identifying numbers. In terms of the number of businesses
out there, some really useful information that came up in the regulatory impact
statement is that there are 1.1 million companies already in New Zealand, 500,000 to
600,000 of which are actively trading, and that thes e companies already have business
numbers. But in addition to that there is another entire half of trading relationships in
New Zealand that are organisations that are not companies. So trusts make up 15
percent of trading relationships in New Zealand, sol e traders make up 19 percent,
partnerships make up 12 percent, and 4 percent is made up of Government agencies,
non-Government organisations, and social enterprises.
So there is a significant number —as many as half of all businesses in New
Zealand—that ar e not currently covered by the existing business numbers that are
already out there. I want to pick up, in particular, on the sole traders and the freelancers,
because they obviously cover a huge portion of New Zealand’s business people, and, in
fact, of o ur total population. There are, by some estimates, 270,000 or so sole traders,
freelancers, one -person companies, and so on. So for those individuals —and having
spent much of the last 10 years of my life as a freelancer —the administrative burden
that comes  when there is only you to run your business and to interact with various
agencies and so on is significant, because every moment that is taken out of my day as a
freelancer dealing with just data entry is an hour that I cannot spend growing my
business.
One of the interesting opportunities in this bill, if it was to cover sole traders, is the
idea of an aggregator effect —being able to, essentially, pull together some bargaining
power across all of those sole traders and freelancers around in New Zealand. I f we had
better access to those people and were able to identify them more clearly, it is
conceivable that we could actually build further services for them and maybe bring
some other costs down —for example, insurance costs or even energy costs, and things
like that.
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3197
It does, however, raise a question of privacy, which I will come to in a minute, and
which some other speakers have already referred to. One of the other benefits that may
be available from this, which is also privacy -related, is the idea that consumers and
employees who have been hard -done-by by some businesses may find it easier to get
recourse to justice if those businesses are easier to track, because there is a sector of our
society in which businesses change their names, or shut up shop an d reopen over the
road, and so on, in order to avoid, for example, court judgment costs. So one of the
benefits of this approach may be that people will actually have more access to justice if
they have been hard-done-by.
All of those things do bring us ba ck to this question of privacy. If there are
something like a quarter of a million or more freelancers and sole traders and so on in
New Zealand, that is nearly one in eight people in the entire country, and most of those
people will be operating their businesses from home. So the question of their residential
address and contact details being tied to their company does raise some privacy
concerns for a very substantial portion of the New Zealand public. It becomes a sort of
proxy personal identity number f or a significant portion of our population. So we do
have some questions about how the data will be managed, what the security and
integrity of that data is, and so on. Of course, this is not an issue that is unique to this
particular initiative, but as has been amply demonstrated across a number of agencies, it
is a real concern.
The other concern that we have, which was raised in the regulatory impact statement,
is about whether this initiative will actually achieve the stated objective —that is, to
increase efficiency. The Government has talked about something like up to $34 million
worth of costs that could be mitigated across the entire economy. That is actually not a
terribly large number, of course, when you consider the overall trading economy.
Apparently, there are no other countries that the Ministry of Business, Innovation
and Employment has been able to find that have the experience of having unique
identifying numbers for their businesses where they have been able to quantify the
efficiency gains to businesses, so there does not seem to be a clear precedent. Although
we have been able to estimate that $34 million worth of benefits are available if we go
down this path, we are not sure whether that will actually eventuate. Other countries’
experience does seem to say that unique identifying numbers have been good for
increasing e-business services. That will clearly be an increased benefit, and you can see
how that will be available to businesses that are using these numbers.
So we do have some  concerns, particularly in the domain of privacy, and it will be
very interesting to see the submissions that come through on the bill and to see how
those go, and to see also the extent to which we are actually confident that, having put
in place this sys tem, New Zealand businesses will be able to capitalise on the savings
that we think that they may be able to.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, it does seem like a very sensible initiative
and pretty uncontroversial, generally. Any initiative that is sensible and does not carry a
great deal of risk and that helps to reduce costs or facilitates the reduction of
administrative time for small businesses, particularly for sole traders and freelancers, we
would like to support. With that, I commend the bill to the House.

items.speaker: FLETCHER TABUTEAU
items.text: Thank you for the opportunity this evening.
I would like to suggest to some of the members who spoke on behalf of the Government
this evening that the prospective benefits of this bill should not be overplayed, and that
we should take this in full consideration and give it the due benefit of time and the input
from business itself. Let us not oversell it, but, on the other hand, after years as a  sole
trader myself and as a business mentor in my local community, I do have to say that one
3198 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
of the common problems that is raised again and again is this compliance issue —this
conversation with Government agencies, and the repetitive nature of it.
There is a lot of common sense behind this piece of legislation. On the other hand,
New Zealand First is worried about several points that do need to be raised this evening.
This bill is necessary for the furthering of the business numbering scheme started in
December 2013. In that short time there has been a huge and broad comprehensive
uptake from New Zealand companies, as has been mentioned several times tonight —
approximately 1.1 million companies, which reflects about half a million actually
operating, active companies at this moment.
This bill would move this number beyond these registered companies, and take it
into the realm of small business —sole traders, partnerships, and trusts were mentioned.
New Zealand First believes they should be active participant s in this scheme. We would
suggest to the business community itself that it is a commendable and necessary system.
Why? Because its ultimate goal is to ensure that there is an improvement in efficiency
in business. This bill and its numbering system are ab out improving the interface
between the Government and said business. So when the goal is to make conversation
between the Government and companies—and now small businesses, like sole traders—
that little bit easier, then New Zealand First will lend its sup port, especially if that
conversation, which most small businesses dread anyway, does not have to happen
again and again, almost ad infinitum, with Government department after Government
department.
This bill has arisen primarily from the Government’s laud able goals about meeting
Better Public Services targets, particularly result No. 9. This specifically means that the
Government should aim to reduce the cost for businesses of having to deal directly with
the Government. This Business Number initiative was  one of the first initiatives arising
from the Better Public Services targets, which is great to see.

items.speaker: But I tell you this
items.text: New Zealand First nearly did not support this bill, even through to
this stage in the House. Here we have on the one hand the Governm ent telling
businesses that the only way that this initiative will work is with rapid and broad uptake
and that providing a better Public Service requires businesses to commit, and then, on
the other hand, I have here before me this document. I hope it was  not the New Zealand
First copy issued by the Government, but this is the regulatory impact statement that I
was provided with, and this is an example of several of the pages provided in the
regulatory impact statement. I have shown this evidence before th e House, and the
particular page I have shown is a device used to measure the efficacy of such pieces of
legislation, and what is the first thing that I notice? These blacked -out pieces of paper
that run all throughout the documentation, with no explanation.
Again, I hope that this is not just the one that was given to New Zealand First, but, on
the other hand, I hope that this is not indicative of the information provided to the
Opposition and to the New Zealand public. This page, which is one of many, is
supposed to show us the building of this New Zealand Business Number system and
Government agency uptake.
What this actually shows us is a Government that is not transparent, a Government
that is not willing to engage, and a Government that does not understand the meaning of
arrogance. What this page shows us is a Government that is not prepared for us to see
the Government agency uptake or, perhaps, the lack thereof. What is it exactly that we
are not seeing? How can the Opposition and how can the public u nderstand just what
this legislation will achieve, or hopes to achieve, if this kind of information is the case?
We know that business will want to have this legislation tidied up. It still needs some
work, and perhaps as we move forward the information pr ovided—or not, as the case
may be—will become available to the Opposition and to members of the public.
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3199
Despite redacted info, and despite issues around its current form in terms of the bill
itself, New Zealand First can see that the intent of this bill is  sensible and reasonable,
and so supporting it through its first reading is a practical step. We hope that then
everyone will understand just what it is that the Government hopes to achieve, but that
will mean that this Government actually needs to engage and work and talk with the
New Zealand public.
The problem that this bill seeks to address is that Government agencies currently take
a siloed approach to dealing with business. This results in duplication and inefficiencies.
So legislation that seeks to r emove duplication and inefficiency is to be commended.
However, New Zealand First would add its voice to the concerns raised around privacy
and, in particular, the privacy of individuals, whether they are sole traders or partners in
a business. This Govern ment’s recent track record around the implementation of good
and sound legislation has, in my opinion, not been that solid. Here is another bill where
getting it right from the outset is absolutely critical in order for the stated outcomes to
be achieved, but there also needs to be consideration and finely crafted legislation that
allows the work to be done but with the privacy of the individual being paramount. So
the data collected must be for business purposes only. Some of the members on this side
of th e House spoke in quite a lot of detail about privacy, and I would support that
further consideration.
Businesses want joined -up Government services and certainty and less confusion
when interacting with the Government. They want an economic infrastructure that better
enables and supports their business. This must be foremost in the minds of the select
committee members and the Minister as the bill proceeds through the House. Let this
number not be just yet another number that businesses have to record and u se to
interface with Government department after Government department.
New Zealand First also sees this piece of legislation as an opportunity —an
opportunity to crack down on the abuse of the bankruptcy system in this country. There
are too many examples where individuals are getting away with too much and they are
not being held to account. We hope that this legislation will ensure that individuals will
become accountable, and we would suggest that this could be done, at least initially, by
linking the business number to the insolvency register, for example.
New Zealand First will support this bill through its first reading, and we ask that this
Government please keep in mind its promise of open transparency, and that it is also
mindful of the individual and their right to privacy. Thank you.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National—Tāmaki): I am pleased to stand to take a call on
this first reading of the New Zealand Business Number Bill. I am actually quite pleased
to speak after the previous speaker, Fletcher Tabuteau, and, in fact, other members who
have spoken before, because I think thi s bill is being given the due consideration
already in its first reading that it deserves, particularly as it moves towards the
Commerce Committee.
I think no one is philosophically opposed, as I can hear it, at the moment against the
notion of having a si ngular number to identify a business. There are naturally some
questions that are arising around privacy and how that will be handled, but I think we on
this side of the House are very proud of the National Party’s engagement with business,
be it large, medium, or small. I know that over many recent weeks, that enthusiasm —in
particular, by the small and medium enterprises —has been shown by the countless
questions given to the Hon Craig Foss and an attempt to continue to show the really
good work that Nation al proudly does with small to medium sized enterprises. I
welcome more questions, not only from this side but, of course, from the Opposition,
once it has finished reading and working out what it is all about.
3200 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
What I have to say as the MP for Tāmaki is that I am very fortunate to have a number
of business owners in the electorate. Tāmaki is not a place of a number of businesses
running per se, other than the usual likes of restaurants and cafes and various activities,
but a lot of Auckland business owners are there—

items.speaker: Andrew Bayly
items.text: A great place.
SIMON O ’CONNOR: A great place, indeed. But although they are pleased with
what is happening within governmental procedures around business, they still want
more change. One of the funda mental areas that comes up is how we can work better in
a digital developing environment. I think one of the key elements of this to make it
happen—I am going to use two analogies in this speech —and to make businesses more
effective and efficient in a digi tal environment, is through the likes of a single business
number.
The first analogy I would draw the House’s attention to is obviously in the health
sector. As the chair of the Health Committee, it is something that I am interested in, the
notion of a national health number. We have had that for a number of years. I think it is
very analogous to this bill —the ability to have a single number that enables the
Government and others to identify a particular person or entity and, in the health
context, of course, to provide the care that is necessary. Like anything that comes down
to a singular number, it often becomes very concerning how it is going to be used or
misused. I think if we look at the health example, those issues really have not come up.
In fact, in more recent weeks —and if it is slightly tangential, I hope the House will
forgive me—in the Health Committee we have had a series of questions raised around
privacy to do with the Health (Protection) Amendment Bill  and the notion of contact
tracing. So if someone has an infectious disease, how do you reach out and make sure
that those who have been infected are well looked after and identified? Some people
were very, very concerned that using a single number, the National Health Index (NHI),
may actually breach someone’s privacy, but expert after expert, lobbyist after lobbyist,
said that, actually, the NHI, this particular single number, is an incredibly strong factor,
if you will, enabling us to provide good and right care, and that it has in the past b een
rightfully used.
So I think, in terms of the New Zealand Business Number, this bill, and the concerns
of privacy, we can turn to the health sector and see an example there of something that
is working rather well. The other element —another metaphor co mes in this case from
the Ministry of Social Development, in which I worked for a number of years. So many
people come into that department, again, with a single number, or are meant to come
into the department with a single number. First and foremost you treat them as an
individual. They come before you as a Mary Smith or as a Joe Jackson, and you engage
with them there. But as we move, again, into a digital environment, you need a number
to enable them to access the systems.
I mention that because, again, like the health number, it is a way to identify, but what
is also important—and I think this Government is clear on it —is that you also need the
systems in the background. In the Ministry of Social Development days, if someone
came in through Work and Income or StudyLink, you had two computer systems to deal
with—the old DOS-based system called SWIFTT and simultaneously a new Windows -
based system called, I think, UCV2. The irony of someone working on the front line
was that if one single person came in, ev en with their client number, you still had to use
two completely different systems to try to work out their full and correct entitlement. So
I use that as a caveat around this bill that although we move, quite rightly, to a single
number to identify busine sses, I think that, from my experience, we want to make sure
that the systems in the background are appropriate, because there is no point in having
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3201
one New Zealand Business Number if we are going to have a multiplicity of systems in
the background—it will just confuse things.
When I go out into the electorate or travel around the country, businesses want to
work more efficiently. They want to, ultimately, save costs, and we as consumers want
to see costs saved because if the business is doing well and can produce something more
cheaply, then, paradoxically, we get it cheaper, as well. Businesses have been asking for
a while now for this single business number, something that they can just use if they
want to call up the Inland Revenue Department, or if they  want to call up Work and
Income, if they are taking a young person on, say, for a role through the myriad of
activities we have there, so the business owners can ring up and be instantly identified.
They know exactly what clients are involved. If they are  going to be calling up even
something like the Commerce Commission —I am not exactly sure how far this
Business Number will be shared across Government departments. I am looking toward
the chair of the select committee, Melissa Lee. I am sure that is somet hing that we will
be looking at as a select committee as this goes through and asking what Government
departments will be using and accessing this number. How will they be interrelating?
But it is very clear, when I have talked to my constituents back in t he fine seat of
Tāmaki, that they want something like this, the ability to just call up.
Some have noted already —and it is more in their personal context —that they are
using the RealMe system. Without being too advertorial, it is where you basically go
down to the post office, or the like, and sign yourself up for a digital identity.

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: If the post office is still open.
SIMON O ’CONNOR: I am very happy to say that post offices are still open,
thriving, and well loved in my electorate. I cannot speak for that honourable member’s,
but they are incredibly well loved. I have to actually thank New Zealand Post for the
engagement that it is giving. I believe, actually, that it is a former member of that party
who is the chair, is it not? Is it Michael Cullen?

items.speaker: Hon Craig Foss
items.text: He’s been closing more than he’s opened.
SIMON O’CONNOR: Oh, he has been closing more than he has opened. That is
very interesting. But anyway, we digress —we digress. We were talking about RealMe.
Again, it is an ability for individual New Zealanders to go down to establish their digital
identity, which means they can walk into a bank, for example, or certain New Zealand
Post services, the Inland Revenue Department, and o ther places to actually access their
services. That is exactly analogous to the New Zealand Business Number Bill that,
actually, a range of New Zealand businesses, large and small, will be able to seek a
number so that they too can most primarily, I would suggest, go online and access the
services that they need.
This is part of the Better Public Services agenda of this Government. It is something
that the Government has been following right since it was elected in 2008, and
something I have been pleased to  be associated with since being elected in 2011. It is
Result 9, for those boffins who are very keen to be looking at the documents, and I am
sure Megan Woods is on to it now. She is going to be going through that paper looking
for Result 9. [Bell rung] Excellent! For whom does the bell toll? We are here to deliver
better public services—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Come on, you can do ten. Keep going.
SIMON O’CONNOR: We are going to do our best, you see. It is all about numbers,
you see. Ten is important. It is around Result 9 where we are delivering better public
services to business customers, and one of the goals we have given to ourselves is to
reduce the cost to businesses dealing with the Government by 25 percent in 2017. That
is only 2 years away. It is something we are very keen on.
3202 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
The business number system is  for a range of groups in New Zealand.  As we said, it
is obviously a unique identifier primarily aimed at the corporate and public entities, and
those that are unincorporated. There is a bit of talk in the bill around natural persons. In
other words, if you have established a body corporate, I assume, or sole trade in a
different name through your trust arrangements, those too can obtain a Business
Number. I think, quite importantly too for those New Zealanders who operate multiple
sole-trading corporate entities and the like, they will be able to obtain several numbers
for those entities. Again, the whole purpose of this bill is to make things easier.
We do note, because it has not been picked up by other speakers, that there is a
whole area within this bill around offences. It is one thing, obviously, to put something
in place, but when you are making laws, making changes, for something as important as
business, you need to make sure that people are using these systems appropriately. We
have seen with other legislation in the House, particularly in the digital or the e -
commerce space, that it is a new area and it is fraught with difficulties, so the bill at the
moment is n oting that a person who commits an offence and who knowingly uses a
number that is a false New Zealand Business Number without a reasonable excuse
could be subject to a maximum penalty and conviction of up to $250,000. Although I
can see Opposition members  smiling, that is incredibly serious and none of us would
want to fall into this area.
There are also offences for people who make or give authorised statements or
documents to the registrar that are false. The integrity of a system like this is incredibly
important. It is like the integrity of the Government —the people know that that is fine
and secure; that is why we continue to ride high in the polls. But it is the same around
the things like RealMe. It has been the same as I talked at the start around t he National
Health Index number, and so forth. People need confidence in the system. So we are
very keen —very keen —that that confidence remains. I am conscious of time. The
numbers are against me. I sit down.

items.speaker: JULIE ANNE GENTER
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker. Tēnā koutou e
te Whare. The Green Party is supporting the New Zealand Business Number Bill. As
members of the House will know —I am sure they listen very closely to Green Party
speeches—the overarching aim of the Green Party’s economic policy is to facilitate a
transition to a smarter, greener, fairer economy —one that ensures that future
generations will have all the benefits that we have, and one that ensures that every
person in New  Zealand has every opportunity to be the best they can be and are not
undermined by, for example, a lack of money on the part of their parents.
Contrary to what our opponents claim, I would say an important part of this
transition is fostering strong New Zealand businesses, particularly those that work to
support communities and the environment. We want to ensure that they are able to do
so, and that they are not undermined by competition that undercuts them by increasing
pollution. To that end, I would sa y the Greens would be very supportive of any
initiatives that reduce the time and costs of doing business without compromising those
higher-level goals of creating a greener and fairer New Zealand.
This bill, on the face of it, looks like a smart initiati ve that should make doing
business easier and more efficient, especially for small to medium sized enterprises —
we think they are quite important. Assigning businesses one unique identifying number
that can be used for a number of different purposes is a se nsible way to reduce
administration costs and make it more efficient. It should make it simpler for businesses
themselves to interact with Government agencies as well as with each other. It could
enable Government to better collect and share information th at would enable targeted
services and policies for business.
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3203
We do, of course, have the same concerns that have been expressed by other
members here in the House tonight about the impacts on privacy, particularly as this
Government, the National Governmen t, has a poor record. We have seen a couple of
Ministers release private information held by Government agencies just to score
political points. We have some real concerns about what that could mean, having this
unique identifying number. Greater interacti on between sharing of data means that the
system becomes a little less resilient. There is this trade -off between efficiency and
resilience, generally, and so although we will have something that is more efficient it is
more susceptible to breaches of priv acy and, potentially, hacking. I note from the
regulatory impact statement that the Privacy Commissioner thought that most of the
privacy concerns, for example, could be addressed. That is something we will be
looking at very carefully and closely during the select committee process.
The devil really is in the detail as to whether or not this will pay off. Obviously, there
have been other moves towards centralisation like, for example, the Auckland super-city
merger, which was supposed to deliver benefits,  but in fact has made the bureaucracy
ever more unwieldy for your average citizen to deal with. So it all depends on how it is
implemented, and I think we will have to watch the submissions in the select committee
carefully and explore the different opportunities. I am sure it will be an iterative process,
if the bill is passed, of learning what works and what does not work.
I would say that the opportunities provided by getting Government agencies to not be
so siloed do not just apply to administration an d the savings costs. For example, in this
bill, according to the regulatory impact statement, we might see something like $30
million to $50 million in savings. When you spread that out across the entire economy,
that is not really a huge impact. I would s ay that the Green Party is interested in finding
even bigger savings for businesses and households in New Zealand. The big ones are
transport, buildings, and energy. If we did those things smarter—and we have the ability
to do that—then we know we could save billions of dollars each year for businesses and
households and reduce environmental pollution. I think surely those sorts of win -wins
are achievable in policy and are something that should be pursued by this Government
if it genuinely believes in long -term sustainable economic development that looks after
people and the environment.
So although we will be supporting this bill, I think that a smarter, greener approach
to policy across the board would deliver much greater savings to business and
households here in New Zealand and ensure that we protect all the things we really love
about New Zealand well into the future. Thank you.

items.speaker: Brett Hudson
items.text: Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Jacinda Ardern.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I am sorry to disappoint the member Brett Hudson;
I will be taking a call on this bill, on the New Zealand Business Number Bill.
I think it is important when discussing a bill like this that we keep at the top of our
minds the context in which business is  operating. It is with some, I guess, irony that we
are debating this bill, which is meant to be about improving the ease of doing business
and improving outcomes for business, when we are so close to a Budget that was
trumpeted by the Government as the Bu dget that would return us to surplus. That,
therefore, would demonstrate to the nation that the economy is in good heart, that the
books have been balanced, and that all is well in never -never land. That is not going to
be what this Budget delivers.
We are now hearing from a Minister of Finance, the one in whom the businesses are
meant to hold great faith, who is the same Minister who stood up in this House today
and likened balancing a Budget to weight loss, which I found extraordinary. So,
3204 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
apparently, if you set a goal of losing 10 kilograms but you reach only 9 kilograms, that
is the same as a Budget surplus not being reached. Well, you cannot be a little bit
pregnant, and the difference for business is that if a business is not able to balance its
books, then it is not just good enough that it had a go at it.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: Business numbers. It’s an identifier.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: So I do think it is important that the context be considered,
because in the Cabinet paper small busi nesses, Melissa Lee, that were asked about what
they thought about the business number legislation, which the Government is now
passing in this debate, said, actually —and this is relevant —that it was not the biggest
issue for them. So that is absolutely re levant. What is relevant to them is whether or not
we do have a well -performing economy that means that their business is doing well
within that context. That is what they want their Government to focus on. That is an
important measure; it absolutely is. M inister Foss knows, because his officials were the
ones who prepared that document and said: “Well, when we consulted with small
business, they weren’t convinced”—they were not convinced—“of the benefits it would
bring for them.”
I can see why they would s ay that, because when you come to Part 1 of the New
Zealand Business Number Bill, it sets out in its preliminary provisions the main
purposes of the bill, which include to “ … enable businesses in New Zealand to interact
more easily with government; and (b ) reduce the costs of business transactions in New
Zealand; and (c) establish and maintain a New Zealand business number register … ”.
There is very little detail on how that will explicitly deliver some of the cost savings
that the Government has been tru mpeting since year dot —very little detail on that
whatsoever. Yet if you directly compare that with some of the really tangible things that
have been put forward by members of the business community or the Institute of
Chartered Accountants, they have said : “Look, if you want to look for things that will
enable business to interact more easily with the Government, that will save them time,
that will save them money, adopt some of the proposal that the New Zealand Institute of
Chartered Accountants put up be fore the election.” They included things like no more
than 1 hour, no more than one form, making it really simple to file for the tax purposes
of the Government. They have set out some of those ideas in a really simple way for the
Government. That has not been picked up.
So if there are things that the New Zealand Business Number is going to deliver,
which we can tangibly say will deliver X amount of time savings, I am pretty sure small
business would like to hear about that, but that is not explicitly cont ained in this bill.
There are probably already areas where we could be sharing information without having
just that one number. I know Xero, for instance, has been putting a case to the
Government over things like allowing Xero to be used as a way of chann elling all the
information that Statistics New Zealand wants directly from Xero —a platform that so
many small businesses are using —to the Government. That would be a massive time
saving. Allowing Xero and things like Mind Your Own Business, for instance, t o speak
directly to the Inland Revenue Department would make a massive difference to those
small businesses.
So, yes, we are willing to explore this. We are willing to send the bill to the select
committee. You are trumpeting a big game here. Let us see what the bill is going to
deliver, but do not do it at the expense of some really practical ideas that the
Government could be delivering on now or at the expense of the bigger picture, which
ultimately is an economy that is delivering for our businesses.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: It is an absolute joy to rise to speak in support of the
New Zealand Business Number Bill in its first reading. For the benefit of the speaker
who has just resumed her seat, w ho is a bit worried that doing this to help business
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3205
might come at the expense of doing something else, well, seemingly unlike the Labour
Opposition, this is a side of the House that can walk and chew gum. We look forward to
doing a number of things, not j ust one at a time. This New Zealand Business Number is
really in part about the Government’s agenda of delivering Better Public Services to
New Zealand. It is an absolutely measurable and concrete way of driving better value
for New Zealanders, reducing co mpliance for businesses, and making it easier for
people and for businesses to engage with the Government.
This is a really simple concept. If you have a business, whether it is small, medium,
or large—but there is a greater compliance cost on small and m edium sized businesses,
I think everyone would argue —that business has to interact with a number of
Government agencies. We have picked just a few, just off the top of our heads.
Obviously, there is the Inland Revenue Department, and if your business perha ps is
employing a very varied workforce you might have Immigration New Zealand contacts,
you might have department of labour contacts, you will have ACC, you have got the
Companies Office—any number of Government agencies that even a small business or
a medium sized business may be obliged to have dealings with.
If you have got a situation where with every one of those agencies you have to have a
unique and different identifier, then it boggles the mind that anyone could suggest that
you need some sort of scientific methodology, rationale, and proof that somehow
having one identifier across all of them could be anything less than more productive and
more cost saving than having a different identifier with every single one of them. This is
exactly what this bill is delivering. It is delivering the one identifier that a business can
use in every dealing it has with any Government agency that it chooses to, or has to,
have dealings with.
That is a simple concept to grasp. It is something that will certainly be  grasped very
readily by small businesses to whom, I would argue, the constant interaction with
Government agencies is more of a bane than a boon to them. The idea that this will
streamline those interactions is something that businesses will welcome, and we are
very, very pleased to be delivering it for them.
One of the things that I think is very, very important about this, and I would make a
note about the previous speaker from the Greens, Julie Anne Genter, who raised issues
of privacy. One of the good  things about this is that supplying their core information
once, that information, the core information about that business, will be shared with
other agencies, and the business, if it needs to make an update, will be able to make the
update once at its p referred point. No longer will it have to advise every Government
agency about a change of address or some subtle change in purpose that the agency
might feel is important. The business will do it once at the agency of its choice, the one
where it likely d oes most of its business. It could be New Zealand Post. That is a
possibility. It will make that change once and that will proliferate across the agencies
that access that New Zealand Business Number.
The issue about data privacy, I think, shows that the members opposite do not
understand the data that is actually going to be captured behind the New Zealand
Business Number and that is going to be shared. That data is the legal entity name, its
registered address, a location identifier, a start date, the ty pe of entity that it is, and its
business status—whether it is active or inactive. There is not a great hacking potential in
that data. Businesses are not storing their customer addresses. They are not storing their
receipts. They are not storing their inv entories. They are not storing the heart of their
businesses. They are saying they are an active business, based at this address, and here
is their number. [ Interruption] Well, sure. I mean it is a bit of a worry if the hackers
want to get in and have a look at that.
3206 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
So you have got to wonder whether the Opposition members actually understand the
information that is going to be captured and shared, because based on what they have
been saying tonight, it does not look to me that they do.
But the point on t his is also that although we are expanding in this bill the New
Zealand Business Number eligibility across a broader range of business, it is worth
noting that we have actually already allocated about 1.1 million of these numbers to
registered companies to  date. In fact, we have got a reference group of about 1,200
small and medium sized businesses that we have been tracking progress with on the
New Zealand Business Number and how it has been working for them. The reports over
the last 6 months or so have reported back a net 7 percent reduction in reported effort in
their dealings with Government agencies since 2012.
So here we have it. We have got a reference group —actual businesses operating in
the real world—using the New Zealand Business Number. Their r eports show, and their
feedback to the Government shows, that this has had a net 7 percent productivity gain
for them in terms of their—well, a net saving for them in terms of their interactions with
the Government since 2012; that is a better way of putting it, I agree. That is definitely a
very, very positive thing for them to have experienced. I tell you what: if I were the
member opposite and I had a business and someone was offering me a 7 percent saving,

items.speaker: I would not be saying
items.text: “No, give me something m ore. Take this one away.” I would be
grasping it with both hands while doing something else as well to further improve my
business.

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: You understand business.

items.speaker: BRETT HUDSON
items.text: Well, thank you, Mr Bishop.
But I would just like to say in concluding that Opposition members have also made a
comment that is just a small thing. And at an estimate of $30 million to $60 million in
savings set against the entire economy, you could say that is a small thing, just as you
could say that half a billion dollars out of the entire GDP of New Zealand is a tiny thing
as well. You could say it is a very small thing, but it is part of a larger plan. It is not one
thing solely in isolation; it is one thing that is part of a plan. Like in ou r Business
Growth Agenda, for instance, there are between 350 and 400 initiatives in that plan that
go together to improve business outlook and promote growth and growth in
employment as well.
So this New Zealand Business Number is part of another plan. W e have already seen
things for small and medium sized businesses like www.business.govt.nz, which is a bit
of a one -stop shop for what a small or medium sized business needs to consider when
setting up and operating, or growing, a company in New Zealand in  respect of its
interactions and compliance obligations with Government agencies. Within that is a
thing called Compliance Matters. This is a tool that sets out for those businesses exactly
what their compliance obligations are, and points them in the dire ction of what they
need to do to make sure that they are compliant.
So let us take this in context. The New Zealand Business Number on its own is not
the only thing that this Government is doing to support small and medium sized
businesses. It is part of a much broader plan both for small businesses and for business
as a whole to promote economic growth in New Zealand and to help to raise confidence
and results in our businesses that lead to greater employment, as we have seen in the
past 12 months and earlier. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Thank you very much for the chance to speak to
this bill. I am looking forward to this bill going to the Commerce Committee because it
has been some time since we have dealt with a piece of legislation of any weight —not
that this piece of legislation is o f any weight. As we have said on this side, when you
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3207
look at what it does and the 7 years of Government that this party has behind it, and the
fact that we are 2 weeks out from an election—

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: From a Budget.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: —from a Budget, sorry—I wish it was an election—shows just how
tired this Government is. Two weeks out from the Budget, this is as good as it gets —a
plan to expand the national business number out beyond what has already gone out to
the public. It is, as Dr Clark said in his speech, a laudable effort to try to make the
interaction between business and Government as efficient as possible.
We have heard from both sides of the House about what kinds of savings we are
trying to get to make business i nteraction with the Government more efficient. But
some of the numbers still need to be fleshed out. You have got to think of it in the
context of what is being promised, and what will actually be delivered. Steven Joyce, in
his opening remarks, said that this piece of legislation will look to reduce the
compliance cost of business by about $60 million. That is nothing to sniff at. It is a
sizable amount of money.
But I think small businesses in New Zealand, 2 weeks out from a Budget, are looking
at more than the extension of the national business number programme. I think they will
be scratching their heads and thinking: “My God. Is this all this National Party has, 2
weeks out from an election?”.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: From a Budget.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: From a Budget—ha, ha! I will get that right eventually.
I would like to sympathise and empathise with some of the things that James Shaw
has said because, as he said in his speech, as a freelancer —I have experienced being a
freelancer as well—from time to time you can get slightly frustrated with the amount of
red tape and interaction you have with Government departments. We will look to the
select committee to flesh out, I guess, some more of the details as to what will be the
real benefit s to the sole traders, to those other small businesses that this national
business number may be extended out to. The select committee consideration will be
very interesting.
I also want to touch on something that Fletcher Tabuteau said. He talked about th e
lack of information and the abundance of redaction in the regulatory impact statement.
That starts pretty early on in the regulatory impact statement. There is a table, at point 5.
For the benefit of those at home, watching at 9.33 on Tuesday night, the line above the
table says: “The table below outlines the net benefits of the preferred options.” As you
can see, it has all been redacted. So maybe—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Blankety-blank.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Yes, in the words of Annette Ki ng, it says: “Blankety-blank, blank,
blank, blank”. Those are the net benefits of the preferred options of this bill. What is so
secret that the Government wants to redact even the net benefits of its preferred option
of this bill? What is going on, when t he Government wants to redact the net benefits of
this extension of a 13 -number programme? You have got to ask some serious questions
about that.
There are also some questions that we will be asking around the costs that are
incurred in this bill, because we have heard that $60 million figure from Steven Joyce.
But, again, in the regulatory impact statement—and if you will let me take some time to
read point 127. For some reason the number 127 has been redacted, but the point has
not been redacted. I do not know what is so secret about the number 127. I will read it—
I am assuming this is No. 127 —below this redaction: “The benefits to business of the
NZBN will only be realised when government agencies change their existing systems to
allow centralised registr ation of businesses and maintenance of their business details
through the NZBN system.” I will go on to the second page, which says: “Government
3208 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
agencies will incur costs in making these changes. It is not possible at this stage to
quantify these costs. In  many cases it may be possible to absorb costs within planned
upgrades of agency systems.”
There are two questions I have here, for when we get to the select committee
consideration. Can we please get an idea of what it will cost to change the systems
within the multitude of Government departments? If it is a huge cost, and we are
looking at saving roughly $60 million for these businesses, or more, then from my
maths that simply does not make sense. There is a track record for this Government
when it gets involved in multi-agency, complicated changes to IT systems.

items.speaker: Hon Todd McClay
items.text: That’s not true.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: Well, it is true. If you would like to dispute that, get up and take a
call. But it is true. This Government does  not have a good track record. Let us look at
some of the IT projects of note recently that it has bungled. The Inland Revenue
Department—who is in charge of inland revenue? The member just over there, who
said: “That’s not true.”

items.speaker: Chris Bishop
items.text: That’s not fair.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: You might think it is not fair, Mr Bishop, but unfortunately it is
true. It is true. I can see how the member might think that is unfair, but unfortunately his
actions and the actions of that ministry, and hi s decisions, are going to cost the New
Zealand taxpayer millions more, which they should not have to pay. There are also other
things that have been mentioned by other speakers, and I would like to talk to the point
around privacy. This regulatory impact statement also talks to that.
Again, and I am talking about the rolling out of IT programs, this Government does
not have a good track record when it comes to the privacy of the private information of
New Zealanders. What department is that? Oh, it is Todd McClay’s department again,
the Inland Revenue Department. Of course, it let a whole spreadsheet list go —just
flicked out in an email the details of hundreds of New Zealanders and their Inland
Revenue Department details. The department just nonchalantly ema iled them out into
the public. Then of course there was the Ministry of Social Development. Someone just
wandered into one of the offices, went to the publicly available booth, and helped
themselves to a lot of information. There are some serious questions  that need to be
asked in the select committee consideration around the safeguards and the privacy of
information to make sure that this Government is getting right, because in the past it has
got it so, so wrong.
This bill, as I said, tries to achieve a l audable aim in trying to make the interactions
of businesses and Government departments more streamlined, so they can save money
and therefore invest more money, pay their staff more, or enjoy more profit. The
example of New Zealand Post has been raised by  a number of speakers on that side of
the House. I just want to take this opportunity to talk about one local example of where
this Government is saying one thing and is doing another. I held a public meeting
recently about the future of the Raumati Beach PostShop, which this Government wants
to close down.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am going to invite the
member to bring his point back to this bill.

items.speaker: KRIS FAAFOI
items.text: I will. In the front seat of that public meeting was a local
businessman who wants to make his life easier with a State -owned enterprise, New
Zealand Post. But this Government, in demanding more of a profit from New Zealand
Post, is forcing the likes of community post shops in my electorate, in Raumati Beach—
which is not the strongest Labour safehold area in my electorate. In fact, the
businessman who spoke to me saying “Well done for bringing up the issue.” said he did
not vote for us, but he is unhappy with this Governm ent and the fact it is extracting
5 May 2015 New Zealand Business Number Bill 3209
more profit out of New Zealand Post and closing down a very important piece of
infrastructure in his community, the local post shop, so now he will not be having that
efficient interaction—

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: I really feel for the member Kris Faafoi
having to interrupt such a wonderful discourse of—whatever.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I did terminate the
member’s speech for being irrelevant. The member is inviting me to do it very early to
him.

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker, for that direction. Can I begin
by congratulating the Minister for Economic  Development on bringing this bill to the
House. Actually, as a businessman —or certainly a former businessman —having dealt
with the Inland Revenue Department and all of the other Government agencies, I think
this is very welcome news. It does not surprise me that, as has been claimed by the other
side of the House, small businesses do not recognise the benefit to them of a bill like
this. Often small businesses are so mired in the day -to-day running of their businesses
that they do not particularly think of  these things and they do not recognise the benefit
of them until they are actually upon them.
I have had experience with a business number, not in New Zealand, but with an
Australian part that we had to deal with in my wine business. Having a business nu mber
over there absolutely made things a lot easier. It seems to me that it is nonsensical that
we have not had one up until now. These little things that Governments do from time to
time, which may seem boring and not earth -shattering, do make a differenc e, and they
do move businesses forward. Those little parts of the New Zealand economy are
actually what drives New Zealand on. It is not the big businesses, as important as they
are to New Zealand’s economy. It is the little businesses that impact on most people in
New Zealand, so it is incumbent upon us to allow them to be as efficient as possible.
The New Zealand Business Number will do that.
I think one of the big things with this bill is, actually, how they are going to maintain
the New Zealand Busines s Number Register. That register is going to be kept by the
registrar appointed under the bill, and it will contain only business -related data. Certain
primary business data contained on the register for the entity must be publicly available
as follows. “[In] the case of a corporate or public entity ,—(i) the data listed in Part 1 of
Schedule 3”, which is “Legal entity name; Registered address; Location identifier;
NZBN; Start date; Kind of entity; Business status (eg, active or inactive)”, and “(ii) any
data prescribed by regulations that the entity elects to make publicly available or that is
otherwise available on a public register;”. “[I n] the case of an unincorporated entity ,—
(i) the data listed in Part 2 of Schedule 3”, which is “Location identifier; NZ BN; Start
date; Kind of entity; Business status (eg, active or inactive)” and “(ii) any data
prescribed by regulations that the entity elects to make publicly available.”
That all sounds like pretty mundane stuff, but I can assure you that once you have
filled out this information once and then you have to do it again —and sometimes four
or five times in a day —it can become pretty tiresome. For a small business —and this
will be rolled out to sole operators in time —it is going to make a tremendous difference
and free them up to do what it is we as an economy want them to do, which is get on
with business. That is what enables us to enjoy the lifestyle we do as a country and
enables us to have enough taxes to look after those people who cannot look after
themselves, which is something that many on the other side of the House claim to
champion.
I note that there are already 1.1 million businesses that have a New Zealand Business
Number, so this has already begun. This bill simply enables it to be rolled out more
widely. I think the small businesses are, quite rightly, the ones, as I said, that need to
3210 New Zealand Business Number Bill 5 May 2015
come on further with this. It will enable us to build a more competitive and productive
economy, which is something that we all benefit from, so I cannot see anyone  having
any issue with that.
Lifting business confidence is also part of the Business Growth Agenda, which this
all ties in very neatly with, and addresses issues that matter most to firms, particularly
building export markets, building capital markets, b uilding innovation, and building
skilled and safe workplaces. I note that this ties in, also, with the Financial Markets
Conduct Act, which allowed crowdfunding to come in. This all ties in with this New
