Zealand Business Number because, actually, that has been a great source of capital for
small businesses, and they have been able to raise funds—in fact, up to $2 million—that
way.

items.speaker: Carmel Sepuloni
items.text: Relevance?

items.speaker: STUART SMITH
items.text: It is great to be able to have all of this pulled int o the bill,
because the New Zealand Business Number enables all of that information to be equally
shared. I think that is really important, so it is very relevant.
Labour market statistics show that self -employed businesses grew by nearly 35,000
in the year to December 2014. If you think about that, there would be at least one person
involved with each. I do not know what the average size of small to medium sized
enterprises is in terms of people involved with them, but I would think it would be
seven or ei ght people maximum —[Interruption] Twenty, is it, and then right down to
one. I would say that the average would be three or four people, so that is a lot of people
involved in those businesses. So there is a significant increase in the numbers of people
involved in small to medium sized businesses.
A lot of small to medium sized businesses fail in their first year. I guess there is an
element of Darwinian selection there, and that is as it should be, because not all
businesses will survive —[Interruption] A bsolutely, but it is a great thing to get these
businesses up and running. One of the things that new businesses often struggle with is
the day -to-day management of their business —their data, filling in all of this
information—so it really is a great step forward, this bill, and with our 3.5 percent GDP
growth that we are running at the moment it is enabling businesses to grow across the
whole economy. I am sure that is something that the other side of the House will be
delighted about—that we have a Govern ment that is focused on business, focused on
growth, and focused on making those businesses able to get as much profit for the
amount of work that they do.
So it is with great pleasure, on that note —[Interruption] And with all the support I
am getting from the other side of the House, I commend this bill to the House.
Bill read a first time.
Bill referred to the Commerce Committee.
Second Reading

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: I move, That the
Environmental Reporting Bill be now read a second time . I want to begin by thanking
members of the Local Government and Environment Committee, particularly the
chairperson, Scott Simpson, and the Officers of Parliament Committee, for the very
sensible refinements that the select committee has made to this imp ortant bill. This bill
has its origins back in National’s Bluegreens —in our efforts to improve the integrity of
New Zealand’s “clean, green” brand. It was part of the policy that we put to the
electorate and I am pleased to be now in Parliament seeing it p rogress through into
legislation. We are actually the only OECD country to not have a statutory framework
5 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3211
for environmental reporting. It is an anomaly, out of step with New Zealand’s “clean,
green” brand. This new Act will rightly put our environmental ma nagement under
scrutiny and improve the integrity of New Zealand’s brand.
We should not underestimate the power of open reporting systems to improve
performance. I remember in my first term of Parliament New Zealand had had 30 years
of pretty appalling ma nagement of New Zealand’s public finances. The Public Finance
(Fiscal Responsibility) Amendment Act, requiring Governments of whatever political
flavour to be absolutely upfront with the electorate about the state of the Government’s
books, has been a game -changer in moving New Zealand from having some of the
worst public accounts in the world to having some of the best. I would also make the
consistent analogy with education. Members on this side of the House, as part of our
policy agenda, introduced the n ational standards legislation, which equally requires
open and transparent reporting of how well our children are doing at school, because we
believe that providing integrity and honest reporting actually helps improve
performance. It has been interesting in the years since 2009 to watch in both the
National Certificate of Educational Achievement results and those national standards a
consistent improvement in the way in which children are learning maths, learning to
read and write, and learning those basic  standards that are so important to New Zealand
achieving better in that area. This Environmental Reporting Bill is about an equally
significant area, where I think New Zealanders want us to do better as a country.
Having standardised reporting in areas l ike water quality, air quality, how well we
are doing in protecting our biodiversity and the survival of important species like the
kiwi, and what sort of job we are doing in managing our oceans —all those areas —in
my view is a very important step. I am pro ud to be part of a Government advancing that
step. It is part of a broader role in terms of what we have been doing as a Government in
strengthening the role of the institutions of, firstly, the Ministry for the Environment as
the policy maker, the environ mental equivalent of Treasury’s role in the economic
space, and, secondly, the Environmental Protection Authority, an agency that was
created by this Government to act as the effective independent regulator, not too
different to the role that is played by the Reserve Bank in the economic sphere. Finally,
just as we have an auditor, we also have an important role for the Parliamentary
Commissioner for the Environment, whose job it is to provide for the overall
independence of our system of environmental mana gement. It is my view that this bill
will actually strengthen those institutional structures, which will also play out well for
our country.
I want to talk to two controversies in the process of the bill’s being processed, to set
the record straight. Ther e are, unusually, parties in this Parliament that I thought would
support a good bill like this, which is absolutely well intended and is best practice by
OECD standards. However, a great deal has been made of clause 18. This is the
provision that sets dow n which topics will be reported. The controversy with which
members in the Green Party and the Labour Party justify their opposition to this bill is
that somehow there is something wrong with the Government’s Minister of Statistics
and Minister for the Env ironment setting the topic areas. The first thing I would point
out is that the legislation makes plain the five domain areas that those topics must cover.
The bill goes further, and requires a process of public consultation with the Government
Statistician, with the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, and with the
public, iwi, and local authorities about each of those topics.
My challenge for members who want to criticise clause 18 is this: the exact parallel
provisions exist in the finance ar ea. So, indeed, if it comes to measuring things like
GDP, the Consumers Price Index, or the labour index, there is no more role here for the
Minister of Statistics and the Minister for the Environment than there is in those parallel
3212 Environmental Reporting Bill 5 May 2015
areas. So why is it tha t they want to have a separate set of rules when it comes to
environmental reporting? I have never heard a member of the Opposition ever raise any
questions of integrity in the economic space about the equivalent of clause 18. Nor did
they do so in their 9  years in Government. So why would they do so here? I simply say
to this House that it is crude oppositional politics rather than actually trying to be
constructive.
The second issue that has been raised is why the bill does not provide for greenhouse
gas emissions, which, of course, are important to report. There is a very simple
explanation. New Zealand is a member of the United Nations Framework Convention
on Climate Change. It requires every single year that greenhouse gas emissions be
reported.

items.speaker: Hon David Cunliffe
items.text: You wouldn’t know it. Why’d you wreck the ETS, Nick? It’s
going to be your legacy, mate.

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: It might be a lesson for David Cunliffe that during the 9
years of the previous Government greenhouse gas emissions rose very steeply. Actually,
I would much rather, Mr Cunliffe, have our record on greenhouse gas emissions than
the previous Clark Government’s, which was all talk and no action. But my point is this,
to Mr Cunliffe and to members o pposite: the framework convention is enlisted in
legislation—the Climate Change Response Act. It requires every single year for us to
both report to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and to
table in this Parliament New Zealand’s gre enhouse gas emissions. So why would you
insist that there be another Act of Parliament to repeat those same reports? Are members
opposite really saying that the very robust process of independent, country auditing of
greenhouse gas emissions is not good en ough for them? If so, again I challenge them
and ask: why was it, then, good enough for them in Government? We are a party of
minimising bureaucracy, reporting information accurately, and doing it once and not
having repeat information in one document afte r another. And in my view the
provisions of the bill in that regard are absolutely sensible.
The last point I wish to make in respect of the role for Ministers and for Government
is let us not pretend there is not a cost with environment reporting. The re ality is that if
we are going to pass regulations requiring regional councils, district councils, and
ministries to collect environmental data —it is actually quite expensive to get good
quality data. The view that is put by Opposition parties, that somehow  parties that are
independent of the Government can make decisions about spending, breaks one of the
fundamental rules of the way in which our system of government works, and that is that
it is only the elected Government of the day that can commit to expe nditure, including
the expenditure on the collection of environmental data. The system that is provided for
in this bill is absolutely transparent, and if Governments of whatever political colour
attempt to misrepresent or not collect robust environmental data on the basis of
budgetary constraint, it will be as transparent as the day is light. That is proper and that
is why the bill is drafted in this way.
This is a good bill. This is a bill that will ensure that New Zealand does not just
brand itself internationally as being clean and green. This is a bill that will give honest,
open reporting on just how we are doing. It is the sort of bill that a National
Government supports. We are a practical Government that wants New Zealand
achieving economically and educationally, as well as in this environment space, and we
are proud to be a party that is making this significant change to our legislative as well as
our constitutional framework —how we manage those natural resources that are so
important to this country.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: It is not with pleasure that I rise to give
this speech. Labour will be opposing this legislation. It is not a position that we wanted
5 May 2015 Environmental Reporting Bill 3213
to be in. We did oppose the bill at its first reading. My predecessor in the role of Labour
spokesperson on the environment, Moana Mackey, made it very clear that we wanted to
work very hard during the select committee process to bring about the changes that
meant we could support it. I think there are very few people in the world who would not
support the stated purpose of the bill, but it is when you get into the detail of the bill that
the problems emerge.
As Dr Smith set out in his contribution, this is something that has  been on the books
of the National Government for a very long time. In fact, it was promised in its 2008
election manifesto that it was going to introduce environment reporting legislation that
required independent 5 -yearly state of the environment reports . Well, I guess that us
being here tonight means that perhaps this Government has beaten itself to a surplus in
terms of the Environment Reporting Bill, because that was also promised in the 2008
manifesto.
What this bill does not deliver is independent r eporting. For Dr Smith to say that he
challenges parties to justify why it is that it needs to be different —well, I would like to
hear from a Government contributor on this bill as to how it is that they disagree with
the vast majority of submitters, many of them very, very deep in the detail of this bill,
who had grave concerns about the independence of the mechanisms that are set up
under this legislation. We heard from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment, who had grave concerns around whet her or not this bill would deliver
independent decision making around which topics are to be covered.
I am of course referring to clause 18 of this bill, which is the central cause of
Labour’s inability to support this bill. You simply cannot have the Min ister for the
Environment and the Minister of Statistics making the decisions on what is to be
reported on and claim that you have independent reporting. What we have consistently
asked for, and will be asking for again, is that that decision be in the han ds of the
Secretary for the Environment and the Government Statistician —who does consult with
other people such as iwi, and such as the Parliamentary Commissioner for the
Environment—and that they arrive at what is to be reported on.
The Minister who has spoken was quite correct. We are the only country in the
OECD not to have this. We really wanted to be able to support this legislation and to
put in place robust and independent environmental reporting.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10 p.m.

TUESDAY, 5 MAY 2015 
Mr Speaker took the Chair at 2 p.m. 
Prayers. 
VISITORS 
Japan—2015 Prime Minister’s Fellow, Vice-Minister of Health, Labour and 
Welfare 
Mr SPEAKER : Honourable members, I am sure that members would wish to 
welcome Mr Gaku Hashimoto, Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Health, Labour and 
Welfare and Japanese Prime Minister’s Fellow 2015, who is present in the gallery. 
MOTIONS 
Congratulatory Message—Birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of 
Cambridge 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister) : I seek leave to move a motion without 
notice on the birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of Cambridge. 
Mr SPEAKER: Is there any objection to that course of action being followed? There 
is not. 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY : I move, That the House put on record its congratulations to 
Prince William, the Duke of Cambridge, and Catherine, Duchess of Cambridge, on the 
birth of Her Royal Highness Princess Charlotte of Cambridge.  The birth of a second 
child is an exciting time for a family. It is a time of great joy and immense celebration, 
and part of th at joy is observing the reaction of the older brother or sister as they meet 
the new little member of the family. I am sure that the duke and duchess are cherishing 
this special time with both Prince George and their new daughter. 
The birth of Prince George was one of the most eagerly anticipated in recent history. 
It is moving to see that the public is just as excited at the birth of the princess. I am sure 
she will bring the same delight as we watch her grow. It is a pleasure to observe the 
strong family unit bonded by love and mutual support that the duke and duchess are 
creating with their children. I have joined with other leaders across the Commonwealth 
and the world in congratulating Prince William and the duchess on the arrival of their 
daughter, and I am sure that the other members of this House and the public of New 
Zealand support the good wishes expressed to them. 
I would also like to note that in a few days’ time New Zealand will be welcoming 
His Royal Highness Prince Harry, who will be visiting our country for the first time. It 
will be an opportunity for New Zealanders to pass on personally their best wishes to the 
royal family on the birth of Princess Charlotte. New Zealand’s official gift to the royal 
couple is a handcrafted teddy bear and a box set of woollen baby items made from wool 
of unique Stansborough sheep bred in the Wairarapa. The teddy will be specially made 
by Cheryl Eldridge of Stansborough and will have the special touches to make it unique 
for the princess. I might add that it is in the colour of dusky pink. 
On behalf of the people of New Zealand, I am pleased to be able to put on the record 
of this House our congratulations to the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge and to Prince 
George, and to welcome the newest member of the royal family into the world. 
ANDREW LITTLE (Leader of the Opposition) : Speaking as the Leader of Her 
Majesty’s loyal Opposition, can I also join the Prime Minister and the many New 
Zealanders congratulating the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge on the birth of their 
second child, Princess Charlotte Elizabeth Diana. Welcoming a child into the world is a 
very happy occasion for any family. Princess Charlotte, of course, arrived under the 
3130 Motions 5 May 2015 
 
scrutiny of hundreds of media and millions more waiting in anticipation, including, of 
course, the street vendors keen to get their supplies of ceramic mugs and tea towels on 
to the streets’ shelves. 
As many in this House will know, I was actually in England for the  days leading up 
to the royal birth . Despite the fact that I am a committed republican, it did not stop my 
wife Leigh from insisting that I bring back a ceramic mug or tea towel, or several of 
them, but, sadly, that did not happen on this occasion. 
In spite of my personal views, I know that the Queen and her family are held in high 
regard by many New Zealanders. I acknowledge the important role different generations 
of the family are making today around the Commonwealth as standard -bearers for 
comity and community. For example, I note that Princess Charlotte’s grandfather Prince 
Charles, after whom I understand Princess Charlotte has been named, gave the most 
eloquent and touching addresses at the Gallipoli commemorations over Anzac weekend. 
I see that the new princess carries the name “Diana”. That will be greeted warmly by the 
millions who continue to hold her grandmother in high esteem for her charity work 
around the world. 
On behalf of the Labour Party I once again respectfully congratulate the Duke and 
Duchess on the birth of their daughter, Princess Charlotte, and look forward to meeting 
her uncle Prince Harry when he arrives this weekend.  
Dr KENNEDY GRAHAM (Green): The Green Party congratulates Prince William 
and the Duchess of Cambridge on the birth of their second child, Charlotte Elizabeth 
Diana, Princess of Cambridge. The birth of a happy and healthy baby girl is always a 
cause for joy, and the name “Charlotte” has, apparently, ranked first in recent years by 
way of choice for a girl’s name in New Zealand. But this royal baby is special for a 
particular reason. Charlotte will be the first female heir to the  British throne to have her 
place in the line of succession guaranteed over younger male siblings and other male 
heirs. Blissfully unaware she may be, but as she beams out on the world she personifies 
constitutional progress for the Realm of New Zealand.  
As we debate this motion today the New Zealand Flag Consideration Panel is starting 
its work. Whether changing the flag is necessary or not is a different issue, but that does 
show that New Zealanders are interested in discussing the issues that symbolise us as a 
nation and tell the story of who we are. The Green Party welcomes that debate. We 
should not take for granted that our symbols of nationhood today will be relevant 
tomorrow. We take this opportunity to wish the British royal family in London well. 
TRACEY MARTIN (Deputy Leader —NZ First) : Kia ora, Mr Speaker. New 
Zealand First joins with the rest of the House in extending our congratulations to the 
Duke and Duchess of Cambridge. W e welcome Charlotte Elizabeth Diana and we wish 
both her and her family, her older brother, and extended family a safe and happy life. 
Kia ora.  
Hon TE URUROA FLAVELL (Co -Leader—Māori Party) : Tēnā koe, Mr 
Speaker. Kia ora tātou. Ko tāku he whaiwhai haere i ngā mihi a te Pirimia ki te uri o 
Irihāpeti, kua puta mai ki te whaiao, ki Te Ao Mārama. 
[Thank you , Mr Speaker . Salutations to us . I am merely following up the Prime 
Minister’s sentiments to the descendant of Queen Elizabeth who has emerged into the 
world of light and understanding.] 
As a representative of some of Her Majesty’s Treaty partners, I stand to follow on 
from the Prime Minister’s statement and acknowledge the bir th of e kī ana te kōrero he 
taonga ki te ao [as it has been stated, a worldly treasure]. 
I acknowledge the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, but I probably want to pay more 
tribute to the grandparents, being a grandfather myself on the birth of my mokopuna. I n 
our household our mokopuna is the princess —in fact, she is probably the queen, to be 
5 May 2015 Motions 3131 
 
truthful, in everything that she does, from the time she wakes up until the time she goes 
to bed. So in our household she is the queen, not just the princess. I wish the m all the 
very best in the years ahead. In particular, I hope that the House thinks very much of the 
grandparents today, as we consider this very important last couple of days for the birth 
of a taonga ki te ao, arā noa atu ngā taonga o te ao [ a worldly tr easure, and there are 
many other treasures of the world]. Tēnā tātou katoa.  
DAVID SEYMOUR (Leader—ACT): On behalf of the ACT Party, I would like to 
offer our warmest congratulations to Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge on 
the birth of Princess Catherine— 
Hon Members: Charlotte. 
DAVID SEYMOUR : —sorry, Charlotte —a healthy,  strapping 8 pound, 3 ounce 
baby. Thank you.  
Motion agreed to. 
SPEAKER’S RULINGS 
Tabling of Documents—Procedure 
Mr SPEAKER : Last Thursday Metiria Turei raised a point of order seeking my 
advice on the procedure for seeking leave to table a document. To assist members, I 
have given this further consideration and I have also examined the rulings of previous 
Speakers. What I will require of members when seeking leave to table a document are 
three things, and that the members identify these three things in this order: the source of 
the document, when it was published or produced, and to very succinctly inform the 
House of its nature. This way an informed decision can be made by members as to 
whether the document should in fact be tabled.  
Seeking leave to table a document is not an opportunity to make a political statement 
that a member wishes to be heard. It is intended for placing before the House material 
that informs members of matters that are not otherwise readily available to them. Briefly 
describing for the House the nature of the document is not an opportunity to quote 
passages from it. If members persist in doing so, the leave will not be put to the House. 
CHRIS HIPKINS (Senior Whip —Labour): I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. 
That is a considered ruling and I understand the point you are raising. The only 
challenge for members in descri bing the document is that I think there must be some 
necessity to explain the relevance for tabling a document at that point. Otherwise, we 
can get into a situation where members can be seeking to table all sorts of things, and 
part of the narrowing -down o f the rules around tabling is to prevent that from 
happening. So although the description does need to be succinct, it also needs to relate 
the nature of the document to the question or the speech in question, otherwise it is 
simply a pointless exercise. 
Mr SPEAKER: I think my ruling is very clear. There is an opportunity to succinctly 
describe the nature of the document, and on various occasions that will require more 
depth than on other occasions. But I repeat the point that it is not the opportunity for 
members to make a political statement, which I see it being used for on many occasions. 
If I sense that that is the purpose of the member who is seeking to table the document, it 
is likely that the leave will not be put in the first place. 
ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Overseas Investment—Agriculture and Housing 
1. Rt Hon WINSTON PETERS (Leader —NZ First) to the Prime Minister: Does 
he stand by all his statements; if so, why? 
3132 Oral Questions 5 May 2015 
 
Rt Hon JOHN KEY (Prime Minister): Yes, because I believe them to be correct at 
the time they were made. 
Rt Hon Winston Peters : Does he stand by his statement that he would “hate to see 
New Zealanders as tenants i n their own country”; if so, why did his Government so

Inflation—Crown Revenue 
2. TIM MACINDOE (National —Hamilton West)  to the Minister of Finance : 
What reports has he received on low inflation in New Zealand, and how does that 
benefit households and businesses? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Minister of Finance): As the published figures have shown, 
New Zealan d is experiencing very low inflation —or, more accurately, in the last 6 
months actually we have had deflation. Usually in an economy growing at 3 percent, 
inflation is rising, not falling. However, it is good news for New Zealand households 
and businesses, which can expect to see interest rates and inflation stay lower for longer 
than they expected, and this is likely to help to reduce unemployment and sustain real 
wage growth. 
Tim Macindoe : What impact does lower than expected inflation have  on 
Government revenue? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Very low inflation and lower interest rates and lower 
commodity prices mean that growth in the dollar value of what New Zealand produces 
each year is a bit lower than expected. Treasury now expects that the dollar value of 
what we produce each year over the next 4 years will be around $15 billion less than 
forecast in Budget 2014, even though the economy will actually grow slightly faster 
than we expected in Budget 2014. This poses some real challenges for Government 
revenue, because it means less PAYE, less company tax, and less GST. In total, 
Treasury expects the Government will collect $4.5 billion less tax revenue over the next 
4 years than it expected at the last Budget. 
Grant Robertson : In light of that question and answer, is it in fact correct that 
“lower than expected inflation” actually means lower Government expenditure as well? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : As it turns out, the inflation impact on Government 
expenditure is considerably less than the impact on spending and the impact on tax 
revenue. That member had better figure it out, because his other members are always 
advocating more spending when he is advocating bigger surpluses. 
Tim Macindoe: How is lower revenue having an impact on the Government’s ability 
to return the books to surplus in 2014-15? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH : Back in December Treasury forecast that the deficit for the 
2014-15 year would be around $570 million, whi ch is just 0.2 percent of GDP. It is fair 
to say that the forecast for the 2014 -15 year has deteriorated a little since December, so 
we expect the Budget to forecast a slightly bigger deficit for 2014 -15, and a slightly 
smaller surplus for 2015 -16. So, whi le progress is slower than expected, we remain on 
track to achieve surpluses and to start repaying debt. 
Tim Macindoe: What steps has the Government taken to get on top of spending and 
return the books to balance? 
Hon BILL ENGLISH: The Government has been very thoughtful about its new 
spending, and very thoughtful about what drives existing spending. If you want a 
measure of that, in the last six Budgets, the total annual cost of new initiatives has been 
just under $3 billio n. By comparison, the last six Budgets of the previous Government 
totalled $20 billion of extra costs —$20 billion as opposed to $3 billion. But despite the 
fact that we have had very constrained spending, we have been delivering better public 
services with better results for New Zealanders.

HUMAN RIGHTS AMENDMENT BILL 
Second Reading 
Debate resumed from 26 March. 
ALFRED NGARO (National) : It is a privilege and an honour to take the final call 
in the second reading of the Human Rights Amendment Bill before the House. This bill 
obviously amends the Human Right s Act 1993. It has two particular areas of purpose. 
The first is to enable the establishment of a full -time commissioner with responsibility 
for leadership in disability rights within the Human Rights Commission and the second 
is to make changes to the rol e and the structure of the commission to strengthen its 
performance.  
People may not know that, actually, this was initiated on 20 October 2010. The 
Minister at that time was the Hon Tariana Turia. As the Minister for Disability Issues 
she announced the es tablishment of a full -time Disability Rights Commissioner within 
the commission, but to formally establish this role would indeed need an amendment to 
the Act. This provided an opportunity to review the structure of the Human Rights 
Commission and to explo re options for change in three key areas: firstly, in the 
composition of the commissioners who were there in place in its status quo; secondly, 
the governance arrangements; and, thirdly, the functions and powers of the commission  
itself.  
5 May 2015 Human Rights Amendment Bill 3147 
 
There were 42 sub missions that were made to the Justice and Electoral Comm ittee 
and 19 oral submissions that were submitted. I would just like to take us through some 
of those submissions that I think are important and that also give weight to the 
recommendations that have  been made by the Justice and Electoral Committee in 
particular. One of the areas was just in regard to one of the challenges of the 
improvements. In consultation with the commission and other Government agencies, 
the Ministry of Justice has identified som e improvements that could be made to the 
composition. These were in regard to improving efficiency, the lack of effectiveness of 
the current composition of part -time commissioners, the inflexibility resulting from the 
way that specialised commissioners rol es are provided for under the Act, and then, 
lastly, there sometimes being an unclear and incomplete description of the functions of 
the commissioners in the Act as it currently stands.  
There are a number of things that I think are quite important in this  legislation, 
especially for the disability community in particular. We know that New Zealand 
ratified the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities on 25 
September 2008. Article 33 of the convention requires States to “maintain,  strengthen, 
designate or establish within the State Party, a framework including one or more 
independent mechanisms, as appropriate, to promote, protect and monitor 
implementation of the present Convention.” We believe that the review and these 
amendments will definitely go a way to approving that.  
A full-time commissioner position with responsibility for leadership and disciplinary 
rights will be created within the commission, and we think this is quite critical. The 
creation of these roles requires an a mendment to the Act, as it currently enables 
commissioners formalised leadership roles in only two areas: race relations and equal 
employment opportunities. The changes to these roles, we think, are going to be quite 
significant. The Act currently provides  for full-time and part-time commissioners. This 
will be changed to permit a composition of three full -time commissioners, and then also 
up to five part -time commissioners who will be part of that composition as well. 
Although we are removing the statutory  roles of the Race Relations Commissioner and 
the Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner, we are requiring commissioners to 
be appointed to lead the work in these areas.  
I just want to quote from the departmental report from which we heard submission s, 
and, again, from the Chief Human Rights Commissioner himself. In 22 of those 
submissions they were in support, indeed, of having the establishment of a disabilities 
commissioner in particular. The Chief Human Rights Commissioner submitted that it is 
quite critically important to be addressing these issues for the disability community as 
well.  
Consultation with the Minister of Justice was also challenged. There was an issue in 
which we felt it would breach the Paris principles of independence of the Huma n Rights 
Commission. This was an issue of concern. In fact, 13 submitters opposed any reference 
to consultation with the Minister being included in this bill. Again, the Human Rights 
Commission actually submitted that this consultation with the Minister cu rrently occurs 
at present, so, in effect, it was not seen that there was a breach, in fact, in regard to the 
Paris principles of independence for the human rights commissioners.  
This bill will enable the chief commissioner to formally designate commission ers. 
We think this area here will then allow them to establish areas of importance that may 
be relevant in that current context in time for our communities. In some of the 42 
submissions that were made there were references to, for instance, areas of the r ights of 
women, and that potentially the Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner role 
could include looking at the rights and responsibilities for women under that as well. 
There was also another submission that talked about issues around the fairness in the 
3148 Human Rights Amendment Bill 5 May 2015 
 
Act around Treaty of Waitangi claims. That was another submission that was made. We 
feel that the amended changes will allow for the commissioner to be able —with 
consultation on the strategic direction of the commission —to potentially appoint part -
time commissioners to this role as well.  
There was some concern that was expressed around the rebranding and existence of 
the specialised commissioners by removing the titles of the Race Relations 
Commissioner and the Equal Employment Opportunities Commiss ioner, which may be 
perceived as lowering the profile of these particular areas of focus. We do not believe 
that the proposed changes will negatively impact on the commissioners’ leadership role 
of protecting and promoting these particular areas of importa nce as well. There will be 
identified commissioners leading the work in each area, and the commissioner will be 
the face and the contact point in being able to negotiate these areas of importance as 
well. 
We feel the recommendations that have been made ade quately address the issues of 
the review plus the concerns. We feel, as a select committee, that our recommendations, 
approved by the Minister, are appropriate but also give both the flexibility and the 
clarity for the commissioner to conduct his roles and  responsibilities. On behalf of the 
Government, I also do commend this bill to the House in its second reading.

them out of our food chain, keeping them out of places that we need to keep secure. We 
also have a great deal of problems with possums, particularly in our native bush and 
forest. Cats, stoats, and rats likewise cause g rievous damage to our native birds. There 
was some quite significant discussion on those topics during the course of the 
consideration of this bill in the select committee, and I think, again, they are well dealt 
with under the relevant codes that apply to those issues.  
In New Zealand we farm some 45 million animals —probably a lot more, in fact, but 
we have an official count of 45 million - odd. We dealt with numerous issues in respect 
of them, including —and I am not counting birds and things like that, so  I am not 
accounting for the poultry industry in that —microchipping, tagging, ear -marking, 
horses’ teeth, blacksmiths’ operations, and all sorts of operations that take place on a

their welfare codes. In my view, New Zealanders are a much mo re adaptable people. I

think there are a large number of those procedures that can be undertaken extremely

I want to talk, briefly, about the live export of animals. Clearly, we have an

I want to talk about codes of welfare for a moment. I have here the Dairy Cattle Code

I just want to talk very briefly about the Minister and the select committee.

Hon DAMIEN O ’CONNOR (Labour —West Coast - Tasman): I must say that,

the previous speaker, Ian McKelvie, is, of course, the chair —I did actually stand aside 
for the Hon Trevor Mallard, who takes the role of animal welfare within our caucus. So

Zealand’s production systems. As a passionate advocate for primary industries, I know 
the things that we need to protect, starting, of course, with biosecurity and food safety. 
Animal welfare probably comes third in terms of the hierarchy of the things that we

3152 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015 
 
Zealand is to continue to export food, then the people who have to pay —or should

way, and in a way that does minimum harm to the animals in the system for th e most 
part. We want to continue with that.  
We are making technical changes with the bill. We are addressing some tricky issues 
like the use of animals in the area of experimentation, and I will say a little bit more

The National Anima l Welfare Advisory Committee, the organisation referred to by

What has happened over recent years is we have moved —as a country and through 
legislation—to expand the areas in which chooks live to give them more movement and 
to give them more freedom. My colleague the Hon Trevor Mallard says that just about 
all those animals should have the right to go outside. We have some systems like that in 
the country but not all of them. If we were to move to those systems within a set period 
of 2, 3, 4, or 5 years, then there would be a cost to the consumer and the producer, and 
some might say that that is a perfectly reasonable cost. There is a reality, of course, in a 
low-paid economy, particularly under a National Government that seems to like zero -
hour contracts, that people cannot afford to pay for that food.  
There are transitional provisions here, and the exceptions and the extensions to what

The difficult issue of dairying is one that is yet to be resolved because o f some

I come back to the legislation. It does include some good objectives. One in

STUART SMITH (National —Kaikōura): It is a p leasure to speak on the Animal 
Welfare Amendment Bill. I was one of the new members to the Primary Production 
Committee and unfortunately did not go through any of the process with this bill, so I 
commend the members of the select committee for the fine jo b that they have done. 
Agriculture underpins our economy —in fact, it pays for our way of life. We would not 
enjoy the same standard of living that we enjoy now if it were not for cows and sheep, 
in particular. So I think to a large extent we ride on their backs in terms of our economic 
well-being. Agriculture earns $25 billion from livestock and it contributes to our 
economy. So it is absolutely huge in terms of New Zealand’s gross national product. I 
use the term gross national product deliberately. Too of ten we focus on GDP. Actually, 
“GNP” is how we pay our way in the world —and that term means “gross national 
product”, for anyone who is not familiar with that term. I think that I would like to see a 
lot more focus on that term.  
Animal welfare is absolute ly vital, but I think that People for the Ethical Treatment 
of Animals are currently running a campaign in Australia that does their cause no good. 
In their latest campaign they claim that 25 percent of the world’s wool is grown in 
Australia and that it is  made from 100 percent cruelty. That is just a ridiculous 
statement. I agree wholeheartedly with the Victorian Farmers Federation, which said 
that the campaign denigrates, offends, belittles, and insults every Australian’s 
intelligence. I think that although we care very deeply about animal welfare, to take it to 
that level in a campaign really just runs the risk of putting everyone offside from that 
organisation’s particular argument. If you keep running into a crowded theatre calling 
“Fire!”, people will not listen to you for very long after that. So I think that they are not 
doing themselves any good.  
New Zealand is, in fact, ranked first equal in the world for animal welfare, and that is 
fantastic. It is great, but that does not mean that we should rest on our laurels; we should 
always attempt to improve. I think that trade is so vital. The previous speaker, Damien 
O’Connor, mentioned that we are a trading nation, we are a niche producer, we sell into 
niche markets, and we actually command a premium for our products. The fact that 
people who buy our products are paying a little more than they pay for those they buy 
from others is based around things like our animal welfare. They do care about that. It is 
not something that they necessarily do a lot of res earch on, but if it comes up, they 
certainly do care about it. Although animal welfare has not been a big issue in Asia —
and the Asian market is becoming an increasingly important market for lots of our 
goods—over time we have seen a distinct change in valu es around the environment in 
Asia, and I believe we will see the same thing with  animal welfare. So it is incumbent 
upon us to have really good rules around that, and this bill really does go a long way 
towards that.  
Sixty-eight percent of New Zealand households own a pet. Although most of our talk 
and focus has been on farm animals, by numbers of population most people’s contact 
with animals is with the family pet, and we should not forget that in this discussion. As 
my colleague said earlier, dogs not on ly damage humans, which we often see when 
there is a dog attack, but they also attack other dogs quite often, and are often trained to 
be vicious.  
This bill deals with a lot of those issues and I commend the Primary Production 
Committee and the Minister f or Primary Industries for dealing with it in that way. This 
bill seeks to amend the Animal Welfare Act 1999. It brings a higher degree of 
transparency to the Act, and I think that is much needed. It has a much greater 
enforceability, it increases the range of enforcement tools, and, in fact, it brings in more 
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3155 
 
appropriate penalties. I think that is really important because we too often see well -
meaning Acts of Parliament with little enforceability or inappropriate penalties. If 
people do offend, then they de serve to feel the full weight of the law, and we need to 
make sure that it really is a deterrent.  
The bill provides a framework for suitable regulations, and the Minister, at their 
discretion, is able to bring in regulations as things change. Over time, attitudes to animal 
welfare change considerably. We have just gone through the Anzac Day celebrations. 
One hundred years ago 10,000 horses went off to the First World War. I can guarantee 
to you that the attitude to animal welfare 100 years ago was consider ably different from 
what it is today. Not many of those horses came back and the way in which they were 
disposed of is perhaps best not focused on too much these days. Those things would not 
happen in the New Zealand of today under the current rules, and t he rules are tightened 
further still under the Animal Welfare Amendment Bill.  
The issues that this bill tackles are complex, and I commend the select committee for 
the work it did on this. It is not easy to deal with these complex issues, but we are not 
elected to do the easy things; we are elected to make good law and do things that are 
sometimes a bit tough. I actually commend both the Minister, in particular, and also the 
select committee for tackling these things head -on and dealing with them in the wa y 
that they did.  
I think it is worth noting that not all New Zealanders —in fact, very few New 
Zealanders—actually deal with farm animals or have any link with farms. Going back 
only a few generations, most New Zealanders had a direct link to a farm throug h their 
family or good friends. Nowadays most people probably do not have any interaction 
with farms at all. Farmers deal with animals every day, and the reality of dealing with 
animals every day is quite different from the interaction that people have wit h a pet. 
Often, seeing what goes on in a farm can be upsetting for some people. A sheep being 
shorn, for example —although the sheep does not actually relish the process, it really 
enjoys getting the wool off its back when it gets outside.  
Surgical and painful procedures were covered, and these were alluded to earlier in 
the process. I have had some feedback from veterinary surgeons in my electorate who 
were concerned about the docking of tails on dogs. In particular, those surgeons did not 
want to see the law changed because they felt that some dog owners would take that 
procedure on themselves rather than doing it through a veterinary surgeon with adequate 
anaesthesia and sterile conditions. Although I have some sympathy with their position , 
the reality is that we do not like that sort of procedure in New Zealand and it has really 
got to end. We do have to draw a line in the sand somewhere, and I am pleased to see 
that that line has been drawn.  
There are 16 codes of animal welfare issued un der the Animal Welfare Act and 
developed by the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee. Those codes are being

that the regulations will have some teeth rather t han just being codes. I think that that is 
a fantastic innovation.  
There has been some talk about factory farming, and I really just want to mention a 
little bit about that. If we do rush into banning so-called factory farming in terms of how 
we treat hens and farrowing crates, etc., there will be a cost. The cost will be borne by 
the consumer, and all we will likely see is consumers switching to cheaper products that 
have come in from offshore, and you are simply shifting the animal welfare  issue out of 
this country and into another country. In terms of the animals you are not really making 
any difference whatsoever. You may be salving your conscience but you are not helping 
animal welfare. I think it is sensible to have a good lead -in time. Patoa Farms , which is 
New Zealand’s biggest pork producer, processes 2,000 pigs a week, so it is a significant

producer. It does not in fact use farrowing crates, but it has taken some time for it to

those practices. I think it is quite right and proper that we give them some time to do 
that.  
Wild animals, pest management, and hunting have been touched on by others, but I 
want to speak just a little bit about those issues. As a hunter myself I know that it is easy

MOJO MATHERS (Green) : I would like to start by thanking previ ous speakers, 
particularly Trevor Mallard and the Minister Nathan Guy, for their generous affirmation 
of my work on this bill. At the second reading, I spoke of our hope that the Government 
would still be prepared to support a ban on animal testing of cosm etics despite having 
rejected it during the Committee of the whole House stage. I am thrilled that my work 
has been justified. I applaud the Government for finally agreeing to a ban on these cruel 
tests, and I thank all parties in the House for supporting this amendment. 
We can be proud of the fact that New Zealand is now the first country in Australasia 
to ban cosmetic animal testing , showing leadership on an important animal welfare 
issue of our time. The announcement of a ban on cosmetic animal testing h as met with 
worldwide acclaim and affirmation, and has spurred renewed efforts to get these cruel 
tests banned in other countries. Doing our part to support a global ban on cosmetic 
animal testing was a major motivation for getting this change incorporated  into the bill, 
and I look forward to the day when no animal, anywhere in the world, is subject, in 
these cruel tests, to chemicals being dripped into their eyes or rubbed into their raw 
skin. 
I also welcome a small but important change in the bill that will require animal ethics 
committees to consider alternatives to animal testing when considering applications to 
test on animals. Alternatives to animal testing is an area that is making rapid progress at 
the moment, but, sadly, it is one that New Zealand i s lagging behind in. Animal testing 
often involves extremely high levels of pain and suffering. One of the most traumatic 
things that I had to do last year, in the discussions on the Pyschoactive Substances Bill, 
was actually to watch a video of what was i nvolved in toxicology testing, and it 
absolutely broke my heart. We should be doing everything that we can to reduce the 
number of animals suffering in these cruel tests, and we have a moral and ethical 
obligation to do so.  
If we are to be confident that unnecessary animal tests are not being carried out, it is 
essential that animal ethics committees are kept up to date with the latest developments 
in non -animal tests. For example, just recently, over in Australia, a major company 
decided to use the liver chip model to test the potential cure for hepatitis B instead of 
using the much more painful and cruel animal test. I want to encourage the Ministry for 
Primary Industries to investigate ways of ensuring that this information about the latest 
developments in alternatives to animal testing is shared between the different animal 
ethics committees in order to guide their decision making. I have spoken to former and 
current members of animal ethics committees, and they have told me that they would 
welcome this information because they do not actually have it. 
This is particularly important in light of the fact that we know that different animal 
ethics committees are making different decisions about controversial tests. At least one 
animal ethics committee has ap proved three applications for the controversial and 
outdated LD50 test, whereas another says it would never have approved these because 
they do not meet the “Three Rs” of animal research. This inconsistency is concerning 
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3157 
 
because it undermines the ministry’ s claims that we can trust the decisions of animal 
ethics committees. In my view, they have a long way to go yet.  
Another welcome change in the bill is the partial removal of the loophole that allows, 
for an indefinite period of time, the development of r egulations that breach the purpose 
of the Act. This is long overdue. These loopholes are the ones that have previously 
allowed cruel factory farming practices such as factory cages and sow crates to remain 
legal. I had an amendment that removed that loopho le, and the Primary Production 
Committee heard good submissions from the public in support of my amendment. The 
Green Party fully agreed with Trevor Mallard that the current transitional provisions in 
the bill are too generous and that 7 years is sufficien t time for farmers to make the 
change away from cruel practices such as farrowing crates. The fact is that there are 
successful pig farmers, such as Havoc farm, that do not rely on farrowing crates, and it 
gives lie to the argument that they are needed. 
Many people in the House will remember the footage shown on Campbell Live last 
year that showed very different conditions on different pig farms. The first programme 
focused on exposing the awful conditions on a pig factory farm in the Waikato. That 
footage was horrific, showing pigs that were absolutely depressed, cramped in confined 
conditions, unable to turn round, and unable to express natural behaviour, and that did 
not have anything like a normal existence. Those conditions were typical of many 
intensive pig farms and they amounted to legalised animal cruelty. Sadly, this bill will 
do little to address these conditions. The second programme showed a completely 
different vision for how farming can be done in New Zealand. It showed Havoc farm, a 
free-range farm in South Canterbury. It said that the mothers there are able to roam 
freely with the piglets and that there is access to warm shelters, litter to snuggle down 
in, and an ability to explore and interact. That is the way that farming should be done if 
we are going to farm for meat, and these are the only kinds of conditions that the Green 
Party considers to be acceptable. 
Despite some of the really positive aspects of this bill, it is our overall view that this 
bill still represents a missed opportunity  to get it right for the millions of animals 
suffering on factory farms. My concern is that this bill will not only continue to sanction 
these kinds of cruel conditions of factory farming but that it may entrench them  even 
further, and that is because it n ow elevates practicality and economic impact in the bill 
as explicit factors that can be considered when developing regulations. There was 
already the ability to take these factors into account, and, historically, these factors —
practicality and economic im pact—were precisely the arguments used to justify codes 
of welfare that enabled animals to be kept in factory cages and in sow crates that were 
in clear breach of the provisions in the Act. In our view, this move sends the wrong 
message about which factors  are important in developing codes of welfare in 
regulations. 
I also want to say that another main area of concern that has just come to light is the 
area of live exports. As everybody has mentioned previously, there is an effective 
prohibition, via an ord er under the Customs and Excise Act, on live exports for 
slaughter, and many submitters wanted an outright ban in this bill. The advice and the 
assurance that we had from Ministry for Primary Industries officers was that the 
intention is for the current pr ohibition to be maintained via regulation under the Act, 
once the bill is passed. I know that many of us have felt very concerned about the recent 
comments by the Prime Minister, when he was visiting Saudi Arabia, that this was one 
of the areas that was being looked at. It would be absolutely shameful if we allowed our 
current policy to be weakened when the regulations are developed, just for the sake of a 
trade deal. That would be horrific. Nothing could be more damaging to our international 
reputation than if we were to resume live exports of animals for slaughter, because we 
3158 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015 
 
know that causes significant suffering, and many farmers do not want it and the public 
do not want it.  
Although we are pleased that some changes will become enforceable, much will 
depend on which standards get lifted into the regulations. We also remain concerned 
about the resourcing of animal welfare monitoring and enforcement. Currently, less than 
1 percent of complaints result in prosecution, and we still want to see significantly 
increased funding for monitoring and enforcement, including proactive enforcement. 
Thank you. 
RICHARD PROSSER (NZ First) : I am very pleased to rise to take a call in the 
third reading of the Ani mal Welfare Amendment Bill on behalf of New Zealand First. I 
want to pick up on a couple of points that Mr McKelvie made earlier, and one of them 
was actually about pest control. He talked about the pest species of animals that we have 
in this country. It is quite interesting that at this time the subject of 1080 is topical, 
because 1080 is actually an extremely inhumane form of pest control. It is curious, in 
fact, that it was not included in the ambit of this bill, but perhaps that is a question for 
another day. It is something we can revisit.  
Mr McKelvie also spoke about the export of live animals for slaughter, and Mr 
O’Connor touched on that, and the Minister has said a word about it as well. I want to 
talk primarily about the export of live animals because it is probably the major lingering 
concern that New Zealand First still has with regard to this bill. During the first reading 
I expressed some reservations that New Zealand First held regarding the export of live 
animals for slaughter. Of course, un der the existing Act, this is prohibited unless it is 
specifically authorised by the Director -General of the Ministry for Primary Industries. 
We asked at the time whether or not, that being the case, this bill presented an 
opportunity to do away with that provision altogether.  
New Zealand used to export animals for slaughter on quite a large scale, and the 
practice was brought to a halt by Parliament some years ago for what were very sound 
reasons at the time. There were, and are, of course, other reasons as well, economic 
reasons, but the motivation at the time was primarily centred on the conditions the 
animals were subjected to while they were being transported to other places and the 
conditions that they were subjected to when they arrived at the other end.  
New Zealand First has got no objection to the export of live bloodstock, because we 
understand full well just how valuable the thoroughbred industry is to this country. We 
know that our bloodstock is highly regarded and highly sought after internatio nally, and 
that many thousands of jobs and literally hundreds of millions of dollars are generated 
in the economy through the export of live horses. But horses are treated in an entirely 
different manner from sheep and cattle intended for slaughter in the way they are 
transported and cared for.  
Horses are airfreighted to their destinations in pressurised, air -conditioned comfort. 
They are housed in safe, secure environments while on the aeroplane and they have 
veterinary care. And, of course, on arrival, t heir fate is not to be taken to the nearest 
abattoir but rather to a training track or a stud farm. These are valuable animals and they 
are cared for accordingly. Breeding heifers are similarly afforded a better lot than the 
cattle and sheep that left thes e shores a decade or so ago destined for the 
slaughterhouses of distant places. New Zealand First does not believe that we should be 
exporting such animals either, but we recognise that while it is legal, there are people 
who will see it as good business and who will look to profit from it.  
We are opposed because we believe that such practices are short -sighted, and, as I 
have said in debates on other legislation, notably the Dairy Industry Restructuring Act , 
we believe that business activity of this type will come back and bite New Zealand. The 
reason for that is that one day the dairy bubble is going to burst. We have allowed 
5 May 2015 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 3159 
 
ourselves in this country to come to the belief that because we hold such a major 
position in terms of global cross -border trade in  dairy products we are somehow 
significant in terms of world milk production, and we are not. New Zealand produces 
only around 3 percent of the world’s milk.  
Most dairy produce worldwide is consumed domestically in the country of origin, 
and international  trade comprises only a very small proportion of the total. At the 
moment, there is a shortfall between supply and demand, and it is this that allows New 
Zealand to profit from being in a position to supply, from our disproportionately large 
dairy producti on relative to our population and domestic demand, to buyers from 
overseas. But in helping to grow production overseas through joint ventures, and by 
selling heifers to foreign dairy producers, we are only hastening the arrival of the day 
when demand for d airy products in the countries that are presently our export markets 
will be met from production in those countries. For that reason, we do not believe that it 
is sustainable or even a good idea to export live dairy cows, regardless of the conditions 
under which they are transported.  
Of course, New Zealand does also export other animals for breeding purposes, 
including cattle, sheep, goats, deer, and even chickens. Our animals are very much 
sought after worldwide because they are known to be, for the most part, from very good 
stock lines and are, for the most part, free from any of the nasty diseases that are 
endemic in some other parts of the world. Again, animals that are exported for breeding 
purposes are treated better and transported in far greater saf ety and comfort than those 
that are destined for the pot.  
The issue of live exports for slaughter has not gone away. In fact, it raised its head 
only last week with the Prime Minister’s efforts towards securing a free -trade deal with 
the nations of the Mi ddle East’s Gulf Cooperation Council . This deal has been on hold 
since 2009. Coincidentally, one of the sticking points is the fact that New Zealand 
halted live sheep exports in 2004. Apparently, an investor from Saudi Arabia lost quite 
a bit of money as a result of the cessation of exports,  and we are told that the Saudis are 
still a wee bit sore about that. But, that aside, these exports were put on indefinite hold 
at that time for very good reason.  
As a nation, we have engaged in live export for slaughter for more than 20 years 
prior to that, but in 2003 something like 5,000 sheep died on one ship under what can be 
described only as quite horrific conditions while being transported from Australia to 
Saudi Arabia. They died from heat stress, overcrowding, and a lack of food, water, and 
sanitation during a sea voyage that had lasted something like 2 months longer than it 
should have. New Zealand First is very much concerned that such exports may be 
resumed and that the provision for their resumption still exists under the bill.  
We are concerned on a number of fronts, but they all come back to animal welfare in 
one way or another. Obviously, we are concerned that if live exports for slaughter were 
to be resumed, we would be faced with a return to the very same conditions that led to 
their being curtailed in the first place. It is hard to see how that can be avoided, because 
these things are driven by money. Sheep are crammed into overcrowded boats because 
the cost of transporting them has to be kept down. A live sheep being exported for 
slaughter is not worth very much. In fact, it is probably the lowest return for both the 
farmer and the nation that can be received for a sheep that has been grown for 
consumption.  
We do know that things have not improved very much in that regard in the last 10 or 
15 years, because live exports from Australia have continued pretty much unabated 
since that time, and the standard of transport today is much as it was then. In fact, 
collateral losses for sheep exports from Australia to other parts of the world are ru nning 
at about 7 or 8 percent —maybe a little bit less than that, but it is still too much, by any 
3160 Animal Welfare Amendment Bill 5 May 2015 
 
measure. It is the minimal value of the animal and the minimal return to the farmer and 
to “New Zealand Inc.” that we oppose, and for the same reasons we do n ot wish to see 
any part of our primary sector reduced to a simple exporter of bulk commodities.  
The second concern that we have is around the conditions that might meet livestock 
exported for slaughter when they arrive at the other end of their journey. W e know that 
the Director-General can grant an exemption if he or she is satisfied that the abattoir in 
the destination country meets the standards that we demand here, but the reality is that 
in too many cases live animals are sought in other parts of the world for reasons of ritual 
slaughter in accordance with the requirements of various religious and cultural 
practices. These practices by their very nature are not able to meet the minimum 
standards of animal welfare that we demand of our own meat processe s. Animals are 
required to be fully conscious when they are put to death, which is at odds with our own 
requirement that they be stunned first. They are frequently transported in the boots of 
cars, even in the back seats of cars. They are not properly rest rained. They are subjected 
to quite brutal and stressful treatment prior to slaughter.  
We have an objection also to the granting of the exemption being placed in the hands 
of the Director -General, however professional he or she might be. The practice of 
exporting live animals for slaughter was stopped by politicians through the 
parliamentary process, and we believe that if it is to be resumed, then that decision must 
be made in the same way. We do not believe that it is good enough for a Minister to be 
able to hide behind a bureaucrat if and when this decision ever is to be made. 
Governments need to take responsibility for changes of this magnitude, and we believe 
that if a Minister wishes to restart the export of live animals for slaughter, then he or she 
should be required to put their money where their mouth is, stand behind that decision, 
and stand up for it if and when necessary. And whether it is necessary is a salient point, 
because over the last decade or so we have shown that exports of live sheep f or 
slaughter from New Zealand are not necessary.  
The New Zealand farming sector has got on quite well without them for the last 
decade, and it appears that customers in the Middle East have got on quite well without 
those exports, as well. So it is simply  not necessary, and we ask again why it has not 
been removed altogether, and why we did not make provision for prohibiting it in total 
when the bill went through. But all that said, on balance this is still a very good bill, 
which will deliver very much be tter and improved outcomes for animal welfare in New 
Zealand, and New Zealand First continues to support it. I commend it to the House. 
Thank you.

STEFFAN BROWNING (Green) : I am pleased to be able to speak to the Animal 
Welfare Amendment Bill and congratulate those involved with getting the 
improvements into the bill, particularly my colleague Mojo Mathers. What I want to see 
when this legislatio n is fully enacted is other elements of animal welfare law that are

speak tonight, of the hundreds of cows that died from the herbicide -tolerant swede issue

subclinical issues. So poor was the condition of some of the surviving cows that there 
was a question of their suitability as culled cows for processing.  
I have been looking at some  Official Information Act material on this. There is what 
they call a natural toxin that seems to be the cause of the distress of these cows. This 
was a serious animal welfare issue. Was that product, which clearly is at the base of this 
issue, withdrawn? Was it banned? Or was there a cover -up? There was a cover -up. We 
still do not have a proper report on what happened last winter, and into early spring, to 
those cows in Southland. The only way we can find anything is through Official 
Information Act materi al, and in that I find the very valid questions that I put to the 
Minister and I see how they were treated as just generalisations. It says that if the group

trying to answer any questions.  
There is a chemical involved here as well. It is not just the glucosinolates —we call 
them GSLs for short, as everybody else does, for good reason. A glucosinolate is natural 
toxin. It forms in the leaves of swedes and other brassicas. It can get to quite high 
levels, and under certain conditions it can get to a toxic level. But what we find here is 
that the herbicide -tolerant swedes have way more than the non - herbicide tolerant 
swedes. The glucosinolate levels are 4 to 16 milligrams per kilo in the leaves—the bulbs 
are lower, down on the ground, 1 to 4 milligrams per kilo —but non - herbicide tolerant 
ones are just 1 milligram. Something is going on in PGG Wrightson’s Cleancrop 
system, with swedes at least, and we are not too  sure about the turnips, rape, and other 
products under that system. It cheated New Zealanders and it cheated farmers by going 
down a system of production of those herbicide -tolerant ones and by dodging the 
genetic engineering route that it already had for  that same product through a chemical

mutagenesis thing—just as much a DNA muck up—so that it did not have to go through 
the Environmental Protection Authority and be open to submissions and testing for 
safety. PGG Wrightson dodged it and this Government has let it dodge it.  
This is an animal welfare issue. It is also an issue for the people who consume the 
products from those animals, and for the other animal products in this country from 
animals that are fed products containing lots of herbicides, whethe r it be glyphosate or 
whether it be chlorothal onil, which is in these herbicide tolerant swedes and is banned

CARMEL SEPULONI (Labour —Kelston): Kia orana, fakalofa lahi atu, and 
taloha ni. It is a privilege to speak to this bill, the Social Assistance (Portability to Cook 
3170 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 5 May 2015 
 
Islands, Niue, and Tokelau) Bill, and out of respect for our Pacific brothers and sisters 
to whom this bill relates, I greet this House in those three languages. 
I want to start by contextualising this bill. Many New Zealanders are, actually, 
unaware of the unique relationship that New Zealand has with our Cook Island, Niuean, 
and Tokelauan nations. Those three Island nations hav e a constitutional relationship 
with New Zealand, which I am sure we are aware of but which many people outside of 
this House have no knowledge of. They are technically part of the Realm of New 
Zealand. As such, they have free association with New Zealand and are New Zealand 
citizens by right. They can move freely between their Island homes and ours. As such, 
we have a responsibility as a Parliament to make sure that we exercise the same duty of 
care to them as we do to New Zealand - based citizens. 
It is appropriate to recognise the service of men and women from those countries to 
our country —particularly in light of the recent Anzac Day commemorations. Our 
Pacific Realm brothers and sisters fought alongside New Zealanders during World War 
I and World War I I—many of them under our flag, the New Zealand flag. The 
contributions that they have made to this country, whether to our economy, our sports 
fields, our workforce, our academia, our arts, or through fighting for this country, are 
unquestionable. The Labo ur Party and, I think, this whole Parliament value the unique 
relationship that we have with these countries and will do what is required to honour 
that relationship. 
In brief, this bill will give effect to the Government policy on portability of New 
Zealand superannuation and the veterans pension to the Cook Islands, Niue, and 
Tokelau. This is an omnibus bill that seeks to amend the New Zealand Superannuation 
and Retirement Income Act 2001, the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and the Social 
Security Act 1964. The aim of this bill is to allow eligible people who live in the Cook 
Islands, Niue, or Tokelau to apply from any of those countries for New Zealand 
superannuation or the veterans pension and to be paid those benefits in those countries 
or in other specified Pacific countries. 
In August 2013 the Hon Murray McCully, Minister of Foreign Affairs, announced 
changes to the special portability arrangement that would allow eligible residents to 
apply for their pension or veterans pension from the Cook Islands, Niu e, or Tokelau. 
Under the current rules, people wishing to retire to the Cook Islands, Niue, or Tokelau 
have to be resident and present in New Zealand at the age of 65. Residents of those 
countries or that territory would still need to qualify for New Zeala nd superannuation. 
They must have been resident and present in New Zealand for more than 10 years since 
the age of 20, including 5 years since the age of 50. This legislation means that people 
who are entitled to New Zealand superannuation, regardless of w hether they are of 
Cook Island, Niuean, or Tokelauan ethnicity, would be able to depart New Zealand to 
live in one of these three countries after the age of 55 and apply for their superannuation 
once they turn 65 without returning to New Zealand. Currently , they would have to stay 
in New Zealand until turning 65 in order to qualify. The new policy would require 
legislation to be passed in the New Zealand Parliament, and is expected to apply from 1 
July 2015. 
We support this bill and believe it is a step in the right direction towards equal 
treatment of New Zealand citizens throughout the Realm. However, we take on board 
some of the concerns that were raised by submitters about the eligibility criteria. My 
colleague Poto Williams actually raised this issue in  a minority report, and she alluded 
to a Supplementary Order Paper she was going to write seeking to remove the 
requirement to be resident and present in New Zealand for 5 years between the ages of 
50 and the qualification age of 65. The purpose of that Su pplementary Order Paper was 
to ensure that residents of the islands of the Realm would not be disadvantaged by being 
5 May 2015 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 3171 
 
forced to absent themselves from family and work commitments in order to receive 
New Zealand superannuation. 
New Zealand citizens, includin g those within the Realm of New Zealand, should be 
treated equitably, and Poto Williams’ idea, which she discussed in that minority report, 
would mean that we are more closely aligning the criteria for all applicants living in 
New Zealand and the countries  of the Realm. I do want to say that despite the fact that 
Poto Williams went to great lengths to write a minority report that reflected her concern 
and also alluded to the fact that she would be writing this Supplementary Order Paper, 
one of our colleague s from New Zealand First decided to go and write the 
Supplementary Order Paper. We are not petty; we will still support that Supplementary 
Order Paper, but I do want to acknowledge my Cook Island colleague Poto Williams for 
the work that she did on the Social Services Committee, for the attention that she paid to 
the submitters, and for the fact that she has been pushing for us to actually take this 
point into consideration. I hope that the Government takes it seriously, including the 
chair of our select co mmittee, who is our other Cook Island colleague in the House, Mr 
Alfred Ngaro. 
I do want to share an experience I had a few years back when I was part of a group 
that travelled to four Pacific Islands as part of New Zealand’s inquiry into our 
relationship with the Pacific. One thing that came up time and time again when we were 
in the Cook Islands and when we went to Niue —unfortunately, we did not get an 
opportunity to go to Tokelau —was the fact that the biggest problem they are facing is 
depopulation. They talked about the fact that they have lost, and continue to lose, their 
biggest resource to New Zealand. And that resource, of course, is their people. 
Sometimes I think that we take it for granted that we have people coming here, living 
here, and contribu ting to our economy, and I want to acknowledge our three Realm 
countries for the contribution that their people —their biggest resource —have made to 
this country. I think one way in which we can honour that relationship is to ensure that, 
yes, we all suppor t this bill in the House, and also that we take into consideration the 
Supplementary Order Paper that has been put up by New Zealand First and that was 
proposed by my colleague Poto Williams. This is a bill that we think will be supported 
across the House, and we do not think there are very many party politics involved with 
this—except for, perhaps, a little bit of debate over who may have come up with the 
idea of a Supplementary Order Paper. It is really about doing what is right. 
I hope that the Governmen t will seriously consider supporting the Supplementary 
Order Paper that I have spoken about, because it is the right thing to do. I think, moving 
forward, that this is just one way in which we can honour the relationship that we have 
with the three Realm c ountries, and ensure that there will be other ways in which we 
can do that, other opportunities that will present themselves to us as a Parliament to 
honour that relationship. I think that it is important, first and foremost, to continually 
raise awareness  with general members of the public that we do have this special 
relationship. Any measures that we put into place to honour that relationship are unique 
to our relationship with those countries, and may not necessarily apply to other 
countries. It is just part and parcel of the fact that they happen to be part of the Realm of 
New Zealand. 
We support this bill, and we ask all of the other political parties in the House to 
support the Supplementary Order Paper that is being put up by New Zealand First but, 
of course, was proposed by my Cook Island colleague, Poto Williams. Thank you.

Dr PARMJEET PARMAR (National) : It is with pleasure that I rise to speak to

3184 Social Assistance (Portability to Pacific Islands) Bill 5 May 2015

unable to do so because of so many other factors kicking in like the age factor.  
So t his bill is actually going to fix this situation. This bill is going to remove this 
requirement of people having to be in New Zealand at the time of applying for their

have lived here in New Zealand for 10 years since the age of 20, including 5 years after

Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau. Other New Zealanders who are eligible for New 
Zealand superannuation can also go and retire in any of these three isla nd countries and

countries of the Cook Islands, Niue, and Tokelau, because of which they enjoy shared 
New Zealand citizenship and unique legal arrangements. The Cook Islan ds and Niue 
have adopted constitutions enabling them to have self -government in free association 
with New Zealand. This allows Cook Islanders and Niuean people to share New 
Zealand citizenship while they run their own affairs, whereas Tokelau is a non - self-
governing territory of New Zealand.  
Another concern that came up was about the depopulation of these three island 
countries. That is, again, understandable because young people and people with special 
skills are always looking for opportunities, and to  get those opportunities they migrate 
to New Zealand, but then these island countries want to get these people back because 
they are facing this issue of depopulation. With this amendment people will be able to

these island countries with this problem as well.
